n: And Benjamin. He is mentioned here, because he was the son of Rachel, as the preceding were the children of Lia. The offspring of the handmaids follow. (Haydock)
Seventy: Septuagint, "75," including the offspring of Joseph. See Genesis xlvi. 26.

Generation, or race of mortals who had seen his wonderful works. The tyrant, who knew not Joseph, began his reign about 58 years after that patriarch's death. (Calmet) --- His name was Pharao Amenophis, (Pererius) or Ramesses Miamum. (Usher)

Numerous. Calvisius observes, that from Ephraim alone might have sprung 4,112,323,729 people. See St. Augustine, q. 43, &c. (Haydock) --- In the space of 215 years, 70 people may produce an immense multitude, as Bonfrere shews by an accurate calculation. God also was pleased to bless the Hebrews with fecundity, so that they sprung up (ebullierunt) like frogs or fishes, ver. 7. In Egypt, the women had sometimes seven at a birth (Pliny, Natural History vii. 3,) and Aristotle (Anim. vii. 4,) mentions one woman who had 20 children at four births. (Tirinus) --- Stronger. This might easily be true, if this king had only Thebais under his command. But if he was king of all Egypt, it seems an exaggeration. (Calmet) --- Indeed, human policy often gives birth to all kinds of wickedness. The king justifies his cruelty on this pretext of self-defence. He wishes to keep the Hebrews under; yet he is not willing to let them depart, as he knew they intended, according to Joseph's prediction. (Haydock) --- God permitted this disposition, in order to punish his people for their idolatry, (Ezechiel xxiii. 8,) to admonish them not to fix their abode in Egypt, and to manifest his power and glory in the destruction of the impious. (Menochius)

Masters. Cruel like himself, who not only made them build without proper materials, (ver. 14, and chap. v. 10, Haydock,) but oppressed them with heavy burdens of brick and tile. Hence Aristophanes calls the Hebrews in derision Plinthophoroi. This servitude is styled the iron furnace of Egypt, Deuteronomy iv. 20; Jeremias xi. 4. --- Of tabernacles, or of storehouses. (Challoner) --- To keep his treasures, Chaldean, or "fortresses," Septuagint. It may also be the name of a city, Miscenoth, chap. xii. 37. Phithom, perhaps the same as the town of Heroum, where the Septuagint say Joseph first met his father, Genesis xlvi. 28. Ramesses was the capital, and situate in the Arabic nome. (Calmet)
Service. They were forced to till the land, reap, &c. (Menochius)

Midwives. Egyptian women, who assisted all of that district. (Josephus, [Antiquities] xi. 5.) There were others under them. Some think all these midwives were of Hebrew extraction, as their names are Hebrew, &c. (Calmet)

The time, &c. Hebrew, "and you shall see them upon the two stones." Abenaim. Jeremias (xviii. 3,) uses the same expression, speaking of a potter hard at work. (Calmet) --- A woman, from whom nothing could be feared, to be reserved for service and for pleasure. (Menochius) --- We must not obey princes in their unjust commands. (Acts iv, and Matthew x. 28.) (Worthington)

Skilful, &c. Hebrew Caioth means midwives: or they are full of vigour, or bring forth alive, like brutes. By this allusion they not only excuse themselves, but seem also to enter into the king's sentiments of hatred and scorn for the Hebrews. (Menochius) --- Women in Egypt, and in the eastern regions, are easily delivered, and hardly stand in need of any assistance. (Ludolf) (1 Kings iv. 19.) Perhaps, therefore, the midwives spoke truth, with regard to the generality of the Hebrew women. But they gave way to a lie of excuse, with regard to some, (ver. 17,) which St. Augustine would not allow, even to save all the Hebrew children. (contra Mend. 15.) It was not so easy to discover this delusion, as women in that country seldom appear in public; and hence Jochabed was enabled to hide Moses so long. (Calmet)

Because the midwives feared God, &c. The midwives were rewarded, not for their lie, which was a venial sin; but for their fear of God, and their humanity; but this reward was only temporal, in building them houses, that is, in establishing and enriching their families. (Challoner) --- This alone the Scripture specifies, though they might also be filled with heavenly graces. (Worthington) --- Some conclude from this verse, that the midwives embraced the true religion. The Hebrew refers built them to the Hebrews, as if they multiplied in consequence of the humanity of these women; (Calmet) and the Vulgate may be explained in the same sense. (Haydock) De Muis supposes, that Pharao ordered houses to be built for the midwives, where the Hebrew women were forced to appear when they were to be delivered, in the presence of commissaries.

The river Nile, where the persecuting successor of this king found his end. (Haydock) --- It seems this inhuman decree was not published till after Aaron was born, and it was probably revoked soon after the birth of Moses; for if it had been rigorously put in execution, there would have been nothing but old men 80 years after, when Moses led the people out of Egypt. (Calmet) --- But perhaps even the Egyptians abhorred and refused to execute this edict. (Menochius) Bible Text & Commentary: The Israelites are multiplied in Egypt. They are oppressed by a new king, who commandeth all their male children to be killed. 1 These are the names of the children of Israel, *that went into Egypt with Jacob: they went in every man with his household: 2 Ruben, Simeon, Levi, Juda, 3 Issachar, Zabulon, and Benjamin, 4 Dan, and Nephthali, Gad and Aser. 5 And all the souls that came out of Jacob's thigh, were seventy:* but Joseph was in Egypt. 6 After he was dead, and all his brethren, and all that generation, 7 *The children of Israel increased, and sprung up into multitudes, and growing exceedingly strong they filled the land. 8 In the mean time there arose a new king over Egypt, that knew not Joseph: 9 And he said to his people: Behold the people of the children of Israel are numerous and stronger than we. 10 Come let us wisely oppress them, lest they multiply: and if any war shall rise against us, join with our enemies, and having overcome us, depart out of the land. 11 Therefore he set over them masters of the works, to afflict them with burdens: and they built for Pharao cities of tabernacles, Phithom, and Ramesses. 12 But the more they oppressed them, the more they were multiplied and increased. 13 And the Egyptians hated the children of Israel, and afflicted them and mocked them: 14 And they made their life bitter with hard works in clay and brick, and with all manner of service, wherewith they were overcharged in the works of the earth. 15 And the king of Egypt spoke to the midwives of the Hebrews: of whom one was called Sephora, the other Phua, 16 Commanding them: When you shall do the office of midwives to the Hebrew women, and the time of delivery is come: if it be a man child, kill it: if a woman, keep it alive. 17 But the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded, but saved the men children. 18 And the king called for them and said: What is that you meant to do, that you would save the men children? 19 They answered: The Hebrew women are not as the Egyptian women: for they themselves are skilful in the office of a midwife; and they are delivered before we come to them. 20 Therefore God dealt well with the midwives: and the people multiplied and grew exceedingly strong. 21 And because the midwives feared God, he built them houses. 22 Pharao therefore charged all his people, saying: Whatsoever shall be born of the male sex, ye shall cast into the river: whatsoever of the female, ye shall save alive. ____________________ * 1: Genesis xlvi. 8. 5: Genesis xlvi. 27. 7: Acts vii. 17.

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 1

It seems to me that each utterance of divine Scripture is like some kind of seed, whose nature is this: that when it has been cast into the earth, it is regenerated into an ear of grain or into whatever other form of its own kind, and is spread abroad manifold — and the more abundantly, the more either a skilled farmer expends greater labor upon the seeds, or grants the benefit of more fertile soil. So then it comes about that by diligent cultivation a tiny "seed", for example "of mustard, which is the least of all, becomes greater than all herbs and turns into a tree, so that the birds of heaven come and dwell in its branches". So too this utterance, which has now been read to us from the divine volumes, if it finds a skilled and diligent husbandman — though at first touch it may seem meager and brief — once it begins to be cultivated and to be handled with spiritual art, grows into a tree, spreads out into branches and into shoots: so that there can come "the disputers and rhetoricians of this world", who like "the birds of heaven" with light wings, that is, with mere pomp of words, pursue lofty and steep things, and, captivated by the reasonings, wish to dwell in these branches, in which there is no elegance of speaking but a rule of living. What then shall we too do with these things that have been read to us? If the Lord should deign to grant me the discipline of spiritual agriculture, if He were to bestow skill in cultivating the field, a single utterance of those that have been recited could be spread out so far and wide — if only the capacity of the hearers permitted — that the day would scarcely suffice us for expounding it. Nevertheless we shall attempt, according to our strength, to discourse on some things, even if it is possible neither for us to explain all things nor for you to hear them all. For to recognize this very thing, that the knowledge of these matters is beyond our strength, I judge to be no small skill. Let us see, then, what the reading contains right at the very beginnings of Exodus, and let us pursue it — with what brevity we can, so far as suffices for the edification of the hearers; if only you help with your prayers that the word of God may be present to us and that He Himself may deign to be the leader of our discourse.

"These are", it says, "the names of the sons of Israel who entered into Egypt together with Jacob their father; each one with his whole household they entered: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah" and the rest of the patriarchs. "But Joseph", it says, "was in Egypt. And all the souls from Jacob were seventy-five". I think that something like this mystery is also that which is said through the prophet, if anyone is able to notice it: "into Egypt my people went down, to dwell there, and by force they were led away to the Assyrians". If anyone, then, is able to compare these things with one another, and from those things which have been discussed either by our predecessors, or even by our contemporaries, and also sometimes by ourselves, to understand what "Egypt" is, into which the people of God went down not so much to dwell as to sojourn, and who also the "Assyrians" are who led them away by force — he will consequently notice what is the number and order of the patriarchs, and what "households" and families of theirs are designated, which are said to have "entered into Egypt together with Jacob their father". For it says: "Reuben with his whole household, and Levi with his whole household", and likewise all the rest. "But Joseph was in Egypt" and took a wife from Egypt, and, though placed there, is nevertheless reckoned in the number of the patriarchs. If anyone, then, is able to examine these things spiritually and to follow the mind of the Apostle, by which he distinguishes and separates Israel and says that there is a certain "Israel according to the flesh", so that without doubt he indicates that there is another according to the spirit; and if anyone also considers more carefully the Lord's saying, by which He designates this very thing, when He says of a certain man: "behold a true Israelite, in whom there is no guile", and gives it to be understood that there are some true Israelites, and some without doubt not true — he will perhaps be able, "comparing spiritual things with spiritual" and joining the old with the new and the new with the old, to notice the mystery of Egypt and of the descent of the patriarchs into it. But he will also contemplate the differences of the tribes, so that he may conjecture what has seemed excellent in the tribe of Levi, that from it the priests and ministers of the Lord are chosen; what also the Lord judged pre-eminent in the tribe of Judah, that from it kings and princes are taken; and — what is the greatest of all — that from it also our Lord and Savior is born according to the flesh. For I do not know whether privileges of this kind are to be referred to the merits of those from whose stock they draw their name or origin, that is, either to Judah himself, or to Levi, or to each one of those who gave a name to a tribe. For in this line of thought that also moves me which John writes in the Apocalypse about this people that believed in Christ. For he says that "from the tribe of Reuben twelve thousand" men and "from the tribe of Simeon twelve thousand", and likewise from each single tribe twelve thousand apiece; all of whom together he says are "a hundred forty-four thousand", who have not defiled themselves with women but have remained virgins. And surely it can be no supposition, however inept, that this can be referred back to those tribes of the Jews — Simeon, Levi, and the rest — which draw their descent from Jacob. To what fathers, then, this number of virgins is to be referred — so equal, so entire, and so evenly ordered, so that none is reckoned higher or lower than another — I for my part do not dare to advance further by inquiring, but even up to this point I proceed almost with some hazard. The Apostle, however, has laid down certain intimations for those who are able to look more deeply, when he says: "for this reason I bend my knees to the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named". And indeed the understanding concerning earthly fatherhoods does not seem to be difficult; for the fathers of tribes or households, to whom the succession of posterity is referred, are together called all fatherhood; but as for what He says regarding heaven, in what way or of what sort the fathers there are, or for what posterities a heavenly fatherhood is named — this belongs to Him alone to know, "whose is the heaven of heaven, but the earth He has given to the sons of men".

The fathers, then, went down into Egypt, "Reuben, Simeon, Levi, each one with his whole household". How would anyone also expound this, that "with his whole household they entered into Egypt"? To which is added: "and all", it says, "the souls that entered with Jacob, seventy-five". Here now, by naming "souls", the prophetic word had almost laid bare the mystery which it had everywhere woven over, so as to disclose that it says these things not of bodies but of souls. Nevertheless it still keeps its veil. For it is believed to be customary for souls to be named in place of human beings. Meanwhile, "seventy-five souls went down with Jacob into Egypt". These are the souls which Jacob begot. I do not think that just any of men can beget a soul, unless perhaps someone is such as he who said: "for even if you have many thousands of tutors in Christ, yet not many fathers. For in Christ Jesus through the Gospel I begot you". Such as these are they who generate souls and bring them to birth, as he also says elsewhere: "my little children, of whom I am again in travail, until Christ be formed in you". For others either will not or cannot have care of this kind of generation. In short, right at the beginnings, what does Adam himself say? "This now is bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh", and yet he does not add: and soul of my soul. But I would have you tell me, O Adam: if you recognized "bone of" your "bones" and perceived "flesh of" your "flesh", why did you not understand that a soul too had proceeded from your soul? For if you handed over all the things that were in you, why do you not make mention of the soul as well along with the rest, which is the better part of the whole man? But it seems that by these words he gives to those who understand an indication that, when he says "bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh", he professes those things which are of the earth to be his own, but does not dare to call his own the things which he knows are not of the earth. But Laban likewise, when he says to Jacob that "you are my bone and my flesh", he too does not seem to dare to call anything more his own than what he recognizes as of earthly kinship. For there is another kinship of souls, which is either associated with Jacob as he goes down into Egypt, or is ascribed to the rest of the patriarchs and saints under the enumeration of a mystical posterity. But we who had resolved to keep our course close to the land as we sail, and in a manner to hug the very edge of the shore — the too-violent surge of the waves is somehow carrying us off into the deep. So let us return to the things which are added in what follows.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 1

"Joseph died", it says, "and all his brothers and all that generation. But the sons of Israel grew and were multiplied, and were spread abroad in a great multitude, and grew exceedingly strong; for the land multiplied them". As long as Joseph lived, it is not reported that the sons of Israel were multiplied, nor is anything at all mentioned in these matters concerning increases and multitude. I, believing the words of my Lord Jesus Christ, do not think that in the Law and the prophets even "one iota or one tittle" is empty of mysteries, nor do I think that "any of these things can pass away until all be accomplished". But since we are of meager capacity, let us now knock only at those things by which we may proceed more safely. Before our Joseph died — he who was sold for thirty pieces of silver by one of his brothers, Judah — the sons of Israel were very few. But when for all men He tasted death, through which "He destroyed him that had the empire of death, that is, the devil", the people of the faithful was multiplied, "and the sons of Israel were spread abroad, and the land multiplied them, and they grew exceedingly". For unless, as He Himself said, "the grain of wheat had fallen into the earth and died", the Church would surely not have brought forth this abundant fruit of the whole world. Therefore, after "the grain fell into the earth and died", all this crop of the faithful arose from it, "and the sons of Israel were multiplied and grew exceedingly strong". For "into all the earth went forth the sound" of the Apostles "and unto the ends of the world their words", and through them, as it is written, "the word of the Lord grew and was multiplied". This much pertains to the mystical understanding. But let us not omit in these things the moral sense also; for it edifies the souls of the hearers. Therefore in you too, if Joseph should die — that is, if you take up "the mortification of Christ in" your "body" and mortify your members to sin — then in you "the sons of Israel are multiplied". By "the sons of Israel" are understood the good and spiritual senses. If, therefore, the senses of the flesh are mortified, the senses of the spirit grow, and as the vices die daily in you, the number of virtues is increased; and "the land" too "multiplies" you in good works, which are administered through the service of the body. But if you wish me to show you from the Scriptures who it is "whom the land has multiplied", look at the Apostle Paul, how he says: "but if to live in the flesh, this is for me the fruit of labor, and what I should choose I know not. For I am hard pressed from the two, having a desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ, for it is far better; but to remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake". You see how "the land multiplies" this man? For while he remains on the land, that is, in his own flesh, he is multiplied by founding churches, he is multiplied by acquiring a people for God, and "by preaching the Gospel of God from Jerusalem round about as far as Illyricum". But let us see what is added in what follows.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 1

"But there arose", it says, "another king in Egypt, who knew not Joseph. And he said to his people: behold, the race of the sons of Israel is a great multitude, and is stronger than we". First of all I wish to inquire who is the king in Egypt who knows Joseph, and who is the one who knows him not. For while that one reigned who knew Joseph, the sons of Israel are not reported to have been afflicted, nor consumed "in clay and brick", nor were their males killed and their females kept alive. But when that one arose who had not known Joseph and himself began to reign, then all these things are reported to have been done. Who then is this king, let us see. If the Lord governs us, and the sense of our mind, illuminated by the Lord, always holds the memory of Christ, doing that which Paul writes to Timothy: "be mindful that Christ Jesus has risen from the dead" — while he remembers these things in Egypt, that is, in our flesh, our spirit holds the kingdom with righteousness and does not consume the sons of Israel, whom we said above to be the rational senses or the virtues of the soul, "in clay and brick", nor wear them down with earthly cares and anxieties. But if our sense has lost the memory of these things, has turned away from God, has come to know Christ no longer, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is an enemy to God, succeeds to the kingdom and addresses its own people, the bodily pleasures, and, with the leaders of the vices called together to counsel, deliberation is entered upon against the sons of Israel — how they may be circumvented, how they may be oppressed, so that they may be afflicted with "clay and bricks", so that they may expose the males, rear the females, so that they may build the cities of Egypt and "fortified cities". These things have not been written for us as history, nor is it to be thought that the divine books narrate the deeds of the Egyptians; but the things that have been written "have been written for our" instruction and "admonition", so that you who hear these things — if perhaps you have already obtained the grace of baptism and have been numbered among the sons of Israel and have received God as king within you, and after this you should wish to turn aside, to do the works of the age, to carry out the deeds of earth and to fulfill muddy services — may know and recognize that "there has arisen in you another king, who knows not Joseph", the king of Egypt, and he himself drives you to his works, he himself makes you labor at brick and clay for him. He it is who, having set taskmasters and drivers over you, urges you with scourges and blows to earthly works, that you may build cities for him. He it is who makes you run to and fro through the age, to trouble the elements of sea and land for the sake of greed. He it is, this king of Egypt, who makes you beat upon the law-court with lawsuits and, for a paltry clod of earth, to wear out your neighbors with quarrels — not to mention lying in wait for chastity, deceiving innocence, committing foul things at home, cruel things abroad, and shameful things within the conscience. When, therefore, you see your deeds to be such, know that you are serving as a soldier for the king of Egypt, which is to be driven by the spirit of this world. But if something is to be understood in this matter more deeply still, this "king who knows not Joseph" can be seen to be the devil, that "fool" who "said in his heart: there is no God", conversing with his people, that is, the apostate angels, and saying: "behold, the race of the sons of Israel is a great multitude" — namely of those who are able to see God with the mind — "and is more powerful than we. Come therefore, let us circumvent them, lest perchance they increase, and, when war befalls us, these too consent with our adversaries, and, overpowering us, they go forth out of our land". But whence does the devil perceive this? Whence does he understand that Israel is a great nation and stronger than they themselves, except that he has often engaged them, has often had wrestlings, and has often been overcome? For he knows that Jacob himself wrestled, and by the help of an angel prevailed over his adversary and grew strong with God. I do not doubt that he has also felt the wrestlings of other saints and has often endured spiritual contests; and hence he says that "the nation of the sons of Israel is exceedingly great, and is stronger than we". But that too which he fears, lest at some time "war befall" them and "they consent with" his "adversaries", and, when these are conquered, they depart out of his land — this, it seems to me, he had a foreboding of from those things which had sometimes been intimated to the holy patriarchs or prophets concerning the coming of Christ, and hence he knows that war is threatening him. He perceives that One will come "who will strip off his principalities and powers, and with confidence triumph over them, and nail them to the wood of His cross". Therefore, having summoned all his people, he desires to circumvent and entrap in men the rational sense, which is now figuratively called Israel; and for that reason he "set over them taskmasters of works", to compel them to learn the works of the flesh, as it also says in the Psalms: "and they were mingled among the nations, and learned their works". He teaches them also to build cities for Pharaoh: "Pithom", which in our tongue signifies the mouth of failing or the mouth of the abyss; "and Rameses", which is interpreted the commotion of the moth; "and On, that is, Heliopolis", which is called the city of the sun. You see what sort of cities Pharaoh commands to be built for himself! A mouth, he says, that fails; for a mouth fails when it speaks a lie, when it fails in truth and in proofs. For he "was a liar from the beginning", and therefore he wills such cities to be built for himself. Or else the mouth of the abyss, because the abyss is the place of his perdition and destruction. And another of his cities is the commotion of the moth. For all who follow him gather their treasures there, where "the moth destroys and where thieves dig through and steal". But they also build a city of the sun by a false name, in that "he transforms himself as an angel of light". In these things, then, he comes beforehand, in these he seizes the minds which were made for this, that they might see God. Yet he foresees that war threatens him and perceives that the destruction of his people will be at hand before long. Therefore he says that "the nation of Israel is stronger than we". Would that he might say this of us too, that he might perceive us to be stronger than he! How will he be able to perceive this? If, when he casts evil thoughts and wicked lusts upon me, I do not receive them, but repel his "fiery darts with the shield of faith"; if in all things, whatever he suggests to my mind, I, mindful of Christ my Lord, say: "get behind me, Satan. For it is written: The Lord your God you shall adore, and Him alone shall you serve". If, therefore, we do these things with all faith, with all conscience, he says of us too that "the nation of Israel is great and is stronger than we". But this also which he says: "lest perchance war befall us, and these too consent with our adversaries" — from the prophetic voices he foresees that war will come upon him, and that he will be forsaken by the sons of Israel, and that they will consent with his adversary and be added to the Lord. For this is what the prophet Jeremiah had foretold concerning him: "the partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth, it made its riches not with judgment; in the midst of its days they will forsake it, and in its last days it will be a fool". He understands, then, that he is called "the partridge, which brought not forth, that gathered", and that those whom "he gathered not with judgment will forsake him in the midst of his days", and will follow the Lord and their creator Christ Jesus, who begot them. But he "gathered those whom he did not beget". And therefore "he will remain a fool in his last days", when "the whole creation", which now "groans together" under his tyranny, shall flee for refuge to its "maker" and its parent. And at this he is indignant and says: "lest", he says, "overpowering us, they go forth out of our land". He does not wish us to go forth out of his land, but wills that we should always "bear the image of the earthly". For if we flee for refuge to his adversary, to Him who has prepared for us the kingdoms of heaven, it is necessary that we leave behind "the image of the earthly" and take up "the image of the heavenly". For this reason, therefore, Pharaoh appoints "taskmasters of works", to teach us his arts, to make us craftsmen of wickedness, to furnish us with a mastery of evils. And because these taskmasters and teachers of wickedness whom Pharaoh has set over us are many, and there is a vast multitude of drivers of this kind, who all exact, command, and extort earthly works, therefore the Lord Jesus, coming, made other masters and teachers, who, fighting against those and subjecting all their "principalities and powers and virtues", defend the sons of Israel from their violence and teach us the Israelite works, and again teach us to see God with the mind, to leave the works of Pharaoh, to go forth out of the land of Egypt, to cast off the Egyptian and barbarous ways, "to put off" the whole "old man with his deeds" "and to put on the new, who is created according to God", to be "renewed" ever "from day to day" unto the image of Him who made us, Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".
COMMENTARY ON THE SONG OF SONGS, BOOK 2

According to these things, therefore, God is perhaps said also to have hardened the heart of Pharaoh, namely because the material of his heart was such that it received the presence of the Sun of justice not on that side by which it illumines, but on that by which it burns and hardens: on this account, without doubt, that he too was afflicting the life of the Hebrews in hard works, and was making them work with clay and brick. … And as this visible sun binds fast and hardens the material of clay, so the Sun of justice, by these same rays with which he was illumining the people of Israel, was hardening the heart of Pharaoh, in which were clayey thoughts, according to the very qualities of its own motions.
HOMILIES ON NUMBERS 27.2

In Egypt were the children of Israel; they were afflicted in the works of Pharaoh the king with clay and brick, until, groaning, they cried out to the Lord, and He, hearing their groaning, sent to them His word through Moses and led them out of Egypt. And we too, therefore, when we were in Egypt — I mean in the errors of this world and in the darkness of ignorance, working the works of the devil in the desires and pleasures of the flesh — the Lord had mercy on our affliction and sent His Word, His only-begotten Son, to rescue us from the ignorance of error and lead us to the light of the divine law.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 2

This "king, who did not know Joseph," devises many things against the people of God, and is forever seeking new arts of doing harm. But now his cunning surpasses all measure, when through the ministry of the midwives he attempts to destroy the offspring of that people — by the very art through which life is usually preserved. For what does he say? "And the king of the Egyptians said," it says, "to the midwives of the Hebrews, to one of them whose name was Sephora, and the name of the other was Phua, and he said: when you deliver the Hebrew women and they are near the birth, if it be a male, kill him; if a female, let it live." But to these words there is joined in what follows: "but the midwives feared God, and did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded them, and they let the males live." If the things that are written were to be taken according to the narrative of the history, then what Scripture says — that "the midwives did not do according to what the king of Egypt commanded them" — would seem unable to stand. For the midwives are not found to have failed to let the females live, whom the king of Egypt commanded to be let live. For thus he says: "if indeed it is a male, kill him; if a female, let it live." And if "the midwives did not do as the king of Egypt had commanded," then surely, just as they "let the males live" against the king's command, so too they ought to have killed the females, that this also might be against the king's command. For to have let the females live was to have done according to Pharaoh's command. These things for the moment I say on account of those who are friends of the letter, and do not think the law to be spiritual and to be understood spiritually. But we, who have learned that all the things that are written were written not as accounts of antiquities, but for our instruction and profit, perceive that these things which are read even now come to pass, not only in this world, which is figuratively called Egypt, but also in each one of us. Let us inquire, then, how the king of Egypt, who is "the prince of this world," does not wish the males to live, but wishes the females to live. If you remember, we have often shown in our discussions that in the females the flesh and the affection of the flesh is signified, but the male is the rational sense and intellectual spirit. The rational sense, therefore, which can have a taste for heavenly things, which can understand God and "seek the things that are above" — this Pharaoh, king and prince of Egypt, hates; this he desires to be slain and destroyed. But he desires that whatever things are of the flesh should live, and the things that pertain to bodily matter — these he desires not only to live, but even to be increased and cultivated. For he wishes that all should have a taste for carnal things, should desire temporal things, should seek "the things that are upon the earth," that no one "lift up his eyes to heaven," that no one inquire whence he came here, that no one call to mind his homeland, paradise. When, therefore, you see men leading their life in pleasures and delights, awash in luxury, giving their labor to feasts, wine, banquets, beds, and unchaste acts — know that in these the king of Egypt is slaying the males and letting the females live. But if you see some rare person, "one out of a thousand," turning to God, lifting his eyes upward, seeking the things that are perpetual and eternal, contemplating not the things "that are seen, but the things that are not seen," hating delights, loving continence, fleeing luxury, cultivating virtue — this one, as a male, as a man, Pharaoh desires to be slain, persecutes, harries, and fights against with a thousand devices. He hates such men, he does not allow them to live in Egypt. Hence, then, it is that in this world the servants of God and all who seek God are held in disdain and contempt. Hence they are exposed to insults, hence they are filled with reproaches, hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them — because Pharaoh hates them, hates males of this kind, he who loves the females. This one also sets about corrupting the midwives, and through them accomplishing what he desires; whose very names are indicated to us by the foresight of the Holy Spirit, who willed these things to be written. "Sephora" it says, "the one" — which is interpreted sparrow (passer) — and "Phua," which among us can be called either ruddy (rubens) or modest. Through these, then, he seeks to have the males slain and the females alone let live.
EXPLANATION OF THE PSALMS 5.7

Many lies indeed seem to be for someone's safety or advantage, spoken not in malice but in kindness: such was that of those midwives in Exodus, who gave a false report to Pharaoh, to the end that the infants of the children of Israel might not be slain. But even these are praised not for the fact but for the disposition shown; since those who only lie in this way will attain in time to a freedom from all lying.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 2

But what does Scripture say? "The midwives feared God," it says, "and did not do as the king of Egypt commanded them." Certain men before us have said that these midwives hold the pattern of rational learning. For midwives are, as it were, in the middle, and tend both the males and the females at their birth. This learning, then, of common rational knowledge reaches to nearly every faculty, instructs all, tends all. If anyone in it be of manly spirit and wish to seek heavenly things and to pursue divine things, he will come, as though healed and warmed by learning of this kind, better prepared for the understanding of divine things. For there is one, as it were the sparrow, which teaches the loftier things and, with the rational wings of doctrine, summons souls to fly on high. The other, which is ruddy or modest, is moral, orders behavior, teaches modesty, instills honesty. To me, however, since Scripture says of these that "because they feared God, they did not do the command of the king of Egypt," these two midwives seem to preserve the figure of both testaments: "Sephora," which is interpreted sparrow, may be compared to the law, which "is spiritual"; but "Phua," which is ruddy or modest, indicates the Gospels, which are ruddy with the blood of Christ and throughout the whole world glow red with the gore of his passion. By these, then, as by midwives, the souls that are born in the church are healed, because from the reading of the Scriptures all the medicine of learning is bestowed upon them. Yet Pharaoh attempts through these things to slay the males of the church, when he suggests heretical notions and perverse doctrines to any who are studious in the divine Scriptures. But the foundation of God stands immovable. For "the midwives fear God," that is, they teach the fear of God, because "the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord." Thus, finally, I think there is fitted still more suitably that which is written in the later passage, where it says: "because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses." This saying can have no coherence according to the letter. For what order of reasoning is it, that it should say: "because the midwives feared God, they made themselves houses"? — as though a house should come to be for the reason that God is feared. If this is taken as it is written, it will seem to have not only no coherence, but also very great emptiness. But if you see how the Scriptures of the new and old testament, teaching the fear of God, make houses for the church and fill the whole circle of the earth with houses of prayer, then what is written will seem to be written reasonably. Thus, then, these midwives, because they fear God and teach the fear of God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt, but let their males live. Nor yet is it said that they obeyed the command of the king so as to let the females live. I dare confidently to say, according to the sense of Scripture: these midwives do not let the females live. For neither are vices taught in the churches, nor is luxury proclaimed, nor are sins nourished — for this is what Pharaoh wishes, when he commands the females to be let live — but virtue alone is cultivated, and virtue alone is nourished. But let us refer these things also to each one of us. And you too, if you fear God, do not carry out the command of the king of Egypt. For he commands you to live in delights, to love the present age, to covet present things. But you, if you fear God and exhibit the office of a midwife toward your soul, if you desire to confer salvation upon it, do not do these things, but let live the male that is in you, tend and cherish your inner man, and through good acts and understandings win for it eternal life.
HOMILIES ON ACTS 54, AT ACTS 20:17

And that you may learn this—Pharaoh commanded the infants to be cast into the river. Unless the infants had been cast forth, Moses would not have been saved, he would not have been brought up in the palace. When he was safe, he was not in honor; when he was exposed, then he was in honor. But God did this, to show His riches of resource and contrivance.
On Lying 15.32

As for its being written that God dealt well with the Hebrew midwives and with Rahab the harlot of Jericho, he did not deal well with them because they lied but because they were merciful to the men of God. And so it was not their deception that was rewarded but their benevolence; the benignity of their intention, not the iniquity of their invention.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 2

But after this, when Pharaoh saw that through the midwives he could not slay the males of Israel: "he commanded," it says, "all the people, saying: every male whatsoever that shall be born to the Hebrews, cast into the river, and every female let live." See what "the prince of this world" commands his own, that they may seize our infants, that they may cast them into the river, and, lying in wait for the very first birth of our own, may straightway, as soon as they have touched the first breasts of the church, rush upon them, tear them away, persecute them, and overwhelm them with the waves and billows of this age. "See what you hear"; the wisdom of God through Solomon says: "understand intelligently the things that are set before you." See, as soon as you are born — nay rather, as soon as you are reborn — what threatens you. This is that which you read in the Gospel, that Jesus, as soon as he came up from baptism, "was led by the Spirit into the desert, to be tempted by the devil." This, then, is what in this passage too Pharaoh commanded his people: to fall upon the Hebrew infants, as soon as they were born, to tear them away, to drown them in the waters. This is perhaps also what is said through the prophet: "for the waters have entered even to my soul. I am sunk fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no substance." But for this reason Christ overcame and conquered, that he might open for you the way of conquering. For this reason, by fasting, he conquered, that you too might know that "a kind of demons of this sort" is to be overcome "by fastings and prayers." For this reason also he despised all the kingdoms of the world and their glory when they were offered to him, that you too, despising the glory of the world, might be able to overcome the tempter. The Egyptians, therefore, to whom Pharaoh gave commands, let only the females live, they hate the males; for they hate the virtues, and nourish only vices and pleasures. And now, therefore, the Egyptians lie in wait, in case perchance some male be born to the Hebrews, so that they may straightway persecute and kill him, unless they take heed, unless they watch and hide the male seed. Finally, Scripture relates that "one of the tribe of Levi, who begot a male and saw that the infant was comely, hid him for three months." See whether it is not for this reason that we are commanded not to perform our good acts in public, not to "do our righteousness before men," but rather, "with the door shut, to pray to the Father in secret," and that "what our right hand does, our left hand should not know." For unless it be in secret, it will be torn away by the Egyptians, it will be assailed, cast into the river, drowned in the waves and billows. Therefore, if I give alms, because it is a work of God, I beget a male. But if I do it so that it may become known to men, and I seek praise from men and do not hide it, my alms has been snatched away by the Egyptians and drowned in the river, and with such great labor and such great zeal I have begotten a male for the Egyptians. Therefore, O people of God, who hear these things, do not think, as we have already often said, that the tales of the ancients are being recited to you, but that you are being taught through these things, so that you may recognize the order of life, the discipline of morals, the contests of faith and virtue.
Commentary on Nahum

Who would not say that beautiful Nineveh, a soul beautiful by nature, beguiled by the luxury and pleasures of this age, has come to womanish delights, and, her manliness lost, has languished into a woman? For if the soul of the righteous man, coming to the perfect man and keeping the firmness of its creation, and cleaving to God, is made one spirit with him, why should not, on the contrary, the soul that loves the world become one with the world, and, reduced to womanly softness, lose its manly firmness? I think that for this reason in Exodus Pharaoh commands that every male born to the Hebrews be thrown into the river, and every female be kept alive. For the Egyptian king, who says elsewhere: The rivers are mine, and I made them, could command nothing other than this, that whatever is strong and manly in the Hebrews, and in those who pass through this age, be thrown into the waters and carried down by their streams into the sea. And on the contrary, whatever seemed womanly and soft and comely in this age, that should be kept alive, should grow up and beget. And consider at the same time that the Egyptian ruler cannot kill the men of the Hebrews, nor those who have already come out of infancy, but only those whose age is still tender, and their body soft, and their progress just beginning; he knows that the females cannot be reared unless the males have been killed. So he wishes to drown in the whirlpool of his river whatever is strong and manly in the Hebrews, so that what is womanly may grow up alone more freely.

n: After this. In process of time, without reference to what immediately precedes. The Hebrew and Septuagint omit these words. (Haydock) --- The marriage of Amram, grandson of Levi, with his aunt or cousin, had taken place before the persecution. Tostat and others suppose, that people were not then forbidden to marry their aunts. But it is probable Jochabed was only the grand-daughter of Levi, and the daughter of one of Amram's brothers, as the Septuagint insinuate. Otherwise their ages would have been very disproportionate. See chap. vi. 20. (Calmet)

Goodly. Handsome, elegant, Hebrews xi. 23; agreeable to God, Acts vii. 20. Josephus says, Amram had been assured by God that the child should be the deliverer of his people. Yet he neglects not to use every prudent precaution. (Worthington) --- Months. Hebrew moons; whence some erroneously infer, that the Hebrew year was not solar. (Calmet)

Bulrushes, or paper plant, growing on the banks of the Nile. Such little vessels were used in Egypt in Lucan's time. Conseritur bibula Memphitis cymba papyro. (Menochius) --- Sedges, to prevent it from being carried away by the stream. Cajetan thinks the Hebrews did not drown their children; but by thus exposing them, abandoned them to the king's use, Acts vii. 19.
His sister, Mary, who was born at the beginning of this persecution, and was therefore called bitterness. (Haydock) --- She was about 12 years old. (Menochius)

Daughter, and sole heiress. She is called Thermut by Josephus, and Meris by Artapanus. She was going to bathe, or to purify herself, according to the custom of the country; or perhaps she was going to wash linen, as Nausicrae, the daughter of Alcinous, was doing, when she met Ulysses. (Calmet)
Hebrews, against whom the persecution raged. She saw it had received circumcision. (Theodoret, q. in Ex.)

Moses, or Moyses, in the Egyptian tongue, signifies one taken or saved out of the water. (Challoner) --- Mo, signifies water in the Egyptian tongue; Mosse, "he drew out," in Hebrew. Philo believes that the princess feigned him to be her own child. Moses denied that he was, and would not take advantage of this adoption, Hebrews xi. 24. He was grown up, and had been well instructed by his parents, ver. 9. He afterwards became well versed in all the sciences, (Acts vii. 22,) rejecting what was idle and superstitious. Josephus assures us he became a great conqueror. (Calmet)

He slew the Egyptian. This he did by a particular inspiration of God; as a prelude to his delivering the people from their oppression and bondage. He thought, says St. Stephen, (Acts vii. 25,) that his brethren understood that God by his hand would save them. But such particular and extraordinary examples are not to be imitated. (Challoner) --- He was inspired, on this occasion, to stand up in defence of the innocent. (Menochius) (St. Thomas Aquinas, ii. 2, q. 60.) --- The laws of Egypt required every person to protect the oppressed; or, if unable to do it, he was to call in the aid of the magistrate. (Diodorus i.) (Calmet) --- Moses looked round to see if there was any help near. He was 40 years old when he was forced to flee.

Feared. St. Paul, (Hebrews xi. 27,) is speaking of his leaving Egypt, at the head of the people, when he says, not fearing the fierceness of the king. Without being dismayed on this occasion, by the unexpected discovery of what he had done, (which was perhaps undesignedly made public by the Hebrew whom he had rescued) he resolves not to tempt God. (Haydock)

Madian. A city and country of Arabia, which took its name from Madian the son of Abraham, by Cetura, and was peopled by his posterity. (Challoner) --- There were, perhaps, some of the descendants of Cham, by his son Chus, intermixed with them; (Haydock) and hence Aaron reproaches the wife of Moses for being a Chusite, Numbers xii. 1. Jethro was a Cinean, descended from the same stock.

Priest. Hebrew cohen, (or cén,) means also a prince, as the Chaldean has it. When put in this manner, with the name of a place, it is generally taken in this sense. But formerly kings were also priests. Jethro served the true God, like Job, in the midst of a perverse generation, and offered sacrifice to him, when he joined the camp of the Israelites, Exodus xviii. 11. (Calmet)

Raguel. He had two names, being also called Jethro, as appears from the first verse of the following chapter. (Challoner) --- He is also called Hobab and Ceni. (Numbers x. 2; Judges i. 16.) Perhaps Raguel was father of Jethro. (Drusius)

Swore. Hebrew Goel is rendered "was willing." --- Sym.[Symmachus?] has, "He conjured Moses;" and Theo., "Moses began to dwell." The Septuagint neglect the word entirely, "But Moses took up his abode."

Gersam, or Gershom. This name signifies, a stranger there: as Eliezer signifies the help of God. (Challoner) --- And she, &c., is wanting both in Hebrew and Chaldean, but found in the Complut. edit. of the Septuagint. It occurs (chap. xviii. 4,) and we might naturally expect to find it in this place. (Calmet)
Died in the year of the world 2494. His successor, Amenophis, treading in his footsteps, was drowned 19 years afterwards. (Usher)
Knew them; that is, he had respect to them, he cast a merciful eye upon them. (Challoner) --- Hebrew, "he had regard for them;" and, as some Latin copies read, delivered them. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 2

"Seeing," then, these of the tribe of Levi "that the infant was comely, they concealed him for three months. And when they could no longer conceal him, his mother took," it says, "an ark and daubed it with bitumen and placed the infant in it and set it in the marsh beside the river. And his sister watched from afar, to see what would happen to him. But the daughter of Pharaoh came down to wash herself in the river, and she heard the infant crying, and she sent," it says, "and took him up, and the daughter of Pharaoh said that this is of the infants of the Hebrews." After this it is then related how his sister spoke, that she might call the mother of the boy to nurse him. "And the daughter of Pharaoh said to her," it says, "keep this infant for me, and nurse him for me, and I will give you your wages. And when she had nursed him, as he grew stronger, she brought him to the daughter of Pharaoh, and he became to her a son, and she named his name Moses, saying: because I took him up out of the water." Each of these things is filled with immense mysteries and demands a great length of time, and if we should spend the space of a whole day upon them, it would perhaps scarcely suffice. Yet briefly some things must be knocked upon by us for the edification of the church. I think the daughter of Pharaoh can be seen as the church, which is gathered from the nations, which, although she has an impious and iniquitous father, yet to her it is said through the prophet: "hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father, because the king has desired your beauty." This, then, is she who goes out from her father's house and comes to the waters, that she may be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father's house. Finally, straightway she takes up "the bowels of mercy" and has compassion on the infant. This church, therefore, coming from the nations, finds Moses lying in the marsh, cast off by his own and exposed, gives him to be nursed, he is nursed among his own, there he passes his infancy. But when "he has grown stronger," then he is brought to her and adopted as a son. That Moses is called the law has already often been treated in many places. Coming, therefore, to the waters of baptism, the church received also the law — the law, however, which was shut up within an "ark," daubed with pitch and "bitumen." An "ark" is a kind of covering woven from twigs or from papyrus, or even formed from the bark of trees, within which the infant, once placed in it, appeared exposed. The law, therefore, lay shut up within coverings of this kind and daubed with pitch and "bitumen"; hedged about by the base and foul senses of the Jews, it lay in squalor, until the church should come from the nations and take it up out of the muddy and marshy places and receive it within the halls of wisdom and the royal roofs. This law, nevertheless, passes its infancy among its own. For among those who do not know how to understand it spiritually, it is a little one and an infant, having the food of sucklings; but when it comes to the church, when it enters the house of the church, Moses is stronger and more robust. For once the veil of the letter is removed, "perfect" and "solid food" is found in the reading of it. Yet what is it that she, among whom the law was both born and nursed, receives the wages of her nursing from the daughter of Pharaoh? What is it that the synagogue receives from the church? I think it can be understood as that which the same Moses writes, saying: "I will lead you into jealousy over that which is no nation, over a foolish nation I will provoke you to wrath." The synagogue, then, receives this as its wages from the church, that it no longer worship idols. For seeing those who are of the nations so converted to God that they no longer know idols, and venerate no one except the one God, she herself is ashamed any longer to worship idols. This benefit, therefore, the synagogue receives from the church, in that she was seen to have nursed the law as a little one. But we too, even if we have had Pharaoh for a father, even if "the prince of this world" begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters, let us take up to ourselves the law of God, and let not the base and obscure covering of its letter be squalid to us; the things that are little and of sucklings in it let us yield up, but the things that are perfect and robust let us take, and let us place these within the royal roofs of our heart. Let us have a great and robust Moses; let us think nothing about him that is little, nothing lowly, but wholly magnificent, wholly excellent, wholly comely. For everything is great, whatever is spiritual, whatever is of sublime understanding. And let us pray to our Lord Jesus Christ, that he himself may reveal and show to us how "great" Moses is and how sublime he is. For he himself "reveals" to whom he wills "through the Holy Spirit." "To Him be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."
The Stromata Book 1

Eupolemus in his work On the Kings of Judea says that Moses was the first sage and the first person to transmit to the Jews the science of writing, which passed from the Jews to the Phoenicians and from the Phoenicians to the Greeks. When he reached the age of manhood he developed his practical wisdom, being zealous for his national, ancestral educational traditions, to the point of striking down and killing an Egyptian who was unjustly attacking a Hebrew. The mystics say that he eliminated the Egyptian simply by speaking, as later in Acts Peter is said to have killed by his words those who had kept for themselves part of the price of the land and had told lies.
On Cain and Abel 2.4.14

Moses indeed killed the Egyptian and became a fugitive from the land of Egypt, in order to avoid the tyrant of that land. But he would not have killed that Egyptian man before he had first killed the Egyptian man of spiritual wickedness within himself, and had renounced the luxury of regal honors, considering the reproach of Christ a greater inheritance than the treasures of Egypt.
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapters 3-4

Every kind of honour and happiness was bestowed upon you, and then was fulfilled that which is written, "My beloved ate and drank, and was enlarged and became fat, and kicked." [Deuteronomy 32:15] Hence flowed emulation and envy, strife and sedition, persecution and disorder, war and captivity. So the worthless rose up against the honoured, those of no reputation against such as were renowned, the foolish against the wise, the young against those advanced in years. For this reason righteousness and peace are now far departed from you, inasmuch as every one abandons the fear of God, and has become blind in His faith, neither walks in the ordinances of His appointment, nor acts a part becoming a Christian, but walks after his own wicked lusts, resuming the practice of an unrighteous and ungodly envy, by which death itself entered into the world. [Wisdom 2:24]

For thus it is written: "And it came to pass after certain days, that Cain brought of the fruits of the earth a sacrifice unto God; and Abel also brought of the firstlings of his sheep, and of the fat thereof. And God had respect to Abel and to his offerings, but Cain and his sacrifices He did not regard. And Cain was deeply grieved, and his countenance fell. And God said to Cain, Why are you grieved, and why is your countenance fallen? If you offer rightly, but do not divide rightly, have you not sinned? Be at peace: your offering returns to yourself, and you shall again possess it. And Cain said to Abel his brother, Let us go into the field. And it came to pass, while they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him." [Genesis 4:3-8] You see, brethren, how envy and jealousy led to the murder of a brother. Through envy, also, our father Jacob fled from the face of Esau his brother [Genesis 27:41-45]. Envy made Joseph be persecuted unto death, and to come into bondage. [Genesis 37:18-28] Envy compelled Moses to flee from the face of Pharaoh king of Egypt, when he heard these words from his fellow-countryman, "Who made you a judge or a ruler over us? Will you kill me, as you killed the Egyptian yesterday?" [Exodus 2:14] On account of envy, Aaron and Miriam had to make their abode without the camp. [Numbers 12:14-15] Envy brought down Dathan and Abiram alive to Hades, through the sedition which they excited against God's servant Moses. [Numbers 16:33] Through envy, David not only underwent the hatred of foreigners, but was also persecuted by Saul king of Israel. [1 Samuel 21:10-15]
HOMILIES ON 2 CORINTHIANS 15.4

For so Moses for the sake of those he ruled left so great riches and treasures untold, "choosing to suffer affliction with the people of God," and before his appointment was leader of the people by his actions. Wherefore also very foolishly did that Hebrew say to him, "Who made thee a ruler and a judge over us?" What sayest thou? Thou seest the actions and doubtest of the title? Just as if one seeing a physician using the knife excellently well, and succoring that limb in the body which was diseased, should say, `Who made thee a physician and ordered thee to use the knife?' `Art, my good Sir, and thine own ailment.' So too did his knowledge make him (i.e., Moses,) what he claimed to be. For ruling is an art, not merely a dignity, and an art above all arts.
HOMILIES ON HEBREWS 26.5

"By faith he forsook Egypt not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured as seeing Him who is Invisible." What dost thou say? That he did not fear? And yet the Scripture says, that when he heard, he "was afraid," and for this cause provided for safety by flight, and stole away, and secretly withdrew himself; and afterwards he was exceedingly afraid. Observe the expressions with care: he said, "not fearing the wrath of the king," with reference to his even presenting himself again. For it would have been [the part] of one who was afraid, not to undertake again his championship, nor to have any hand in the matter. That he did however again undertake it, was [the part] of one who committed all to God: for he did not say, `He is seeking me, and is busy [in the search], and I cannot bear again to engage in this matter.' So that even flight was [an act of] faith. Why then did he not remain (you say)? That he might not cast himself into a foreseen danger. For this finally would have been tempting [God]: to leap into the midst of dangers, and say, `Let us see whether God will save me.' And this the devil said to Christ, "Cast Thyself down." Seest thou that it is a diabolical thing, to throw ourselves into danger without cause and for no purpose, and to try whether God will save us? For he [Moses] could no longer be their champion when they who were receiving benefits were so ungrateful. It would therefore have been a foolish and senseless thing to remain there. But all these things were done, because, "he endured as seeing Him who is Invisible."
Interrogation of Job and David 4.4.14
Moses went out from Egypt and was made a prophet and sent back to the people that he might free their souls from the land of affliction.
HOMILIES ON ISAIAH 5

In Exodus something of this kind is written: "and it came to pass after many days, the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel groaned, and their cry went up to God". As long as Pharaoh lived, the "children of Israel" did "not groan", and, placed under punishments, they did not even have the free faculty of "groaning"; for the king was alive, who commanded them to make "bricks and straw". As long as Pharaoh lived, they did "not groan to God"; when Pharaoh died, then they had the strength to lift up their faces wet with weeping. The wicked king lives in our breast as long as Pharaoh the devil lives. Then we labor at "bricks" and "straw", then we swallow our tears in silence and do the first works of iniquity; but when he has died, at the visitation of the Lord our God, then we "groan to the Lord".
On Paradise 15.75

Finally, the Hebrews who groaned in the labors of Egypt obtained the grace of the righteous. And because they ate bread in sorrow, they were given spiritual food. But the Egyptians, who celebrated such works with exultation, serving a detestable king, did not obtain any forgiveness.
Commentary on Isaiah

When Ahaz, who is interpreted κατάσχεσις, that is, holding, or possession, whom we read was a most ungodly king, had died, this weight, or word, comes upon the Philistines. For while he lived and reigned among sinners, neither a weight against the foreigners nor the word of God could come to the Prophet. Indeed I remember having said this above too, when, Uzziah having died, Isaiah saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. And in Exodus we read (Exod 2:23) that after the king of Egypt died, the children of Israel groaned from their works, and cried out, and their cry went up from their works, and the Lord heard their groaning. For unless what was said were mystical, they ought rather to have cried out while he was reigning, when they were slaving at mud and bricks.

n: Fed for the space of forty years. During which time, he composed the books of Genesis and Job, for the consolation of his countrymen; (Menochius) though others believe he wrote all the Pentateuch in the desert. (Theodoret; &c.) --- Of God, on account of its height; or on account of God's appearing to Moses. --- Horeb is so close to Mount Sinai, that the shadow of the latter reaches it when the sun rises. It is watered with three fine springs; and the summit is adorned with fruit trees. (Calmet)

The Lord appeared. That is, and angel representing God, and speaking in his name. (Challoner) (Acts vii. 30; Galatians iii. 19.) --- The apparitions of God to the patriarchs are generally understood in this sense. (St. Augustine, de Trin. iii. 11.) (Worthington) --- Yet many of the Fathers suppose, that this angel was no other than the Son of God, the angel of the great council, (Malachias iii. 1,) and St. Augustine (q. 2, in Ex.) does not disapprove of this opinion. QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 42: WHY DID THE ANGEL APPEAR TO MOSES IN FIRE AND A BUSH?

WHY WAS THE ANGEL WHO WAS SENT TO SPEAK TO MOSES APPEARED TO HIM ON THE MOUNTAIN IN THE MIDST OF FIRE AND A BUSH? — God is most high; therefore it was fitting that He should appear on a height, that is, in a place close to heaven. And because fire always strives upward, growing toward heaven, the Lord of heaven ought to appear in it, He who urges what is earthly toward what is above. As for the bush, He caused His appearance there on account of sins. For since He had come down to give the Law because of sins, and thorns signify sins, because, he says, “I looked that it should yield grapes, but it yielded thorns” (Isa. 5:2), and the Law did not come at once to punish, but first to reveal, therefore the fire did not burn the bush; that is, the Law when given did not make sinners guilty for past sins. For sins are not of nature, but arise by accident; so the material of the bush, that is, of thorns, does not have a root armed with thorns. Reason therefore shows why the Lord appeared to Moses in this way.
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 7: WHY DID THE ANGEL APPEAR TO MOSES IN FIRE AND A BUSH?

WHY DID THE ANGEL SENT TO SPEAK TO MOSES APPEAR IN THE FIRE AND IN THE BUSH? — The angelic nature in itself is simple, and its substance as such desires higher, not lower things. Therefore the Lord appeared in fire, whose nature is always reaching upward, where Christ is. But He appeared in the bush for this reason: because it has thorns that hurt, and it is easily combustible, and yet it was not burned by the fire. Take the fire as representing the Law, because for sinners it is fire. The bush, however, signifies sins, because in comparison with other trees the bush is shown by the Savior to be an evil tree; and sins are nothing other than evil. Therefore, although the fire appeared in the person of the Law, it did not consume the bush: just as the Law, given with regard to past sin, did not in fact punish, but rather restrained the full force of its justice, so that later, once given, if it were despised, it would punish. For this reason, then, the Lord appeared in fire and in a bush, because in the bush the fire signified the Law.

To God. Hebrew, "thou shalt be to him in the place of God." He shall hear and obey thee, explaining to the people the instructions thou shalt give him. I have established thee the god of Pharao, and Aaron shall be thy prophet, chap. vii. 1. (Calmet) --- I will address myself immediately to thee. (Tirinus)
Rod. So the devil taught Mercury and Bacchus to mimic Moses, and to carry a wand. Tum virgam capit, hâc animas ille evocat orco. (Virgil, iv.) (Calmet)

Life. "After those many days were elapsed, the king of Egypt died," who had obliged Moses to flee, as the Septuagint, Josephus, and Philo add at the end of ver. 18. Upon which God, who had already commissioned him to go, and saw him willing, gives him this farther assurance that he has nothing to fear for his own person. (Haydock)

I shall harden, &c. Not by being the efficient cause of his sin; but by withdrawing from him, for his just punishment, the dew of grace, that might have softened his heart; and so suffering him to grow harder and harder. (Challoner) --- Non impertiendo misericordiam. (St. Augustine, ep. 194, ad Sixt.) Thus God permitted the false miracles of the magicians, and did not suffer the scourges to continue long, so that the tyrant soon relapsed and forgot his promises. (Origen, Philos. xx; Theodoret in Rom. ix. 17.) (Calmet)
First-born, heir to my promises, and the object of my complacency.
Thy son. This was the tenth and last scourge, which forced the king to relent. (Menochius)

The Lord met him, and would have killed him. This was an angel representing the Lord, who treated Moses in this manner, for having neglected the circumcision of his younger son: which his wife understanding, circumcised her child upon the spot, upon which the angel let Moses go. (Challoner) --- Both his children were born about this time. But Eliezer, the younger, had not been circumcised; and therefore remained under the power of the destroying angel. (Origen, contra Cels. v.) Others think the angel was going to kill Moses. (Calmet)

Stone, like a flint. Such stones are very common in Egypt, and are used by the embalmers to open the side of the deceased. The Galli priests make themselves eunuchs without danger, by means of sharp stones. (Pliny, Natural History xxxv. 12.) Josue circumcises with the like, Josue v. But any instrument will suffice. (Calmet) --- Sephora seized the first thing that came in her way, to save the life of her husband, with whom God was displeased for this neglect of complying with the law, whatever might be his pretext. It was not fit that he should be a legislator, who was not a pattern of obedience. (Tirinus) --- Spouse. I have redeemed thee from destruction, by shedding the blood of my son; therefore, I will deem this a ratification of our marriage. Never forget our union, which costs me so much, and which has placed you in such imminent danger. The Hebrew mothers style their newly circumcised infants bloody spouses, in imitation of Sephora, who on this occasion perhaps addresses the words to Eliezer. The Septuagint read, "Sephora...fell at his feet, and said, the blood of my son's circumcision has ceased to flow," &c., which is not very easy to understand.
Of God. Horeb, where both brothers met, after Sephora was returned to her father.
The three signs, prescribed above, in proof of their mission. (Calmet)

f: ON THE RESURRECTION OF THE FLESH 28.1-2

But we know that prophecy expressed itself by things no less than by words. By words and also by deeds is the resurrection foretold. When Moses puts his hand into his bosom and then draws it out again dead, and again puts his hand into his bosom and plucks it out living, does not this apply as an anticipation of the resurrection to all humankind?—inasmuch as those three signs denoted the threefold power of God: when it shall, first, in the appointed order, subdue to man the old serpent, the devil, however formidable; then, second, draw forth the flesh from the bosom of death; and then, at last, shall pursue all blood [shed] in judgment.
SERMON 6.7

Let me try to explain, as far as the Lord enables me to, what these signs mean. The rod stands for the kingdom, the snake for mortality; it was by the snake that man was given death to drink. The Lord was prepared to take this death to himself. So when the rod came down to earth it had the form of a snake, because the kingdom of God, which is Jesus Christ, came down to earth. He put on mortality, which he also nailed to the cross. Your holinesses know that when that proud and stiff-necked people grumbled against God in the desert, they began to be bitten by serpents and to die of the bites. In his mercy God provided a remedy, a remedy that restored health at the time but also foretold the wisdom that was to come in the future.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 32.268

It is difficult to see what this sign can symbolize for us. But since we must not stop seeking and must deliver to the reader what occurs to us as an interpretation, we will say that in many passages the hand is a symbol of deeds. Now the bosom of Moses has two meanings. The first, in accordance with the sense of the letter, makes the deed of the doer like snow, as it says in the Hebrew, and leprous. The second, however, in accordance with the spiritual law, shows that the conduct is pure and that it is restored to the will of the nature of the Word.
On the Duties of the Clergy 3.15.95

Again, another sign which Moses gave points to our Lord Jesus Christ. He put his hand into his bosom and drew it out again, and his hand had become as snow. A second time he put it in and drew it out, and it was again like the appearance of human flesh. This signified first the original glory of the Godhead of the Lord Jesus and then the assumption of our flesh, in which truth all nations and peoples must believe. So he put in his hand, for Christ is the right hand of God; and whosoever does not believe in his Godhead and incarnation is punished as a sinner; like that king who, while not believing open and plain signs, yet afterwards, when punished, prayed that he might find mercy.
Clement's First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 17

Let us be imitators also of those who in goat-skins and sheep-skins [Hebrews 11:37] went about proclaiming the coming of Christ; I mean Elijah, Elisha, and Ezekiel among the prophets, with those others to whom a like testimony is borne [in Scripture]. Abraham was specially honoured, and was called the friend of God; yet he, earnestly regarding the glory of God, humbly declared, "I am but dust and ashes." [Genesis 18:27] Moreover, it is thus written of Job, "Job was a righteous man, and blameless, truthful, God-fearing, and one that kept himself from all evil." [Job 1:1] But bringing an accusation against himself, he said, "No man is free from defilement, even if his life be but of one day." [Job 14:4-5] Moses was called faithful in all God's house; and through his instrumentality, God punished Egypt with plagues and tortures. Yet he, though thus greatly honoured, did not adopt lofty language, but said, when the divine oracle came to him out of the bush, "Who am I, that Thou sendest me? I am a man of a feeble voice and a slow tongue." [Exodus 4:10] And again he said, "I am but as the smoke of a pot."
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 5

And of old indeed Moses said: "but I am ἄλογος (without speech or reason)" — which, though the Latin has rendered it otherwise, can nevertheless be more properly translated: "without speech or reason" —, and after he said this, he received reason or speech, which he had confessed that he did not before possess. But the people of Israel in Egypt, before it received the law, was in a certain way "mute", without speech and reason; then it received speech, of which Moses was an image. This people, therefore, does not now confess what it then confessed in Moses, namely that it is "mute" and ἄλογος, but by nods and silence indicates that it does not have speech and does not have reason. Does it not seem to you to be a confession of foolishness, when none of them can render a reason for the legal precepts and the prophetic oracle?
HOMILIES ON GENESIS 3.5

But I will bring forward to you yet another thing, which you cannot contradict. In Exodus, where we in the books of the Church have it written that Moses answered the Lord and said: "Provide, Lord, another whom you may send. For I am of a thin voice and slow of tongue," you in the Hebrew copies have: "but I am uncircumcised in lips." Behold, you have circumcision of the lips according to your copies, which you say are truer. If, then, according to you Moses says he is still unworthy, because he is not circumcised in lips, it is certain that he thereby indicates this, that he is worthier and holier who is circumcised in lips. Apply, then, the sickle also to your lips and cut away the coverings of your mouth, since such an understanding in the divine letters pleases you. But if you recall the circumcision of the lips to allegory, and likewise call the circumcision of the ears allegorical and figurative, how do you not also seek an allegory in the circumcision of the foreskin?
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

So long as Moses was in Egypt and "was being instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians", he was not "of a thin voice" nor "slow of tongue", nor did he profess himself to be lacking in eloquence. For, as far as the Egyptians were concerned, he was both of a sonorous voice and of incomparable eloquence. But when he began to hear the voice of God and to receive the divine utterances, then he perceived his own voice to be feeble and thin, and he understood his tongue to be slow and hampered; then he pronounces himself mute, when he began to recognize that true Word which "was in the beginning with God". But that what we are saying may more readily be grasped, let us make use of a comparison of this kind. If a rational man, however unskilled and untaught, be compared with dumb animals, he will seem eloquent in comparison with those which are devoid both of reason and of voice; but if he be set beside learned and eloquent men, men most approved in all wisdom, he will seem inarticulate and mute. And if someone should contemplate the divine Word itself and look upon the divine wisdom itself, then, however great his learning and however great his wisdom, he will profess himself before God a mute animal, far more than the beasts are before us. This surely was what the blessed David also, gazing upon it and weighing himself in such a manner against the divine wisdom, was saying: "I became as a beast of burden before you". According to this, therefore, Moses too, the greatest of the prophets, says to God in the present reading that he is "of a thin voice" "and slow of tongue", and that he is not eloquent. For all men, in comparison with the divine word, are to be reckoned not only inarticulate, but even mute.
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF LUKE 16

Thus I understand also that which God says: "Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Was it not I, the Lord God?" There is an eye of the body, with which we behold these earthly things, an eye according to the sense of the flesh, of which the Scripture says: "walking vainly, puffed up by the sense of the flesh". To this we have another, contrary and better, that savors of divine things; and because it was blind in us, Jesus came to make it see, that those who did not see might see, and those who saw might be made blind.
Treatise XI. Exhortation to Martyrdom 10

Just as in Exodus God speaks to Moses, when he delays and fears to go to the people, saying, "Who gave a mouth to man and who made the dumb and the deaf, the seeing and the blind? Did not I the Lord God? Go now, and I shall open your mouth, and I will teach you what you shall speak." It is not difficult for God to open the mouth of a man devoted to him and to inspire constancy and confidence in speaking in one who confesses him, who in the book of Numbers made even a female ass speak against Balaam the prophet. Therefore let no one consider in persecutions what danger the devil brings, but rather let him bear in mind what assistance God affords.
