Let not the disturbances of men weaken the mind, but let divine protection strengthen the faith, since each one according to the Lord's promises and the merits of his faith receives so much of God's help as he thinks he receives, and since there is nothing which the Almighty cannot grant, except if the frail faith of the recipient be deficient.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

Because, therefore, he had advanced so far in understanding as to recognize his own self—in which lies the greatest part of wisdom—the divine favor rewards him. Hear with what rich and magnificent gifts. "I," he says, "will open your mouth, and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". Blessed are those whose mouth God opens, that they may speak. To the prophets God opens the mouth and fills it with his own utterance, as he says in the present passage: "I will open your mouth and will instruct you in what you ought to speak". But through David also God says: "Enlarge your mouth, and I will fill it". Likewise Paul too says: "that speech may be given me in the opening of my mouth". The mouth, therefore, of those who speak the words of God, God opens. But I fear that there may be some whose mouth, on the contrary, the devil opens. For whoever speaks a lie, it is certain that the devil has opened his mouth, that he might speak the lie. Whoever gives false testimony, whoever utters buffooneries, whoever brings forth filthy things and the rest of this kind out of his mouth—the devil has opened their mouth. I fear that the devil opens also the mouth "of whisperers and detractors", and also of those who "utter idle words, of which an account is to be rendered in the day of judgment". And indeed, as for those who "speak iniquity on high", "who deny that my Lord Jesus Christ has come in the flesh", or "who blaspheme the Holy Spirit", to whom "it shall be forgiven neither in the present nor in the age to come"—who doubts that the devil opens their mouth? Do you wish me to show you this also from the Scriptures, how the devil opens the mouth to men of this kind, who speak against Christ? See what is written of Judas, how it is related that "Satan entered into him", and that "the devil put it into his heart to betray him". He, then, opened his mouth, that "he might confer with the chief priests and Pharisees how he might betray him" for money received. Whence it seems to me to be no small grace to discern the mouth which the devil opens. It is not without the grace of the Holy Spirit to distinguish a mouth of this kind and its words; and therefore in the distribution of spiritual graces this too is added, that to some is given "the discernment of spirits". It is therefore a spiritual grace by which the spirit is discerned, as also elsewhere the Apostle says: "test the spirits, whether they be of God". But as God opens the mouth of the saints, so I think that God opens also the ears of the saints to hear the divine words. For thus says the prophet Isaiah: "The Lord will open my ear, that I may know when the word ought to be spoken". So too the Lord opens the eyes, as "the Lord opened the eyes of Hagar, and she saw a well of living water". But Elisha the prophet also says: "Open, Lord, the eyes of the servant, that he may see that there are more with us than with the adversaries. And the Lord opened," he says, "the eyes of the servant, and behold, the whole mountain was full of horsemen and chariots and heavenly aids". For "the angel of the Lord encamps round about those who fear him, and will deliver them". God therefore opens, as we have said, both the mouth and the ears and the eyes, that we may either speak or discern or hear the things that are God's. But that also I do not take idly, which the prophet says: "the instruction," he says, "of the Lord opened my ear". This seems to me to pertain to us, that is, in common to the whole Church of God. For if we are engaged in "the instruction of the Lord", "the instruction of the Lord" opens the ear for us also. But the ear which is opened through "the instruction of the Lord" is not always open, but at one time open, at another closed. Hear the lawgiver saying: "you shall not receive a vain report". If, then, at any time vain things are spoken, if at any time empty, foolish, base, profane, wicked things are brought forth, he who knows "the instruction of the Lord" closes his ears and turns away his hearing and says: "but I, like a deaf man, was not hearing, and like a mute man who has not opened his mouth". But if the things that are spoken pertain to the profit of the soul, if the discourse is about God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, cuts away vices, the ears ought to lie open to utterances of this kind—and not only the ears, but also the heart and the mind, and the whole gate of the soul is to be thrown open to hearing of this kind. Yet with the utmost moderation of precept the law expressed itself, so as to say: "you shall not receive a vain report"; it did not say: you shall not hear a vain report, but "you shall not receive". For we frequently hear vain things. What Marcion speaks are vain things; what Valentinus speaks are vain things; and all who speak against God the creator—vain are the things they speak. But nevertheless we frequently hear them, that we may be able to answer against them, lest perchance they steal upon any of the simpler of our brethren through the ornament of speech. We hear these things, then, but we do not receive them. For they were spoken from that mouth which the devil opened. And therefore we must pray that the Lord may deign to open our mouth, that we may be able both to refute those who contradict and to stop up the mouth which the devil opens. So much for what is written: "I will open your mouth, and will instruct you in what you ought to speak".
Letter 65.4

The Lord also said to the Apostles, opening their mouths, Receive ye the Holy Ghost, whereby He declared that He is the same Who said to Moses, I will open thy mouth, and teach thee what thou shalt say. Wherefore this wisdom, divine, unspeakable, unadulterated and incorruptible, pours her grace into the minds of her saints, and discloses to them knowledge that they may behold her glory.
Commentary on Isaiah

So Moses too, to whom the Lord had said: Come, I will send you to Pharaoh king of Egypt (Exod 3:10), and he said: I beseech you, Lord, I am not worthy; provide another whom you may send, or as is read in the Hebrew, Send whom you are going to send (Exod 4:13), answered not out of contempt but out of humility, because he who had been instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians had heard nothing about his lips being cleansed. And Isaiah, not by his own merit but by the grace of the Lord, by which he was cleansed, offers himself for the ministry.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

But not to Moses only is it promised that his mouth shall be opened by the Lord, but to Aaron also. For it is said concerning him too: "I will open your mouth and his mouth, and will instruct you in what you are to do".
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 3.1.7

Now many have been troubled by the story of Pharaoh, in dealing with whom God says several times, "I will harden Pharaoh's heart." For if he is hardened by God and through being hardened sins, he is not himself responsible for the sin; and if this is so, Pharaoh has no free will. And someone will say that in the same way those who are lost have no free will and will not be lost on their own account. Also the saying in Ezekiel, "I will take away their stony hearts and will put in them hearts of flesh, that they may walk in my statutes and keep my judgments," might lead one to suppose that it was God who gave the power to walk in the commandments and to keep the judgments, by his removing the hindrance, the stony heart, and implanting something better, the heart of flesh.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 3.1.9

Why too does he blame Pharaoh, saying, "You will not let my people go; behold, I will smite all the firstborn in Egypt, even your firstborn," and all the rest that is recorded as being said by God through Moses to Pharaoh? It is incumbent on him who believes that the Scriptures are true and that God is just, if he is a thoughtful man, to take pains to show how God, in using such expressions as these, can be clearly conceived to be just.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 28.185

And is there anything more profound to say of Israel, not of nature but of grace, of whom it was written, "Israel is my firstborn son," when Israel was in dispersion? You yourself will also understand that these are the scattered children of God for whom Jesus was to die in order to gather them together into one.
Catechetical Lecture 11.4

When you hear "firstborn," do not think of this in human fashion; for among humans the firstborn have other brothers; and it is somewhere written, "Israel is my son, my firstborn." But like Reuben, Israel was a rejected firstborn; for Reuben went up to his father's bed, and Israel cast the Son of the Father out of the vineyard and crucified him. To others also Scripture says, "You are children of the Lord your God" and elsewhere, "I said, you are gods; all of you sons of the Most High." Note "I said," not "I begot." They, from the fact that God said it, received adoption which they did not have, but he was not begotten to be other than he was before. Rather he was begotten Son from the beginning, Son of the Father, like in all things to his Genitor, begotten Life of Life, Light of Light, Truth of Truth, Wisdom of Wisdom, King of King, God of God, Power of Power.
Commentary on Isaiah

From this point the Prophet relates what the Lord has spoken: that the people of Israel, whom he had created as servants under the common law, he changed into sons, and said: Israel is my firstborn son. Then too the Lord in the Gospel promises the Apostles that if they do his will he will no longer call them servants but friends (John 15:15). But if Israel should grow proud on hearing that he is the firstborn, let him understand that he is called firstborn for this reason, that second sons are signified from among the nations. For he is not called only-begotten, which would exclude other brothers, but firstborn, to show that others too will follow; and yet, according to the mysteries of the Scriptures, it is not the firstborn who receive the inheritance but the second. Cain was the firstborn, but the gifts of Abel pleased God. Ishmael was the firstborn, but Isaac received the inheritance. Esau was the firstborn, but Jacob the supplanter snatched away the father's blessing. Reuben was the firstborn, but the blessing of the seed of Christ is nevertheless transferred to Judah. Thus they were first according to the order of calling, and were called the head; we, the second, who were called the tail, have been turned into the head and are called sons of God.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 3.2.1

We must also inquire who that being was of whom it is said in Exodus that he wished to kill Moses because he was setting out for Egypt. And afterwards, who is it that is called the "destroying angel," and who also is he who in Leviticus is described as Apopompeus, that is, the Averter, of whom the Scripture speaks thus: "One lot for the Lord, and one lot for Apopompeus"?
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 16: WHY THE ANGEL WHO WANTED TO KILL MOSES WAS APPEASED BY CIRCUMCISION

WHY DID THE ANGEL WHO WANTED TO KILL MOSES, IN THE ROUTE, BE APPEASED BY THE CIRCUMCISION OF HIS CHILD? — What Moses had done without taking counsel was corrected by the appearance of the threatening angel. Finally, when the angel saw being done what had been neglected through carelessness, he ceased from his wrath. Therefore Moses saw the angel so hostile against him and ready for punishment, because the fault of a man of high rank is a grave sin. For the more exalted his position is, the more serious is his offense. Therefore whatever is done by a man of highest standing, as the leader of the people, is a most bitter sin. He was going to the sons of Israel, sent by the God of Abraham, and he was not bearing the sign of Abraham’s righteousness, in which he knew the Jews took pride, so that he would either be called a deceiver, or not be considered sent by that same God who had chosen Abraham. For while living in Midian he had by no means circumcised his sons: whom he ought either not to have taken with him to Egypt, since he was going there to lead the others out; or certainly to have taken them circumcised, for the reasons we stated above. Therefore Zipporah, the wife of Moses, because Scripture speaks briefly, knowing well for what reason the angel appeared hostile to her husband, took a stone, circumcised her son, and the angel departed. For by that action the anger was softened by the same cause by which it had been kindled. Sometimes Scripture speaks in brief form, wanting things to be understood from the reasoning presented: just as in that passage where the Savior says among other things to the Jews, Why do you also transgress the commandment of God in order to establish your tradition? For God said, Honor your father and mother; and, Whoever curses father or mother, let him surely die. But you say, Whoever shall say to his father or mother, Whatever gift you might have had from me shall profit you, shall not honor his father or mother (Matt. 15:3–6). Without doubt the Savior said this in summary, so that the Jewish priests may be understood, in that, being devoted to greed, they despised the Law of God. For in sinful conspiracy they gave counsel to sons that, when they cursed father or mother, whatever they might offer as if a gift to God would dissolve the sentence previously given against those who curse: and therefore the sons, made secure, in defiance of God’s commandment despised their parents. So also Moses, when he saw the angel hostile to him, understanding the cause, showed his wife what ought to be done so that the angel who sought to kill him would depart from him. This is to be understood covertly in this case, just as in the passage we mentioned above concerning the priests.
LETTER 23

If I had been a Jew in the times of the ancient people, when there was nothing better to be, I would surely have accepted circumcision. That "seal of the justice of the faith" had so much power at that time, before it was rendered void by the coming of the Lord, that the angel would have strangled the infant son of Moses if his mother had not taken up a stone and circumcised the child and thus by this sacrament warded off his imminent destruction. This sacrament even tamed the river Jordan and reduced it to a brook. The Lord himself received this sacrament after birth, although on the cross he made it void.
ON BAPTISM 4.24.32

Why, therefore, was it commanded him that he should circumcise every male child in order on the eighth day, though it could not yet believe with the heart, that it should be counted unto it for righteousness, because the sacrament in itself was of great avail? And this was made manifest by the message of an angel in the case of Moses' son; for when he was carried by his mother, being yet uncircumcised, it was required, by manifest present peril, that he should be circumcised, and when this was done, the danger of death was removed. As therefore in Abraham the justification of faith came first, and circumcision was added afterwards as the seal of faith; so in Cornelius the spiritual sanctification came first in the gift of the Holy Spirit, and the sacrament of regeneration was added afterwards in the laver of baptism.
ON THE GRACE OF CHRIST AND ORIGINAL SIN 2.31.36

Now there was a forecast of His coming undoubtedly contained not only in other sacred institutions of the ancient Jews, but also in their circumcision of the foreskin. For the eighth day, in the recurrence of weeks, became the Lord's day, on which the Lord arose from the dead; and Christ was the rock whence was formed the stony blade for the circumcision; and the flesh of the foreskin was the body of sin.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

For Aaron also "met" Moses, and he went out of Egypt. But "he met" him where, in what kind of place? For it matters where "he meets" him—Moses, that is, whose mouth is to be opened by God. "He met him," he says, "in the mountain of God". You see that his mouth is deservedly opened, who is able to "meet in the mountain of God". Peter and James and John ascended the mountain of God, that they might be counted worthy to see Jesus transfigured and to see Moses with him and Elijah in glory. And you too, therefore, unless you ascend to "the mountain of God" and there "meet" Moses—that is, unless you ascend to the lofty sense of the law, unless you win your way up to the summit of spiritual understanding—your mouth is not opened by the Lord. If you stand in the lowly place of the letter and bind the text of the history to Jewish narratives, you have not met Moses "in the mountain of God", nor has God "opened your mouth" nor "instructed you in what you ought to speak". Unless, then, "Aaron had met Moses in the mountain", unless he had seen his lofty and arduous sense, unless he had discerned his exalted understanding, Moses would never have spoken to him the words of God, nor handed over to him the power of signs and wonders, nor associated him as a partaker of so great a mystery.

n: Went in alone. Aaron was substituted instead of the ancients, chap. iii. 16. --- Pharao Amasis, Cenchres, or Amenophis. (Usher.) --- Sacrifice, which is the principal part of a religious festival. (Menochius)
The Lord. Is there any one above me?
Upon us. They include themselves in the common danger, in case of disobedience; and they admonish the king respectfully, that there is no resisting the God of the Hebrews with impunity.
Get you. He knew not that Moses had been so long absent; and if he had known, he would not probably have treated him more mildly. (Haydock)
Increased, the edict against children being abrogated. (Menochius) --- He insists upon their labour being so intense and toilsome, as to thin their ranks.
Overseers, natives of Egypt, who had under them some Hebrews for task-masters, as the people were more willing to obey them, ver. 14.
Straw, beaten small and mixed with clay, to make brick and mortar. See Ezechiel xiii. 11, 15; Chardin, Perse ii. p. 76.
Idle. Thus the impious speak of those who consecrate any part of their time to the service of God: and thus Protestants often condemn the holy-days prescribed by the Catholic Church!
Lying words, alluding to the proposals of Moses. (Haydock) -- Let them not spend their time in idle conversation. (Calmet)
Straw. While some continued at the works, (Menochius) others went about the fields to gather up every grain of chaff and piece of straw which they could find.

And they, the officers of the children of Israel, established over their brethren, as the Hebrew more clearly insinuates, were scourged, or bastinadoed on the soles of the feet, as smaller faults are commonly punished in the East; (Calmet) or they were beaten also with rods, ver. 16. (Haydock)
Withal. Hebrew, "the fault is in thy own people," who require impossibilities. (Calmet) --- They throw the blame upon the king's officers, (Menochius) though it was his own. (Haydock)

Kill us. You are the occasion of our more cruel treatment. You have made the king have a bad opinion of us. Hebrew, "you have made our savour to be abhorred in the eyes of Pharao." So Jacob said, (Genesis xxxiv. 30,) you have made me stink or become odious. Those who attempt to do a kindness, unsuccessfully, often experience a similar ingratitude, chap. xiv. 11. (Menochius) --- It does not appear from the original, whether the officers or Moses was coming from the king's presence. They met in some appointed place. (Calmet)

Wherefore. These are not words of anger, but of earnest prayer. (St. Augustine, q. 14.) Moses does not attempt to satisfy the exasperated officers, but commits the whole to God. (Menochius) --- In great undertakings, there are commonly many difficulties; which ought not to discourage us. (Tirinus)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

But since it is a long matter to speak of each thing in order, let us see what "Moses and Aaron", "having gone in" to Pharaoh, say: "Thus says the Lord: let my people go, that they may serve me in the wilderness". Moses does not will that the people, while placed in Egypt, should serve the Lord, but that it should go out into the desert and there serve the Lord. This is without doubt what he shows: that so long as anyone remains in the dark deeds of the world and is engaged in the obscurity of affairs, he cannot "serve the Lord"; for he cannot "serve two masters", he cannot "serve the Lord and mammon". We must, therefore, go out of Egypt; the world must be forsaken, if we wish to "serve the Lord". But it must be forsaken, I say, not in place, but in mind; not by setting out on a journey, but by advancing in faith. Hear John saying these same things: "little children, do not love the world nor the things that are in the world; for all that is in the world is the desire of the flesh and the desire of the eyes".
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

But Pharaoh resists; "the ruler of these darknesses" does not wish to release you; he does not wish you to be drawn away from his darkness and led to the light of knowledge. And hear what he says: "who is he," he says, "whose voice I should hear? I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go". You hear what "the prince of this world" answers: he says that he does not know God. Do you see what raw pride does? So long as "he is not in the labors of men and is not scourged with men", for that reason pride held him fast. Then, a little later, you will see how much he profits under the scourges, how much better he is made when beaten. He who now says: "I do not know the Lord", afterward, when he has felt the force of the blows, is going to say: "pray the Lord for me"; and not only this, but even, when his own magicians testify, he will confess that "it is the finger of God" in the power of the signs. Let no one, then, be so untaught in divine discipline as to think the divine scourges a ruin, as to believe the blows of the Lord a punishing destruction. Behold Pharaoh too, most hardened; yet he profits when beaten. Before the blows he does not know the Lord; when beaten, he asks that the Lord be entreated for him. It is an advance under punishments to recognize this very thing—why you have deserved the punishment. "I do not know," then, he says, "the Lord, and I do not let Israel go". But see in the Gospels how, when beaten, he amends this saying. For it is written that the demons cried out to the Lord and said: "why have you come before the time to torment us? we know you, who you are: you are the Son of the living God". When they have felt the torments, they know the Lord. Before the scourges he says: "I do not know the Lord, and I do not let Israel go"; but he will both let Israel go, and not only let it go, but will himself urge it to go out. For there is no "fellowship of light with darkness"; no "part of the faithful with the unfaithful".
HOMILIES ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 65

Let us then become lowly, that we may be high. For most utterly doth arrogance abase. This abased Pharaoh. For, "I know not," he saith, "the Lord," and he became inferior to flies and frogs, and the locusts, and after that with his very arms and horses was he drowned in the sea. In direct opposition to him, Abraham saith, "I am dust and ashes," and prevailed over countless barbarians, and having fallen into the midst of Egyptians, returned, bearing a trophy more glorious than the former, and, cleaving to this virtue, grew ever more high. Therefore he is celebrated everywhere, therefore he is crowned and proclaimed; but Pharaoh is both earth and ashes. For nothing doth God so abhor as arrogance.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

And yet what does he say? Let us see how or how far he bids us set out from Egypt: "we will go," he says, "a journey of three days into the wilderness, and there we will sacrifice to the Lord our God". What is "the way of three days" which we must travel, that, going out from Egypt, we may be able to arrive at the place in which we ought to sacrifice? I understand that way to be he who said: "I am the way, the truth, and the life". This way must be traveled by us in three days. For whoever "shall confess with his mouth the Lord Jesus and shall believe in his heart that God raised him from the dead" on the third day, "shall be saved". This, then, is the "three days' way" by which one arrives at the place where one may sacrifice to the Lord and render "the sacrifice of praise". This, as far as pertains to the mystical understanding. But if we seek also the moral sense, which is most useful to us, we set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if we so preserve ourselves from every defilement of soul, body, and spirit that, as the Apostle said, "our spirit whole, and soul, and body, may be kept in the day of Jesus Christ". We set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if, taking away rational, natural, and moral wisdom from worldly things, we turn it to the divine ordinances; we set out "a three days' journey" from Egypt if, purifying in ourselves words, deeds, and thoughts—for these are the three by which men can sin—we are made "pure in heart", that we may be able to "see God". But do you wish to see that such are the things which the Holy Spirit indicates in the Scriptures? This Pharaoh, who is the prince of Egypt, when he sees himself more vehemently pressed to let the people of God go, in the second place desires to obtain this, "that they should not go far off", that they should not set out the whole three days, and he says: "do not go far off". He does not want the people of God to be made "far" from himself; he wants it, if not in deed, at least to sin in word; if not in word, at least to offend in thought. He does not want them to set out from him the whole three days. He wants to have at least one of his days in us; in others two, in others he possesses the whole three days. But blessed are those who withdraw from him the entire three days, and he possesses no day of his own in them. Do not think, then, that Moses led the people out of Egypt only at that time: now too Moses, whom we have with us—"for we have Moses and the prophets"—that is, the law of God, wishes to lead you out of Egypt; if you hear it, it wishes to make you "far" from Pharaoh; it desires to rescue you from the work of mud and straw, if only you hear the law of God and understand it spiritually. It does not want you to remain in the deeds of the flesh and of darkness, but to go out to the wilderness, to come to a place empty of the disturbances and waves of the world, to come to the quiet of silence. For "the words of wisdom are learned in silence and quiet". When, therefore, you come to this place of quiet, there you will be able "to sacrifice to the Lord", there to recognize the law of God and the power of the divine voice. For this reason, then, Moses desires to cast you out from the midst of tossing affairs and from the midst of clamoring peoples. For this reason he desires you to go out of Egypt, that is, out of the darkness of ignorance, that you may hear the law of God and receive the light of knowledge.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

But what does he yet add in his answers? "Why," he says, "O Moses and Aaron, do you turn my people away from their works? Depart, each one of you to your work". So long as the people is with him and works "mud" and "brick", so long as it is occupied in "straw", he does not think it perverted, but that it walks in the right path. But if it should say: I wish to go "the way of three days" and "to serve the Lord", he says that the people is perverted by Moses and Aaron. This indeed "was said to the ancients". But even today, if Moses and Aaron—that is, the prophetic and the priestly word—should rouse the soul to the service of God, invite it to go out of the world, to renounce all that it possesses, to give heed to the divine law and follow the word of God, immediately you will hear it said by those who are of one mind with Pharaoh and his friends: 'see how men are seduced and perverted—what young men, that they may not toil, may not do military service, may not do anything that would profit them, forsaking necessary and useful things pursue trifles and idleness. What is it to serve God? They do not wish to labor and seek occasions for slothful idleness.' These were the words of Pharaoh then, and these his friends and intimates speak now too.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

The matter is carried on not by words only; blows follow too—he orders the scribes of the Hebrews to be scourged, straw not to be given, the work to be exacted; these things the fathers endured, in the figure of whom the people of God also, which is in the Church, often suffers as well. For you will find, if you consider them, that those who have wholly handed themselves over to "the prince of this world" act with prosperous successes, that everything, as they themselves think, turns out happily for them; but that to the servants of God often not even these humble and small things of human sustenance turn out well. For these things I think seem to be the straw that is furnished by Pharaoh. It often happens, then, that those who fear God lack even this cheap sustenance, like straw; often too they endure the persecutions of tyrants, they bear tortures and savage torments, so that some, worn out, say to Pharaoh: 'Why do you afflict your people?' For some, overcome by the blows, fall away from the faith and confess themselves to be the people of Pharaoh. "For not all who are of Israel are Israelites; nor because they are the seed are they all sons as well".
LETTER 93

When both the good and the bad do the same things and suffer the same things, they are to be distinguished by their intentions, not by their acts and penalties. Pharaoh oppressed the people of God with hard labors; Moses afflicted the same people, who had fallen into idolatry, with severe punishments. They did the same things, but they did not aim at the same result. The former was puffed up with pride of power, the latter was animated by love.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

These, then, who are doubtful and are worn out in tribulations, even speak against Moses and Aaron and say: 'from the day you go in and go out to Pharaoh, you have made our odor abominable before him.' These men speak truly, though perhaps they know not what they say, just as that Caiaphas too spoke truly that "it is expedient for you that one man should die for the people", but he knew not what he was saying. For, as the Apostle says, we are the "good odor" of Christ; but, he says, "to some an odor from life unto life, but to others an odor from death unto death". So the prophetic word too is a "sweet odor" to those who believe, but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves to be the people of Pharaoh, it becomes an abominable odor.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 3

But Moses himself too says to the Lord: "from the time I spoke with Pharaoh, he has afflicted your people". For it is certain that, before the word of God is heard, before the divine preaching is made known, there is no tribulation, there is no temptation, because, unless the trumpet sound, battle is not joined; but when the trumpet of preaching has given the signal of war, there affliction follows, there all the fighting of tribulations rises up. From the time Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God is afflicted. From the time the word of God is brought into your soul, of necessity a struggle is stirred up within you, of the virtues against the vices; but before the word came which would rebuke, the vices endured within you in peace; but when the word of God began to make the distinction of each, then a great disturbance rises up and war is born without treaty. "For when can iniquity accord with justice", unchastity with sobriety, falsehood with truth? And therefore let us not be greatly disturbed if our "odor" seems to be abominable to Pharaoh; for virtue is a thing of abomination to the vices. Nay rather, as he says in what follows, that Moses stood "before Pharaoh", let us too stand "against Pharaoh" and not be bent nor bowed, but let us stand "girt about our loins in truth and our feet shod in the preparation of the gospel of peace". For thus the Apostle exhorts us, saying: "stand, therefore, and do not again cleave to the yoke of servitude". And again he says: "in which we stand, and glory in the hope of the glory of God". But we stand confidently if we beseech the Lord to "set our feet upon a rock", lest that befall us which the same prophet says: "but my feet were almost moved, and my steps were almost poured out". Let us stand, then, "before Pharaoh", that is, let us resist him in the struggle, as the Apostle Peter too says: "resist him, strong in faith". But Paul likewise says: "stand in faith and act manfully". For if we stand bravely, that too follows which Paul prays for his disciples, saying: "God will crush Satan under your feet speedily". For the more constantly and bravely we stand, the weaker and more feeble will Pharaoh be; but if we begin to be either weak or doubtful, he will become stronger and more constant against us. And truly that is fulfilled in us of which Moses gave a figure: for when he himself "lifted up his hands", Amalek was overcome; but if, as though they were weary, he "let them down" and laid low his feeble arms, "Amalek prevailed". So, then, let us too, in the power of the cross of Christ, lift up our arms and "raise up" in prayer "holy hands in every place without wrath and disputation", that we may deserve the help of the Lord. For this same thing the Apostle James too exhorts, saying: "but resist the devil, and he will flee from you". Let us act, then, with all faith, that Satan may not only "flee from us", but also "be crushed under our feet", just as Pharaoh too was sunk in the sea and extinguished in the deep of the abyss. But we, if we withdraw from the Egypt of the vices, will escape the waves of the world as though by a solid road, through Jesus Christ our Lord, "to whom is the glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".

n: Said, in answer to his prayer. --- Cast out, so eager he will be to have you dismissed, after he has repeatedly felt my hand, chap. iii. 19. (Haydock)

My name Adonai. The name which is in the Hebrew text, is that most proper name of God, which signifieth his eternal self-existing being, (Exodus iii. 14,) which the Jews, out of reverence, never pronounce; but instead of it, whenever it occurs in the Bible, they read Adonai, which signifies the Lord; and therefore they put the points or vowels, which belong to the name Adonai, to the four letters of that other ineffable name, Jod, He, Vau, He. Hence some moderns have framed the name Jehovah: unknown to all the ancients, whether Jews or Christians: for the true pronunciation of the name, which is in the Hebrew texts, by long disuse, is now quite lost. (Challoner) --- This name was first clearly revealed to Moses, that he might have confidence in his special protection and love. (Menochius) --- To know one by his name is to treat him with familiarity and distinction, Exodus xxxiii. 17. The pronunciation of the name of God might be known to Abraham, &c., but it was not so fully explained, nor the power and excellence of it declared in such a stupendous manner, as it was to Moses. (Du Hamel) --- Or perhaps Moses made use of this name in the history of the patriarchs, because he wrote his account of them after this revelation. (Calmet) --- The Septuagint always put Kurios, "the Lord," instead of the ineffable name; and our Saviour and his apostles, citing text where it occurs, follow their example. (Matthew iv. 7, 10; Romans xv. 11.) (Worthington) --- Philo informs us, that it was death to pronounce it out of the temple; and since that was destroyed, it has never been heard. (Calmet) --- Galatinus, who wrote in 1518, is supposed to have invented the word Jehovah, (see Amama Antib. p. 319,) the year after the pretended reformation began. (Haydock) --- St. Jerome (ep. 136 ad Marc.) explains the ten names of God, but never reads Jehovah. (Tirinus)
God, Elohim, who will pass sentence in your favour, as a just judge. (Menochius)
Hand; swearing. (Chap. xiv. 22; 2 Esdras. ix. 15.)
Anguish: Septuagint, "pusillanimity." They would not even hope for a change. (Menochius) --- The Samaritan copy records the speech which they made to Moses. (Kennicott, p. 313.)

Uncircumcised lips. So he calls the defect he had in his words, or utterance. (Challoner) --- The Hebrews call the heart, &c., uncircumcised, when it has any natural or moral defect, Acts vii. 15. (Tirinus) --- "I do not speak the language in its purity." Sym.[Symmachus?], "I express my sentiments with difficulty," chap. iv. 10. (Onkelos.)

These. From this place to ver. 26, is written in a kind of parenthesis: the remainder of the chapter is a recapitulation of what had been said. (Calmet) --- Moses intends to give his own genealogy, and the state of affairs when he began to afflict Egypt. (Haydock) --- He mentions three tribes, which Jacob had rebuked, lest any one might think they had forfeited their title to some distinctive tribes. (Menochius)
Levi died the last of his brethren, and Joseph the first. (Worthington)

Aunt: Hebrew Doda is applied to various degrees of kindred. The Chaldee says, Jochabed was daughter of Amram's sister, the Septuagint assert of his brother, and consequently his own cousin. But she might be his aunt, chap. ii. 1. (Calmet)
Nahason, prince of the tribe of Juda, Numbers i. 7. Observe the modesty of Moses, who passes over his own family almost in silence. (Menochius)
Aaron is sometimes placed first, as the elder; sometimes last, as inferior in dignity, ver. 27. --- Companies, or bands, in order of battle, chap. xiii. 18. (Calmet)

f: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF MATTHEW 14.1

For though there were three sons of Korah whose names we find in the book of Exodus—Aser, which is, by interpretation, "instruction," and the second Elkana, which is translated "possession of God," and the third Abiasaph, which in the Greek tongue might be rendered "congregation of the father"—yet the prophecies were not divided but were both spoken and written by one spirit and one voice and one soul, which worked in true harmony. And the three speak as one, "As the hart pants after the springs of the water, so pants my soul after you, O God."

n: The God of Pharao, viz., to be his Judge; and to exercise a divine power, as God's instrument, over him and people. (Challoner) --- Artapanus says, Moses was afterwards adored by the Egyptians. --- Prophet, or interpreter. Thou shalt reveal my orders to him. (Calmet) --- Moses participated in the divine nature, as judge, priest, prophet, &c. (Worthington)

I shall harden, &c.; not by being the efficient cause of his hardness of heart, but by permitting it; and by withdrawing grace from him, in punishment of his malice; which alone was the proper cause of his being hardened. (Challoner) --- He took occasion even from the miracles to become more obdurate. (Haydock) --- Yet Pharao was less impious than Calvin, for he takes the sin to himself, chap. ix. 27. (Tirinus)
Took, or "threw down," as the Hebrew and Septuagint read.

Magicians. Jannes and Mambres, or Jambres, 2 Timothy iii. 8. (Challoner) --- The pagans represented Moses as the greatest of magicians. (Pliny, Natural History xxx. 1; Justin xxxvi.) --- They also, &c. Hebrew has three terms: "wise men, diviners, and magicians;" but the two last seem to be of the same import. "The enchanters did the like by their secret practices," either by words or by actions. Some say these operations were real; others affirm they were only apparent, and mere delusions. (Calmet) --- "Whoever believes that any thing can be made, or any creature changed or transmuted into another species or appearance, except by the Creator himself, is undoubtedly an infidel, and worse than a pagan." (Council of Orange.) See St. Augustine, q. 21, de Trin. iii. 7; St. Thomas Aquinas, 2, 2, 9, 17, a 2. --- The devil deceived the senses of the beholders; or brought real serpents, &c., thither. (Menochius)
Devoured. Thus the superiority remained with Aaron. The rod was then restored to its pristine form, ver. 15. (Haydock)
My hand. The rod was in the hand of Moses, but he was God's agent. (Menochius)

River. The Samaritan copy repeats here the very words of God to Pharao, as the other speeches are also twice put at length. "Moses and Aaron went to meet Pharao, and said to him, 'The Lord,'" &c., as ver. 16, 18. See chap. xi. 7. (Calmet) --- This is very agreeable to the style of Homer; and Kennicott believes that the repetitions have been omitted in the Hebrew for brevity's sake, (Diss. 1 Chron. p. 383,) and that before the Greek version had been made. (Haydock)
All the land, even in that of Gessen, which belonged to the Egyptians; while the Hebrews had good water. (Menochius)

Like. They got a small quantity of water, either from the sea, from Gessen, (Wisdom xi. 5,) or by digging wells, ver. 24. (Calmet) --- This plague lasted a full week, ver. 25. The water which they found in the mean time in the wells was mixed with blood. (Philo; St. Augustine, in Psalm lxxvii.) Wisdom xi. 7, thou gavest human blood to the unjust.

f: On Cain and Abel 1.2.7

So also in Moses there was the figure of the future Teacher, who was to teach the law, preach the gospel, fulfill the old covenant, establish the new, give heavenly nourishment to the people, exceeding even human dignity to such an extent that he was given the name of God, as we have it written, with the Lord saying: 'I have made you like God to Pharaoh' (Exod. VII, 1). For he, the conqueror of all passions, not being captivated by any worldly allurements, who had, according to the purity of his heavenly demeanor, withdrawn all that conversation of his after the flesh from him, governing his mind, subjecting his flesh, and chastising it by a certain royal authority, was called by the name of God, after whose likeness he had formed himself by the abundance of perfect virtue.
Exposition of the Christian Faith 5.1.23

But if they think [Christ] is called God because he had an in-dwelling of the Godhead within him, as many holy men were (for the Scripture calls them gods to whom the word of God came)—they do not place him before other men but think he is to be compared with them. They consider him to be the same as he granted other men to be, even as he says to Moses: "I have made you a god unto Pharaoh." Similarly it is also said in the psalms: "I have said, you are gods."
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 34

And there are some who so dominate all vices and all desires within themselves that by the very right of their purity they are called gods among men; whence also it is said to Moses: "Behold, I have made you a god to Pharaoh." Where then do these run except among the numbers of Dominations? For since that heavenly city consists of angels and men, to which we believe the human race ascends in such number as equals the elect angels who remained there, we too ought to draw something from those distinctions of the heavenly citizens for the use of our own way of life, and inflame ourselves with good pursuits toward growth in virtues. For the different ways of life of men correspond distinctly to the orders of individual hosts, and they are assigned to their lot through similarity of life.
The Stromata Book 3

On the same basis, you would not be able to point to anyone of the past generations approaching a pregnant woman in the pages of Scripture. Only later, after the birth and weaning of the child, would you again find the wives in physical relations with their husbands. You will find that Moses' father observed this point. He left a three-year gap after Aaron's birth before fathering Moses.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 4

The narrative that has been read to us is indeed most renowned, and, by reason of its greatness, is known to the whole world; through it is signified how Egypt, together with king Pharaoh, was chastised by the mighty blows of signs and wonders, so that it might restore to its native liberty the Hebrew people, which, though born of free forefathers, it had "by violence" reduced to servitude. But the account of these deeds is so interwoven that, if you inspect the several details carefully, you will find more matters in which the understanding sticks fast than in which it can extricate itself. And because it is a long task to set forth each thing said by Scripture in its order, let us review the substance of the whole history in a more compendious way. So then, at the first sign "Aaron cast down his rod, and it became a dragon"; and the enchanters and sorcerers of the Egyptians were summoned, and "they did likewise" out of their rods, making dragons. But the dragon that had been made from Aaron's rod swallowed up the dragons of the Egyptians. And whereas this ought to have caused Pharaoh astonishment and to have profited toward belief, it was turned to the contrary. For Scripture says that: "the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, and he did not hearken to them". And here indeed it says that "the heart of Pharaoh was hardened"; but no less in the first plague also, where the water is turned into blood, it is written in like manner, and in the second when the frogs bubble up, and also in the third when the gnats come on; in the fourth too when the dog-fly is brought forth, and in the fifth, where "the hand of the Lord comes upon the cattle" of the Egyptians, things equal and similar are said on this point. But in the sixth, where Moses "took ashes of the furnace" "and sprinkled them, and there arose sores and burning blisters upon men and upon the four-footed beasts, and now the sorcerers could not stand in the presence of Moses", it is not said that the heart of Pharaoh was hardened, but something more terrible is added; for it is written that: "the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh, and he did not hear them, even as the Lord had appointed". Again in the seventh, when hail and fire lay waste all Egypt, "the heart of Pharaoh" is indeed "hardened", but not by the Lord. But in the eighth, where the locust is brought forth, "the Lord" is said "to harden the heart of Pharaoh". And in the ninth also, when "palpable darkness comes over the whole land of Egypt", "the Lord" is written "to harden the heart of Pharaoh". And at the very last too, when, the firstborn of the Egyptians having been destroyed, the Hebrew people had departed, after many things it is thus said: "and the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt and of his servants, and he pursued after the children of Israel". Moreover, when Moses is sent from the land of Midian to Egypt and is commanded "to do all the wonders which the Lord had put into his hands", it is added: "thou shalt do them", he says, "in the presence of Pharaoh. But I will harden the heart of Pharaoh, and he will not let the people go". Here first it was said by the Lord: "I will harden the heart of Pharaoh". And a second time also, where the princes of Israel have been enumerated, after a little he adds in the person of the Lord: "I", he says, "will harden the heart of Pharaoh, and I will multiply my signs".

But if we believe these letters to be divine and written by the Holy Spirit, I do not think that we should feel so unworthily of the divine Spirit as to suppose that in so great a work this variation was made by chance — that now indeed God is said to have "hardened the heart of Pharaoh", but now it is said to have been hardened not by God, but as it were of its own accord. For my part, I confess myself too little fit and too little capable to be able to search out the secrets of the divine wisdom amid variations of this kind. Yet I see Paul the Apostle, who, because of the Spirit of God dwelling in him, dared to say with confidence: "but to us God has revealed it through his Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God". — him, I say, I see, as one understanding what difference there is between "the heart of Pharaoh being hardened" and "the Lord having hardened the heart of Pharaoh", saying elsewhere indeed: "or dost thou despise the riches of his goodness and forbearance and long-suffering, not knowing that the patience of God leads thee to repentance? But according to thy hardness and impenitent heart thou treasurest up for thyself wrath against the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God"; whereby without doubt he blames him who has been hardened of his own accord. But elsewhere, as though proposing a certain question upon this matter, he says: "therefore on whom he will he has mercy, and whom he will he hardens. Thou wilt then say to me: why then does he yet complain? For who shall resist his will?". He adds also to these: "O man, who art thou that repliest against God?". Whereby concerning him who is said to be hardened by the Lord he answers, I believe, not so much by the resolution of the question as by Apostolic authority, not judging it worthy, because of the incapacity of his hearers, to commit the secrets of resolutions of this kind to "paper and ink"; just as in another place also he himself says concerning certain words that he had "heard" certain things "which it is not lawful for men to speak". Whence too in what follows he deters, with the severity of a great teacher, the man who, not so much by the merit of his studies as by a craving to know, plunges himself curiously into more hidden questions, when he says: "O man, who art thou that repliest against God? Does the thing formed say to him who formed it: why hast thou made me thus?" and the rest. Whence for us too let it suffice only to have observed and inspected these things, and to have shown our hearers how great are the mysteries plunged in the depths of the divine law, on account of which we ought to say in prayer: "out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O Lord".

But that observation too seems to me to be no less worthy of consideration, that certain blows are said to be inflicted upon Pharaoh or upon Egypt by Aaron, certain by Moses, and certain by the Lord himself. For in the first plague, when "he turned the waters into blood", Aaron is said to have lifted up the rod and to have struck the water. And in the second also, when he struck the waters "and brought forth frogs", and in the third, when "he stretched out the rod with his hand and struck the dust of the earth, and there were gnats". In these three blows there was the ministry of Aaron. But in the fourth the Lord is said to have done it, so that "the dog-fly should come" and fill "the houses of Pharaoh". And in the fifth also, when "the cattle of the Egyptians are destroyed", the Lord no less is said to have done "this thing". But in the sixth Moses "sprinkles ashes of the furnace, and there arise sores and blisters with burning upon men and cattle". And in the seventh too "Moses lifts up his hand to heaven", and there arise "thunders and hail, and fire runs about upon the earth". In the eighth likewise the same Moses stretches out his hand to heaven, "and the Lord brings a wind all that day and all that night", and brings the locusts. And in the ninth also the same "Moses stretches out his hand to heaven, and there arise darkness and gloom over all the land of Egypt". But in the tenth the end and completion of the whole work is administered by the Lord. For thus it is written: "and it came to pass about midnight, and the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat upon the throne, unto the firstborn of the captive woman who is in the pit, and every firstborn of the cattle".

There is also another difference in these matters, which we have observed: that in the first plague indeed, when the water flows into blood, it is not yet said to Moses that he should go in to Pharaoh, but it is said to him: "go to meet him at the bank of the river, when he comes out to the water". But in the second plague, after the first had been ministered by them constantly and faithfully, it is said to him: "go in to Pharaoh", and going in he says: "thus says the Lord", and the rest. But now in the third, where the gnats are brought on, the magicians, who had before withstood, yield, confessing that "this is the finger of God". In the fourth too Moses is bidden to "rise early in the morning and to stand before Pharaoh as he goes forth to the water", when the houses of the Egyptians are filled with the dog-fly. In the fifth no less, where the cattle of the Egyptians are destroyed, "Moses is bidden to go in to Pharaoh". In the sixth, however, Pharaoh is despised, and it is not related that Moses or Aaron went in to Pharaoh, because "there arose sores and blisters with burning even upon the sorcerers of Egypt, and they could not withstand Moses". In the seventh he is bidden to "rise very early in the morning and to stand before Pharaoh", when he brings forth hail and fire and thunders. In the eighth he is commanded to go in to him, when the locust is brought forth. In the ninth again Pharaoh is despised, and "Moses is commanded to stretch out his hand to heaven, that there may be darkness over all the land of Egypt, palpable darkness", and indeed he does not go in, but is called to Pharaoh. Likewise also in the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed and he is compelled with haste to go out from Egypt. There are also very many other observations, in each of which the tokens of the divine wisdom are shown. For you will find that at first Pharaoh is not bent nor yields to the divine blows, when the waters have been turned into blood. But in the second he seems to be somewhat softened: for "he called", it says, "Moses and Aaron, and said to them: pray for me to the Lord, and let him take away the frogs from me and from my people, and I will let the people go". In the third the magicians yield and say to Pharaoh: "this is the finger of God". In the fourth, beaten by the dog-fly, he says: "go, sacrifice to the Lord your God, but you shall not go too far on your way. Pray therefore for me to the Lord". In the fifth, where he is smitten by the slaying of the cattle, he not only does not yield, but is hardened all the more. Likewise also in the sixth he does the same over the plague of sores. But in the seventh, when he is laid waste by hail and by fires: "Pharaoh sent", it says, "and called Moses and Aaron and said to them: I have sinned even now; the Lord is just, but I and my people are ungodly. Pray therefore for me to the Lord". In the eighth, when he is pressed by locusts: "and Pharaoh hastened", it says, "and called Moses and Aaron, saying: I have sinned before the Lord your God and against you. Take away my sin even now, and pray to the Lord your God". In the ninth, when he is covered with darkness: "Pharaoh called", it says, "Moses and Aaron, saying: go, serve the Lord your God". But now in the tenth, when the firstborn of men and of the cattle are destroyed: "Pharaoh called", it says, "Moses and Aaron by night and said to them: arise and go out from my people, both you and the children of Israel; go, serve the Lord your God, as you say: and taking your sheep and your oxen, depart, as you have said. But bless me also. And the Egyptians urged the people to go out of the land of Egypt as quickly as possible. For they said: we shall all die".

Who is he whom God may fill with that Spirit with which he filled Moses and Aaron, when they were accomplishing these wonders and signs, so that, illumined by the same Spirit, he might be able to expound the things done through them? For otherwise I do not think that these varieties and differences of mighty matters can be explained, unless they are expounded by the same Spirit by which they were done, since Paul the Apostle too says that: "the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets". Not therefore to any persons whatsoever are the sayings of the prophets said to be "subject" for their explanation, but "to the prophets". But since the same blessed Apostle bids us become imitators of this grace, that is, of the prophetic gift, as being in some part and within our power, saying: "but be zealous for the better gifts, and rather that you may prophesy", let us too attempt to take up a zeal for good things and to exert whatever is in us, but to await from the Lord the fullness of the gift. For with regard to the one it is said by the Lord through the prophet: "open thy mouth, and I will fill it", but with regard to the other another Scripture says: "prick the eye, and it brings forth a tear; prick the heart, and it brings forth understanding". Let us not therefore out of despair give ourselves over to silence, which certainly does not edify the Church of God; but let us briefly go back over the things of which we are able and in so far as we are able.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 4

But now, if the moral figure too is to be treated by us, we shall say that every soul in this world, while it lives in errors and in ignorance of the truth, is placed in Egypt. If the law of God begins to draw near to this soul, it turns its waters into blood, that is, it converts the fluid and slippery life of youth to the blood of the old or new testament. Then next it draws out of it the vain and empty talkativeness and the frog-like complaint against the providence of God. It also purges its malignant thoughts and shakes off the stings of craftiness like the biting of the gnats. It drives away too the bites of lusts like the darts of the dog-fly, and destroys in it the folly and the understanding like the cattle's; through which "man, when he was in honor, did not understand, but was compared to the senseless beasts of burden and became like unto them". It convicts also its sores of sins, and extinguishes the swelling of arrogance and the burning of fury in it. After these it applies also the voices of the "sons of thunder", that is, the evangelical and apostolic teachings. And it brings to bear also the chastisement of hail, that it may restrain luxury and pleasures. It applies at the same time also the fire of repentance, so that it too may say: "did not our heart burn within us?" Nor does it withdraw from it the examples of the locusts, by which all its restless and turbulent motions may be bitten and fed upon, so that it too may learn what the Apostle teaches: "that all its things may be done according to order". But when it has been sufficiently chastised as to its morals and constrained toward the correction of an amended life, when it has perceived the author of the blows and has now begun to confess that "it is the finger of God", and has received some little of recognition, then especially does it see the darkness of its own deeds, then does it feel the gloom of its own errors. And when it has come to this, then will it deserve that the firstborn of Egypt be extinguished in it. In which I think something of this sort can be understood: every soul, when it has come to the completion of its age and, as it were, a certain natural law in it has begun to defend its own rights, without doubt produces first the motions according to the desire of the flesh, which the incentive force stirs up from the tinder of concupiscence or of anger. Whence, as of something special and not common with the rest of men, the prophet says concerning Christ alone: "he shall eat butter and honey; before he does or brings forth evil things, he shall choose the good, since, before the child knows good or evil", he resists malice, that he may choose that which is good. But another prophet, speaking as it were of himself, said: "remember not the sins of my youth and of my ignorance". Since therefore these first motions of the soul, produced according to the flesh, rush into sin, rightly in the moral sense the firstborn of the Egyptians will be set down, which are then extinguished, if the conversion of the remaining life directs a more amended course. Thus therefore in the soul, which the divine law, having taken it up from its errors, chastises and corrects, the firstborn of the Egyptians too are understood to be destroyed — unless after all these things it persists in unbelief and refuses to be joined to the Israelite people, so as to go out from the deep and escape unharmed, but remains in iniquity and goes down "like lead in the mightiest water". For iniquity, according to the vision of the prophet Zachariah, sits upon a talent of lead, and therefore he who remains in iniquity is said to be sunk "like lead" into the deep. Indeed, as to what we observed above, that certain wonders were ministered through Aaron, certain through Moses, and certain through the Lord himself, they can be understood thus far, that we recognize that in certain things we are to be purged through the sacrifices of the priests and the intercessions of the pontiffs, which the person of Aaron designates; but in certain things we are to be amended through the knowledge of the divine law, as the office of Moses designates; but in others, without doubt those which are more difficult, we have need of the power of the Lord himself.

But neither is that to be thought to have been observed by us in vain, that at first indeed Moses does not go in to Pharaoh, but meets him as he goes out to the waters, but afterward goes in to him, and after this does not go in, but is summoned and approaches. And in this too I think it can be understood thus: that whether we have a contest against Pharaoh in the word of God and the assertion of religion, or whether we also strive to snatch souls besieged by him out of his power and there is for us a wrestling in disputation, we ought not at once at the very front to enter into the ultimate places of the questions, but we must meet the adversary, and meet him at his waters; for his waters are the authors of the Gentile philosophers. There therefore, when we first wish to dispute, he must be met, so that we may convict them and teach that they too have erred. After this we must now enter even into the inner parts of the contest. For the Lord too says: "unless one first binds the strong man, he cannot go into his house and plunder his goods". First therefore the "strong man" must be bound by us and constrained with the bonds of the questions, and thus we must go in to plunder "his goods" and to free the souls which he had possessed by the fraud of deception. And when we have done this rather often and have stood against him — and we have stood in that manner in which the Apostle says: "stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth", and again: "stand in the Lord, and act manfully" — when therefore we have stood in this manner against him, that ancient and crafty artificer will feign even to be conquered and to yield, if perchance through this he may make us more negligent for the contest. And he will feign repentance too and will beseech us indeed to depart, but not to depart far. He wishes us to be in some part near to him, he wishes us not to depart far from his borders. But unless we withdraw farther from him and pass over the sea and say: "as far as the east lies from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us", we cannot be saved. Wherefore let us beseech the mercy of the Lord, that he too may snatch us out of the land of Egypt, out of the power of darkness, and may sink Pharaoh with his army "like lead in the mightiest water". But let us, being freed, with joy and exultation sing a hymn "to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored", because to him is "honor and glory unto the ages of ages. Amen".
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 4

I think therefore, so far as I am able to perceive, that Moses coming to Egypt and bearing the rod with which he chastises and beats Egypt with ten plagues — this Moses is the law of God, which has been given to this world, that it may correct and amend it with ten plagues, that is, with the ten commandments which are contained in the Decalogue; but the rod, through which all these things are wrought, through which Egypt is subdued and Pharaoh is overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which this world is conquered and "the prince of this world" with his principalities and powers is triumphed over. And that the rod, when cast down, becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians, who had done "likewise" — that the serpent is put for wisdom or prudence the Gospel word indicates, when it says: "be prudent as serpents", and elsewhere: "the serpent was more prudent than all the animals and beasts that were in paradise". The cross of Christ, therefore, whose preaching seemed "foolishness", which Moses, that is the law, contains, as the Lord said: "for he wrote of me" — this cross, I say, of which Moses wrote, after it was cast down upon the earth, that is, after it came to the belief and faith of men, was turned into wisdom, and into so great a wisdom that it should devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world. For behold how "God made foolish the wisdom of this world", after he manifested "Christ, who was crucified, to be the power of God and the wisdom of God", and now the whole world has been caught by him who said: "catching the wise in their own craftiness".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 8: ON THE SERPENT MOSES MADE BEFORE PHARAOH

THERE WAS NO OTHER SIGN THAT MOSES PERFORMED OPENLY BEFORE PHARAOH EXCEPT THE SERPENT (Exod. 7:10) — Whoever considers this blameworthy should say what else ought to have been done. For indeed he made a serpent, which both inspired terror yet did not harm, because it is somewhat slow to injure due to a certain stupor. For if he had made a lion, or a bear, or something of that sort, how would those present have escaped? He did not wish to kill anyone, but only to instill fear and to show power; so that since the first transgression began through a serpent, in like manner the calling to mind of the knowledge of God and the correction of conduct might come through the sign of a serpent, so that as sin came about, so it might also be corrected. Just as sin came through a woman, so it was taken away through a woman, namely Mary, the Mother of the Lord, from whom Christ was born and condemned sin. Eve was still a virgin when she transgressed, just as Mary was a virgin. In this way, therefore, the things that had perished were recalled to their former state: for the kingdom too had been lost through the tasting of wood, and again through wood it was sought. For “the Lord,” it is said, “reigned from the tree” (Ps. 95:10). In a similar way, the world in which it was made, in it also must be reformed, that is, at the beginning of the first month, which is Passover. Therefore no nature will be evil except transgression alone; since sin has been corrected through that by which it was also committed.
On the Duties of the Clergy 3.15.94

He cast down his rod, and it became a serpent which devoured the serpents of Egypt. This signified that the Word should become flesh to destroy the poison of the dread serpent by the forgiveness and pardon of sins. For the rod stands for the Word that is true, royal, filled with power and glorious in ruling. As the rod became a serpent, so he who was the Son of God begotten of the Father became the Son of man born of a woman. Like the serpent, he was lifted up on the cross, poured his healing medicine on the wounds of humanity. Wherefore the Lord himself says, "As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up."
LETTER 137

We read that the magicians of the Egyptians were very skilled in those arts, but they were outdone by Moses, the servant of God. Yet when they performed certain wonders by their forbidden arts, he overturned all their trickery by simply calling on God.
City of God 10.8

The magicians of Pharaoh, the king of Egypt who was tyrannizing over this people, were permitted to accomplish certain wonders merely that they might be outdone by more genuine miracles. These magicians worked by the kind of sorceries and incantations to which evil spirits or demons are addicted, while Moses was powerful by his holiness and helped by the angels, and so, in the name of God, creator of heaven and earth, he easily triumphed over them.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 4

But that the waters of the river are turned into blood is fitted suitably enough. First indeed, so that that river, to which they had handed over the little ones of the Hebrews by cruel slaughter, might render to the authors of the crime a cup of blood, and that by drinking they might feel the gore of the polluted flood, which they had stained with parricidal killing. Then next, so that nothing might be lacking to the allegorical laws also, the waters are turned into blood and its own blood is given to Egypt to drink. The waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of the philosophers; because these have deceived all who are little ones in perception and children in understanding, when the cross of Christ showed the light of truth to this world, they are required to pay the penalties of their slaying and the guilt of blood. For thus also the Lord himself says that: "all the blood which has been shed upon the earth, from the blood of Abel the just unto the blood of Zachariah, shall be required of this generation".
LETTER 143

You asked … how, when all the water of Egypt was turned into blood, the magicians of Pharaoh found any [water] with which they could transform in like manner. This difficulty is usually solved in two ways. They did it either because some sea water could be brought or, what is more likely, because in that part of the country where the children of Israel were those plagues did not take place. In certain passages of that Scripture this is very clearly expressed, and it warns us what is to be understood even when it is not expressed.

n: Frogs, not by a new creation; but the spawn was miraculously brought to maturity. (Calmet) --- Angels, or a divine instinct, brought them to infest all places; and thus they became a more grievous plague than that of blood. (Menochius)

Servants. The Abderites and Dardanians were formerly obliged to abandon their country by such a plague. (Orosius iii. 23; Pliny, Natural History viii. 29.) (Calmet) --- Here the Samaritan copy adds, that Moses delivered this message to Pharao. (Haydock)
Frogs, few in number, and brought by the ministry of devils. (Menochius)

Pray ye to the Lord, &c. By this it appears, that though the magicians, by the help of the devil, could bring frogs, yet they could not take these away: God being pleased to abridge in this the power of Satan. So we see they could not afterwards produce the lesser insects; and in this restraint of the power of the devil, were forced to acknowledge the finger of God.

A time. Moses thus prevents the king from attributing their departure to natural causes. Pharao was perhaps inclined to suspect this would be the case, and therefore had a mind to wait till the morrow. (Menochius)
Corrupted. This helped to produce the ensuing plague of flies, &c. (Calmet) --- The Egyptians might then recollect the putrid carcasses of the children, whom they had drowned. (Haydock)

Pharao hardened his own heart. By this we see that Pharao was himself the efficient cause of his heart being hardened, and not God. See the same repeated in ver. 32, Pharao hardened his heart at this time also; likewise chap. ix. 7, 35, and chap. xiii. 15. (Challoner) --- This is the constant doctrine of the holy fathers, St. Augustine, ser. 88, de Temp. q. 18, 28, 36; St. Basil, orat., "that God is not the author of evil;" St. Chrysostom, hom. 67, in Jo.; &c. Hence Origen, periar. 3, says, "The Scripture sheweth manifestly that Pharao was hardened by his own will; for God said to him, thou wouldst not: if thou wilt not dismiss Israel." Even the priests of the Philistines were so well convinced of this, that they said, (1 Kings vi. 6,) Why do you harden your hearts? God therefore hardened them only by not absolutely hindering their wickedness, and by punishing them with less severity, as they did not deserve to be corrected like dear children, Hebrews xii. --- Perdition is from thyself, Osee xiii. 9. As cold naturally congeals water, so we of ourselves run to evil. Thus God cast Pharao into the sea, by permitting, not by forcing, him to enter, Exodus xv. 4. How shocking must then the blasphemous doctrine of Zuinglius, (ser. de provid. 5,) Calvin, (Instit. 8, 17,) &c., appear, who attribute every wicked deed to God, though they pretend at the same time that he is not unjust, even when he commands and impels a man to commit murder or adultery. Idem facinus puta adulterium...quantum Dei est auctoris, motoris, impulsoris opus est, crimen non est; quantum hominis est, crimen ac scelus est. (Zuinglius, sup.) The light of reason may suffice to confute such absurdity. (Worthington)

Sciniphs, or Cinifs, Hebrew Cinnim, small flying insects, very troublesome both to men and beasts. (Challoner) --- Like midges. (Origen, hom. 4.) Others think they were lice. (Bochart) Pharao is not forewarned of this plague.

Practiced, fecerunt; the same expression as ver. 7: whence some argue, that the former were delusions, not real changes. (Haydock) --- God was pleased to shew here the vanity of their attempts, and the imbecility of the devil, who could not even bring a single animalcule or insect, though he had before appeared to work great wonders. (Tirinus)

Finger, the spirit, (Luke xi. 20; compare Matthew xii. 28,) or power of God, Isaias xl. 12. The magicians here confess, that Moses is something more than themselves. (Calmet) --- Thus God interferes, whenever a contest of miracles, real or apparent, might lead any sincere seeker astray. He caused the priests of Baal to be confounded; (3 Kings xix,) and Simon Magus, flying in the air, was hurled down at the prayer of St. Peter. (Hegesip.) Cyrola, the Arian patriarch, attempting to deceive the people, by giving sight to a man whom he bribed to feign himself blind; and Calvin, who wished to have the honour of raising a man to life, at Geneva, by the like imposition, were both deservedly covered with confusion; while, of those unhappy men who joined in the collusion, one lost his sight, and the other his life. (Gregory of Tours, ii. Hist. 3; Bolsec.) On such occasions, we are admonished to be on our guard, and to adhere to the old religion. (Deuteronomy xiii.; Matthew xxiv.) (Worthington) --- The magicians, though fully convinced, were not still converted.

Flies. Hebrew heharob. Septuagint, "dog-flies." Some include under this plague all sorts of wild beasts. (Josephus, [Antiquities?] ii. 13; Wisdom xi. 9, 16, 18.) Insects are very troublesome, and the pagans honoured Jupiter with the title of Apomuios, because he delivered them from flies. Beelzebub, "the god-fly," got his name for the same reason, 4 Kings i. 1. (Calmet)
Gessen, where the Hebrews dwelt. The Egyptians who lived among them would not, however, escape this plague.
Be. Here again the Samaritan copy observes, that Moses told this to Pharao. (Haydock)

The Lord, without the intervention of the rod, lest any inherent power might be supposed to rest in it. (Menochius) --- Corrupted, ravaged; men and beasts being destroyed by their bite or sting. (Psalm lxxvii. 45; Wisdom xvi. 9.)

The abominations, &c. That is, the things they worship for gods: oxen, rams, &c. It is the usual style of the Scriptures to call all idols and false gods, abominations; to signify how much the people of God ought to detest and abhor them. (Challoner) --- The Egyptians adored the stars, and even the vilest creatures, on account of some advantage which they derived from them. (Cicero, N. Deor. i.) They sometimes sacrificed animals; though, at first, "they offered only prayer and incense." (Macrobius, Satur. i. 7; Genesis xliii. 16.) Their belief in the transmigration of souls, perhaps, induced them to abstain from the immolation of beasts. (Calmet)
Hardened. Hebrew and Septuagint, "Pharao hardened his heart this time also." (Menochius)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 4

But by the second plague, in which the frogs are brought forth, I judge that the songs of the poets are figuratively indicated, who, by a certain empty and inflated modulation, like the sounds and songs of frogs, have brought upon this world the fables of deception. For that animal is useful for nothing else except that it renders the sound of its voice with wicked and importunate clamors.
ON PRAYER 3.2-3

One should also observe that the term prayer,which often differs in meaning from "invocation," is here employed in the case of one who promises in a vow to do certain things if God grants him certain other things. But the term is also used in the ordinary way. For example, we found this to be so in Exodus after the description of the plague of the frogs, which was the second of the ten plagues: … "But Pharaoh called Moses and Aaron and said to them: 'Pray to the Lord on my account to take away the frogs from me and my people; and I will let the people go to sacrifice to the Lord.' " When Pharaoh employs the word prayer the habitual meaning of "prayer" is conveyed in addition to the above meaning. If anyone finds this difficult to see, it becomes clear in what follows, namely: "And Moses said to Pharaoh: 'Set me a time when I shall pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, that the frogs may be driven away from you and from your house and from your people, and may remain only in the river.' "We noted, however, that in the case of the sciniphs, the third plague, Pharaoh does not ask that prayer be made, nor does Moses pray. And in the case of the flies, the fourth plague, he says, "Pray therefore for me to the Lord." And then Moses said, "I will go out from you and will pray to the Lord. And the flies shall depart from Pharaoh, and from his servants, and from his people tomorrow." And a little further on we read: "So Moses went out from Pharaoh and prayed to God." Again in the case of the fifth and also of the sixth plague Pharaoh did not ask that prayer be made, nor did Moses pray. In the seventh plague "Pharaoh sent and called Moses and Aaron, saying to them, 'I have sinned this time. The Lord is just, but I and my people are wicked. Pray to the Lord, that the thunderings of God and the hail and the fire may cease.' " And a little further on we read: "And Moses went from Pharaoh out of the city and stretched forth his hands to the Lord; and the thunders … ceased." We shall discuss more suitably at another time why it is not said as on the previous occasions that "he prayed" but rather that "he stretched forth his hands to the Lord." And in the case of the eighth plague Pharaoh says, "And pray to the Lord your God, that he take away from me this death. And Moses going forth from the presence of Pharaoh, prayed to the Lord."
On Cain and Abel 1.9.33

But Pharaoh, who was devoted to beliefs and vain superstitions (Egypt being filled with frogs, which produced empty sounds and noisy clamor), when Moses said to him: 'Appoint a time for me to pray for you, and for your servants, and for your people, so that the Lord may exterminate the frogs' (Exod. VIII, 9); though he should have been compelled by such great necessity to pray, and not delay any longer, he replied: 'Tomorrow'; idle and negligent, intending to destroy Egypt by incurring the punishment of delay.
