A graven thing, nor the likeness of any thing, &c. All such images or likenesses, are forbidden by this commandment, as are made to be adored and served; according to that which immediately follows, thou shalt not adore them, nor serve them. That is, all such as are designed for idols or image gods, or are worshipped with divine honour. But otherwise images, pictures, or representations, even in the house of God, and in the very sanctuary, so far from being forbidden are expressly authorized by the word of God. See Exodus xxv. 15, &c.; chap. xxxviii. 7; Numbers xxi. 8, 9; 1 Chronicles xxviii. 18, 19; 2 Chronicles iii. 10. (Challoner) --- Protestants insidiously translate "any graven image," though pesel, eidolon, glupton, and sculptile, in the Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, denote a graven thing or idol. They will, however, hardly condemn his majesty for having his representation stamped upon the coin of the nation, nor so many of our wealthy noblemen, who adorn their rooms with the choicest efforts of painting and of sculpture. They know that the object of prohibition is the making and adoring of idols. But they probably wish to keep the ignorant under the stupid delusion of supposing, that Catholics are idolaters, because they have images, and that they themselves are not, though they have them likewise at home; and even in their churches admit the absurd figures of the lion and the unicorn, stretching their paws over the tables of the law, instead of the pious representations of Jesus expiring on the cross, &c., which were set up by their Catholic ancestors. Let them read, and adopt herein just weights and measures, proposed to them by Thorndike, one of their most discerning and moderate teachers. In the mean time, we will assure them, that we abhor all idols; both those made with hands, and those which are formed by the head of heretics, who set up their own fancies and delusions, to be adored instead of the true God. Our general councils of Nice and of Trent define what we ought to believe on this head; and the matter is so fully explained in our catechisms and books of instruction, as well as from our pulpits, that no person can well remain in ignorance. If we perform various actions of respect before pictures, which are also done in honour of God, can any man of sense infer, that we look upon both with equal respect? Do we not read of the people falling down to shew respect to the king, and supreme worship to God, by the same act of the body? (Haydock) --- Altars and sacrifice we reserve solely for God, as St. Augustine (contra Faust. xx. 21,) well observes. Other indifferent practices must be determined by the intention. --- Latria, or supreme worship, can be given to none but the Deity. But we shew our respect and veneration for his servants in glory, by an inferior service called Dulia, giving honour to whom honour is due. How profane and impious must the words of the first reformers appear, who, after saying most falsely, that "papists make the Virgin Mary a god, (Luther. postil.) and worship images in heathenish manner," (Melanct. Loc. com.) attribute various fictitious crimes to the blessed Virgin and other saints! (Centuriators of Magdeburg; Calvin, &c.) They knew that all the saints abhorred their impiety; and therefore, in revenge, they vilify the saints, and condemn all the doctors and fathers of the Church, since the death of the apostles, as guilty of superstition and idolatry. (Haydock) --- "By this occasion, dead creatures, and bloodless half worm-eaten bones, began to be honoured, invocated, and worshipped with divine honour. All which the doctors of the Church not only winked at, but also set forward." (Centuriators of Magdeburg, C. vi.) What is then become of the promises of God, to teach all the truth by the mouths of his pastors? (Matthew xxviii, &c.) Let others judge, whether we ought to pay greater deference to Saints Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, &c., or to Luther, Calvin, and the Centuriators of Magdeburg. But some will even admit that images were commanded by God, chap. xxv. 18, &c. Hence they lay great stress upon the words to thyself; as if all images were forbidden that man should make, without the express sanction of God. So Parkhurst Lexic. But those who are conversant in Hebrew, know that these words have no such import; and if things were inseparable from idolatry, they could not be sanctioned by God. (Haydock) --- No creature must be represented as a deity. But sovereign worship, both internal and external, must be given to the great Author of all good, while we abstain from every superstitious act, and from all dealings with the devil and false religions. (Calmet) --- Protestants, therefore, who only forbid images, diminish God's law. Were not the idols of Chanaan, Chamos, &c., which represented nothing in nature, also condemned?

Adore. Protestants translate again, with the same view, as in the preceding verse, "thou shalt not bow down thyself to them," in condemnation of Catholics, who kneel before the cross. But do not they kneel, when they receive their sacramental bread, or when they ask for their parents' blessing? Did not St. John, and other saints, bow down out of respect to angels? And were these all idolaters! We are forbidden, therefore, to shew any respect to strange gods. But we must honour the true God in his saints, referring all the glory to him. (Haydock) --- Hate me. Those who do not imitate their wicked ancestors, need not fear being involved in their punishment. (Menochius) (St. Augustine, q. 42; St. Gregory, mor. 15. 22; St. Jerome in Ezechiel xviii.) --- Sometimes, indeed, God takes away the lives of children and of subjects, to punish the sins of parents and of kings; but this may be no real detriment to the deceased. (Haydock) --- Grotius thinks, that this menace is directed against idolaters. Others believe, it may be placed at the conclusion of each of the commandments. (Calmet)
In vain. On trifling occasions, rashly, or falsely. "Those who swear often, diminish their credit among the wise." (Philo)

Sabbath day, on which rest from servile work is prescribed, that we may worship God with greater fervour. Saturday was kept holy by the Jews, in honour of God's resting. The apostles have authorized us to keep Sunday instead, to commemorate the mysteries of Christ's resurrection, &c.
Six, &c. This must be understood if no festival of obligation occurred. For many were in force in the old law; such as the Passover, Encenia, Purim, &c., as there are still in the Church. (Haydock)

Stranger. Of some other nation. Good policy required, that all should conform to this regulation, whatever their religion might be. (Grotius) --- Maimonides says, without any probablility, that "a Gentile observing the law, was guilty of death. (Calmet)

Honour. Love, respect, feed, if requisite; support the infirmities of parents. See Numbers xxiv. 1; 1 Timothy v. 3, 17. They are ministers of God, in the production of children; and those who offer an affront to his minister, irritate God. (Philo) --- Land of Chanaan. The promises are of a temporal nature; but they should bring to our reflection the eternal rewards which attend the virtuous. The duties of parents are not specified, as nature would shew their extent, and as the obligations of parents and children are reciprocal. (Calmet)

Kill. These precepts are to be taken in their full extent, as prohibiting not only the ultimate act, but every thing which leads to it. Magistrates are authorized to inflict capital punishments. We are allowed also to defend ourselves against an unjust aggressor. But we must never intend to kill him. (Calmet) --- The laws will not condemn us, perhaps, if we do; but God sees the heart, and judges. A night thief may be slain, because we know not how far our own lives may be endangered, chap. xxii. 2. (Haydock)

Adultery. This precept is placed before the former one, in the Septuagint; St. Mark x. 19; and St. Luke xviii. 20. Adultery was punished with death, Leviticus xx. 10. All civilized nations have held it in abhorrence, as destructive of all peace, Job xxxi. 11. All other impure actions are forbidden, under different penalties.
Steal; by which name fraud of every description is condemned. Some have erroneously restrained this prohibition to the stealing of men for slaves, chap. xxi. 16. (Calmet)

False. Calumniators were subjected to the law of retaliation, and were forced, by the Egyptians and others, to undergo the same punishment, which they would have inflicted upon others. This law is the guardian of good faith and honesty in all our dealings. It is explained more in detail [in] chap. xxiii. 1, and Leviticus xix. 11.

House. Septuagint places wife first, as all do, Deuteronomy v. 21. The express prohibition of lustful and unjust desires, might suffice to have obviated the mistake of Josephus, and of the Jews, in our Saviour's time, who looked upon them as indifferent, provided they were not carried into effect. They render us guilty in the sight of God, (Matthew v. 28,) whenever we give consent to them, as even Ovid and the pagan philosophers acknowledged. (Grotius) --- At the conclusion of this 10th commandment, we find five verses in the Samaritan copy and version, as well as in the Arabic, and a sufficient vacant space is left in an ancient Syriac manuscript translated from the Hebrew, which induce Kennicott (Dis. 2. p. 97,) to conclude that they are genuine; particularly as they explain what law was to be engraven on the two stones set up by Josue, which the Hebrew leaves ambiguous. They are as follows, repeated, for the most part, Deuteronomy xxvii. 2. "And it shall come to pass, when the Lord thy God shall bring thee into the land of the Chanaanites, whither thou goest to possess it, then thou shalt set thee up great stones; and thou shalt plaster them with plaster, and shalt write upon the stones all the words of this law. --- And it shall come to pass, when ye are passed over the Jordan, ye shall put these stones, which I command you this day, upon Mount Gerizim. --- And thou shalt build there an altar to the Lord thy God, an altar of stones; thou shalt not lift up any iron tool upon them. --- Thou shalt build the altar of the Lord thy God of whole stones, and shalt offer thereon burnt-offerings to the Lord thy God, and shalt sacrifice peace-offerings; and thou shalt eat there, and rejoice before the Lord thy God. --- That mountain is on the other side Jordan, by the way where the sun goeth down, in the land of the Chanaanites, which dwell in the flat country over-against Gilgal, beside the plain of Moreh, near Sichem." This particular designation of Gerizim, makes Calmet suspect, that it is an interpolation of the Samaritans. But Kennicott hesitates not to lay the blame of omission upon the Jews; as he endeavours to shew, that they have corrupted Deuteronomy xxvii. 4, substituting Hebal, instead of Gerizim. "Certainly the Jews might omit, as easily as the Samaritans might insert." (p. 100.) (Haydock)

Saw. The Hebrews often substitute one organ of sense for another. (St. Augustine 9. 72; Jeremias ii. 30.) --- The Samaritan reads, "the people heard the thunders and the sound of the trumpet, and beheld the lightning." Henceforward till chap. xxiv., Moses and Aaron alone heard the voice of God; and the laws delivered, chap. xxv. to xxxi., were revealed to Moses only.
Die. The Samaritan copy inserts here what we read [in] Deuteronomy v. 24, 25, 26, 27.
Seen: no visible form; (Calmet) but I have spoken from the top of Sinai. (Haydock)
Make. Hebrew adds, "with me," ver. 3. This people was prone to idolatry, and stood in need of having the first commandment often inculcated. (Menochius)

Earth, which may be destroyed with ease, to prevent any profanation. --- Place. Where the tabernacle shall be fixed, you shall offer sacrifice, and I will hear you. The ark was afterwards deposited in the temple, where alone the Jews were, consequently, allowed to sacrifice. (Haydock) --- Samuel offered victims at Mespha and Ramatha, by the dispensation of God, 1 Kings vii. 9, 17. (Menochius)

Defiled; because done in opposition to God's order, who required, on this occasion, the utmost simplicity, to prevent any undue veneration. Iron was not used about the tabernacle or temple, as brass was more common. Altars raised in haste, like that, Deuteronomy xxvii. and Josue viii. 30, and that which was designed for the ratification of the covenant, (chap. xxiv. 4,) were required to be of this construction, unpolished and simple, as was the altar erected, 1 Machabees iv. 47. But other altars were not built after this model. (Calmet)

Steps. These were afterwards allowed in the temple, Ezechiel xliii. 17. The Egyptians made use of their pyramids for altars; and some suppose, that the high places of Juda were of a similar nature, and exposed the priests, who wore long robes without breeches, to the danger of being seen, chap. xxviii. 42. The steps allowed by God were therefore very low, and enclosed with boards, after the Greek fashion. Such were used by the priest and priestess of Jupiter. (Servius in Æneid iv. 646.) Linen breeches, or girdles, were afterwards required, Leviticus xxxix. 27. and Exodus xxviii. 42. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

Everyone who has learned to despise the present age, which "is figuratively called Egypt", and who through the word of God has—to speak according to the Scriptures—"been translated, and is not found", because he hastens and presses on toward the age to come: concerning a soul of this kind God says, "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt". These things, therefore, are not said only to those who set out from Egypt, but much more to you who now hear them, if only you set out from Egypt and no longer serve the Egyptians; to you God says these things: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage". See whether the affairs of the world and the deeds of the flesh are not a "house of bondage", just as, on the contrary again, to leave behind worldly things and to live according to God is a house of liberty, as the Lord also says in the Gospels: "if you abide in my word, you shall know the truth, and the truth shall set you free". Therefore Egypt is a "house of bondage", but Judaea and Jerusalem are a house of liberty. Hear also the Apostle proclaiming concerning these things "according to the wisdom which had been given to him in his ministry": "but the Jerusalem" he says "which is above is free, which is the mother of us all". Just as, therefore, Egypt, that earthly region, is called for the children of Israel a "house of bondage" in comparison with Judaea and Jerusalem, which are made for them a house of liberty, so in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is, so to speak, the mother of liberty, this whole world and all things that are in this world are a "house of bondage". And since from the paradise of liberty, as a penalty for sin, there had been a coming into the bondage of this world, for that reason the first utterance of the Decalogue, that is, the first voice of God's commandments, is brought forth concerning liberty, saying: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage". This voice, while set in Egypt, you could not hear, even if it be enjoined upon you to keep the Passover, even if you "gird your loins" and take "sandals on your feet", even if you hold "a staff in your hand" and "eat unleavened bread with bitterness". And why do I say that, set in Egypt, you could not hear these things? Nay, not even having set out from there could you hear these things at your very first halting-place, nor at the second, nor at the third, nor when you crossed the Red Sea; even if you come to Marah and the bitterness be turned for you into sweetness, even if you come to Elim to the "twelve fountains of waters and seventy palm trees", even if you pass Rephidim and ascend through the remaining stages, you are not yet judged fit for words of this kind—but only when you come to Mount Sinai. Therefore, after many labors have first been accomplished, after many hardships and temptations have been overcome, hardly at length will you be made worthy to receive the precepts of liberty and to hear from the Lord: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage". Yet this utterance is not yet the utterance of a commandment, but it shows who it is that commands. Now, therefore, let us see what is the beginning of the ten commandments of the law, and, if we do not reach them all, let us at least unfold the beginnings, according as the Lord may grant.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

The first commandment, then, is: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me". And after this there follows: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness, whatever things are in heaven above and whatever are in the earth below and whatever are in the waters under the earth; you shall not adore them nor worship them. For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God, who repay the sins of the fathers upon the sons, unto the third and fourth generation, upon those who hate me, and showing mercy unto thousands to those who love me and who keep my precepts". All these things together some suppose to be one commandment. But if it be so supposed, the number of ten commandments will not be filled out—and where then will be the truth of the Decalogue? But if it be divided in the manner in which we too distinguished it in the utterance above, the whole number of ten commandments will appear. Therefore the first commandment is: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me", and the second: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness", and the rest. Let us begin, then, with the first commandment. But I too have need of the help of the very God who gave these precepts, in order to speak, and you have need of purer ears in order to hear. If, therefore, any of you has "ears to hear", let him hear how it was said: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me". If he had said: there are no gods besides me, the utterance would seem more absolute. But now, since he says: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me", he did not deny that they exist, but he restrained them from being gods for him to whom these precepts are given. From this, I think, the Apostle Paul also took what he writes to the Corinthians, saying: "for even if there are those that are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth". And he adds: "as indeed there are many gods and many lords, but for us there is one God the Father, from whom are all things and we unto him, and one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and we through him". But in many other places of Scripture also you will find gods named, as there too: "for the Lord is most high, terrible, a great king over all gods", and: "the God of gods, the Lord, has spoken", and: "in the midst he distinguishes gods". Concerning lords the same Apostle says: "whether thrones, or dominions, or powers, all things were created through him and in him". But dominions are nothing other than a certain order and multitude of lords. In which, as it seems to me, the Apostle Paul made the sense of the law clearer. For what he says amounts to this: although there are "many lords" who rule over other nations, and "many gods" who are worshiped by others, "yet for us there is one" "God and one Lord". But what is the cause of there being "many gods" or "many lords", if you listen intently and patiently, Scripture itself will be able to teach us. For the same Moses says in the canticle of Deuteronomy: "when the Most High divided the nations" he says "and scattered abroad the sons of Adam, he set the bounds of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. And the Lord's portion became his people Jacob, the cord of his inheritance, Israel". It is established, then, that the angels to whom the Most High committed the nations to be governed are called either gods or lords: gods, as though given by God, and lords, as being those who received their power by lot from the Lord. Hence the Lord too said to the angels who did not keep their princedom: "I said: you are gods, and all sons of the Most High. But you shall die as men, and shall fall like one of the princes"—imitating, that is, the devil, who was made prince of all unto ruin. Hence it is established that transgression, not nature, made those accursed. To you, therefore, O people of Israel, who are "the portion of God", who have been made "the cord of his inheritance", he says: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me", because truly the "one God" is God and truly the "one Lord" is Lord. But upon the rest, who were created by him, he conferred that name not by nature, but by grace. Yet, lest you suppose these things are said only to that "Israel" which is "according to the flesh", much more are they said to you, who have been made Israel by seeing God in mind and have been circumcised in heart, not in flesh. For even if in the flesh we are Gentiles, in the spirit we are Israel, on account of him who said: "ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance and the ends of the earth for your possession", and on account of him who again said: "Father, all that is mine is yours and yours mine, and I have been glorified in these"—if only you so act that you may be worthy to be "the portion" of God and to be measured in "the cord of his inheritance". Otherwise, if you act unworthily, let those be an example to you who had been called to this, that they should be "the portion" of God, and by their sins earned this, that they should be "scattered among all nations". And those who had first been led out "from the house of bondage", now once again—because "he who sins is the slave of sin"—serve not the Egyptians alone, but all nations. Therefore it is said to you also, who through Jesus Christ came out of Egypt and were led out "from the house of bondage": "there shall be for you no other gods besides me".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 7: ON THE TEN WORDS OF THE TABLETS

WHAT ARE THE TEN WORDS GIVEN ON THE TABLETS; OR WHAT DID EACH TABLET CONTAIN, AND HOW MANY WORDS DID EACH HAVE? — He called ten sentences “ten words,” because the Savior also used the word “word” to mean a sense or meaning, when he said among other things to the Jews, I also ask you one word; answer me: the baptism of John, where was it, from heaven or from men? (Matt. 21:24). This sense he called a word. In a similar way, the ten words written on the two tablets are said to be ten meanings. Indeed, he says, You shall not have other gods besides me (Exod. 20:3): this is the first word. And he added the second, You shall not make for yourself any likeness in heaven above, or on the earth beneath, or in the water under the earth. (Exod. 20:4) Then he added the third, You shall not take the name of your God in vain. (Exod. 20:7) For the Lord will not cleanse him who takes his name in vain: that is, You shall not take the name of your God in a lie, so that you swear falsely by it. Then in the fourth place he says, You shall keep the sabbath of the Lord your God, (Exod.20:8) and you shall do no servile work on it. These four words properly belong to God, and are contained on the first tablet. The remaining are these: the first word is, Honor your father and your mother; the second, You shall not murder; the third, You shall not commit fornication; the fourth, You shall not steal; the fifth, You shall not bear false witness; the sixth, You shall not covet anything of your neighbor’s (Exod. 20:3–17). The Apostle Paul proves that these were written on the second tablet, saying, Honor your father and your mother, which is the first commandment with a promise (Eph. 6:2). For how could it be the first, unless he had begun with it on the second tablet itself? He says “with a promise” for this reason, because he immediately added, That you may live long upon the earth, and that it may go well with you. This is the promise made to those who keep the commandments. Therefore you have both the commandments distinguished, and their number completed, and what and how many were written on each tablet.
ON THE FAITH

God commands us by His prophet not to esteem any new God to be God, and not to worship any strange God. Now it is clear that that is called new which is not from everlasting, and on the contrary, that is called everlasting which is not new. He, then, who does not believe that the Only-begotten God is from everlasting of the Father does not deny that He is new, for that which is not everlasting is confessedly new; and that which is new is not God, according to the saying of Scripture, "there shall not be in thee any new God." Therefore he who says that the Son "once was not," denies His Godhead. Again, He Who says "thou shalt never worship a strange God" forbids us to worship another God; and the strange God is so called in contradistinction to our own God. Who, then, is our own God? Clearly, the true God. And who is the strange God? Surely, he who is alien from the nature of the true God. If, therefore, our own God is the true God, and if, as the heretics say, the Only-begotten God is not of the nature of the true God, He is a strange God, and not our God. But the Gospel says, the sheep "will not follow a stranger." He that says He is created will make Him alien from the nature of the true God. What then will they do, who say that He is created? Do they worship that same created being as God, or do they not? For if they do not worship Him, they follow the Jews in denying the worship of Christ: and if they do worship Him, they are idolaters, for they worship one alien from the true God. But surely it is equally impious not to worship the Son, and to worship the strange God. We must then say that the Son is the true Son of the true Father, that we may both worship Him, and avoid condemnation as worshipping a strange God.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

After these things let us see what the second commandment also seems to contain: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness of the things that are in heaven or that are in the earth or that are in the waters under the earth". Idols are one thing, and gods far another, as the Apostle himself likewise teaches us. For concerning gods he said: "as there are many gods and many lords"; but concerning idols he says: "for an idol is nothing in the world". Hence it seems to me that he read what the law says not carelessly. For he saw the difference between gods and idols, and again the difference between idols and likenesses; for he who said of idols that they do not exist did not add that likenesses also do not exist. But here it says: "you shall not make for yourself an idol nor a likeness of any things". It is one thing, then, to make an "idol", another to make a "likeness". And if indeed the Lord deign to enlighten us as to the things that must be said, I think it should be understood thus: that, for example's sake, if someone in any metal of gold or silver, or of wood or of stone, make the shape of some quadruped, or of a serpent, or of a bird, and set it up to be adored, he has made not an idol, but a likeness; or even if he set up a painting for this very purpose, he must nonetheless be said to have made a likeness. But that man has made an "idol" who, according to the Apostle who says that "an idol is nothing", makes what is not. And what is it that is not? A shape which the eye has not seen, but which the mind itself fashions for itself. For example's sake: as if one should form, upon human limbs, the head of a dog or of a ram, or again should fashion two faces on one human form, or join to a human breast the hinder parts of a horse or of a fish. He who makes these things and things like them makes not a likeness, but an idol. For he makes what is not, nor has it anything like itself. And therefore, knowing this, the Apostle says: "for an idol is nothing in the world"; for the shape is not taken from any of the things that exist, but is what the idle and curious mind has itself devised for itself. But a likeness is when something is formed from those things which are "either in heaven or in earth or in the waters", as we said above. Nevertheless, it is not as ready at hand to pronounce concerning heavenly things as concerning the likenesses of those things which are in the earth or in the sea—unless one should say that this can be perceived concerning the sun and moon and stars; for indeed the heathen are wont to express the forms of these too. But because Moses "was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians", he desired to prohibit also those things which among them were among their hidden and secret matters; as, for example's sake, so that we too may use their own appellations, the one they call Hecate and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls "the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places". Concerning which perhaps the prophet also says: "my sword has been made drunk in heaven". For with these forms and likenesses it is the custom to invoke demons for those who have such matters as their concern, whether to repel or even to invite evils; all of which the word of God, embracing them all together, at once abjures and casts away, and forbids not only that an idol be made, but also "a likeness of all things that are in the earth, and in the waters, and in heaven".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 69: ON CHRIST FULFILLING THE LAW

IF, WHEN JOHN OR THE SAVIOR WAS PREACHING, THE LAW CEASED, HOW DOES THE SAVIOR SAY, “I HAVE NOT COME TO DESTROY THE LAW OR THE PROPHETS, BUT TO FULFILL” (Matt. 5:17)? FOR IF IT HAS BEEN FORBIDDEN, HOW IS IT NOT ABOLISHED, SINCE IT HAS LOST THE AUTHORITY TO BE CARRIED OUT? — Everything that was spoken about Christ has been fulfilled; and the Lord Himself therefore fulfilled the Law and the Prophets, since He did everything that was written about Him, and did not dissolve anything, but confirmed it. For the Law and the Prophets were until Him. The Prophets spoke about Him; therefore beyond Him, what was said by them about this, namely, about Christ, cannot extend; nor after Him could the Prophets find anything of this sort, because they have neither one to speak about, and He about whom it was spoken has already come. Indeed they encompassed in their books all things: His incarnation, His manner of life, His passion, His resurrection, the revealing of His divinity, and the revelation of His future judgment. And therefore the Prophets ceased when the work of the dispensation was completed. But the Law ceased in a twofold way, and not entirely; for even that which has ceased can remain, if the condition be observed. One thing ceased in its sentence, another in the Law itself. When John preached the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, the sentence of the Law ceased, which held sinners guilty; the burdens of the Law also ceased, which had been given on account of the hardness of the Jewish heart in foods, new moons, sabbaths, and the rest. For when mercy came, vengeance ceased. But the burdens of the Law have ceased forever. The sentence, however, ceases and is abolished for those who remain in the benefit obtained. But for those who return to the old man, the authority of the Law is revived, because, forgetful of benefits, they return under the sentence of the Law. Circumcision and the sabbath indeed were in force until that time when the commandment of the new law was preached. For they were given in such a way that, when the law of faith arrived, they should cease. Therefore the Apostle says, “Christ is the end of the Law” (Rom. 10:4). And Daniel signifies this also, when he prophesies both concerning the coming of the Lord and the weeks of time, that the anointing and judgment and sacrifice and the city itself were to cease (Dan. 9:24–27). For when the spiritual law arrived, it was necessary that the carnal things should cease. Then God was served in part by the body, now in part by the soul; formerly visibly, now invisibly; then in the flesh, now in the mind. For to God, who is spirit, one must serve in spirit (Jn. 4:24). Therefore the Law is not undone because it has ceased, but something has succeeded it when the time was fulfilled. Nor is its administration or judgment accused if indulgence is given to sinners; for from this it is rather clearly shown to have been rightly and justly given, since it is not denied that those over whom it ruled were sinners, because, “The Law,” he says, “is not laid down for the righteous” (1 Tim. 1:9). Therefore, because mercy is to be preferred, righteousness must not on that account be thought shameful; for if there were no reverence for it, mercy itself would have no fruit. For unless they keep righteousness after receiving mercy, indulgence will profit them nothing. For the Law said, “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor adore the things that are in heaven above or on the earth beneath”; and, “You shall not swear falsely”; and, “Honor your father and mother”; and, “You shall not kill, nor commit fornication, nor steal, nor bear false witness, nor covet anything that is your neighbor’s” (Exod. 20:4–17). Are these to be said to have ceased? Far from it. For without these, who could even in this life be judged acceptable? And therefore the other things which we mentioned above have ceased, new moons, sabbaths, the law of foods, sacrifices, circumcision, and so on. From this it is that the Apostle says among other things: “Rulers are not a terror to good work, but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the power? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it” (Rom. 13:3). Observing these makes men good, though not yet perfect. Therefore the Savior: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5:20). By adding better things to these, the Savior did not in any way dissolve the Law, but fulfilled it. For the intention of the Law pertains to man’s salvation, for example, “Eye for eye, tooth for tooth” (Lev. 24:20): so that, fearing lest he suffer what he is forbidden to do to another, he might restrain himself from wickedness. But the Savior, adding a higher righteousness to this sense, says, “But I say to you, do not resist the evil; but if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the left also” (Matt. 5:39); so that by not returning evil in kind, he may be perfect. For to repay in kind is righteousness, but not full; but if he overlooks the injury, it is full and overflowing righteousness. To retaliate brings joy for a time; to forgive brings joy for the future. Therefore the Savior fulfilled the Law, in that those whom it taught to be righteous, He made more righteous, which it could not do. Wherefore it is the joy of the Law that its disciples have become more skillful. He would indeed have destroyed the Law if He had taught men to sin with freedom. But rather He suspended the sentence, so that he who acts wickedly may have time to repent; if not, the sentence returns upon him with increase, because he did not understand that he was forgiven for this purpose, that he might improve himself.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

Let us now see also what follows, how the "sins of the fathers" are said to be repaid "upon the sons unto the third and fourth generation". For in this saying the heretics are wont to jeer at us, that it is not the saying of a good God, who says that one is punished for the sins of another. But even according to their own reasoning, who say that the God who commanded these things in the law is, though not good, yet just, not even they can show how, according to their own sense of justice, it seems to accord that one should be punished when another sins. It remains, therefore, that we beseech the Lord to show us how these precepts accord with a just and good God. We have often said already that the divine Scriptures speak not everything to the outer man, but very much to the inner. Our inner man, therefore, is said either to have God as father, if he lives according to God and does the things that are God's, or the devil, if he be in sins and does his wills; as the Savior evidently shows in the Gospels, when he says: "you are of your father the devil, and you wish to do the desires of your father. He was a murderer from the beginning, and stood not in the truth". Just as, then, the seed of God is said to remain in us, when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin in ourselves, as John says: "but he who is of God does not sin, because the seed of God remains in him", so also, when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed. But when we even fulfill in deed what he has counseled, then indeed he has also begotten us; for we are born his sons through sin. But since it scarcely almost happens that we who sin should sin without a helper, but we always require either ministers or helpers of sin—for example's sake, if someone contrives adultery, he cannot accomplish this alone, but there must needs be also an adulteress as partner and companion of the sin; and moreover, even if not several, yet there must needs be some man or some woman in the services and companionship of the sin; all of whom, begotten as it were one from another according to the order of persuasion, "from their father the devil" draw the progeny of a harmful birth. And, to come to the things that are written, the "Lord of majesty", Jesus Christ our Savior, was crucified. The author of this crime and the father of the wickedness is without doubt the devil. For thus it is written: "but when the devil had entered into the heart of Judas Iscariot, that he should betray him". The father of the sin, then, is the devil. He, in this wickedness, first begets a son, Judas; but Judas alone could not accomplish this. What, then, is written? "Judas went" it says "to the scribes and Pharisees and to the chief priests, saying to them: What will you give me, and I will betray him to you?" There is born, then, from Judas a third and fourth generation of sin. And you will be able to detect this order in each single sin as well. Now, therefore, let us see, according to this progeny of which we have spoken, how God "repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons and unto the third and fourth generation", and does not repay upon the fathers themselves; for he said nothing about the fathers. The devil, then, who has already exceeded the measure of sinning—as the prophet says, "as a garment congealed in blood shall not be clean", so he too shall not be clean in this age, nor is he rebuked for his sin, nor scourged; for all things are reserved for him unto the future. Hence he himself too, knowing that a set time of punishments is appointed for him, said to the Savior: "why have you come to torment us before the time?" While, therefore, this world stands, the devil, who is the father of those who sin, does not receive his sins; but they are repaid upon the sons, that is, upon those whom he begot through sin. For men, set in the flesh, are rebuked by the Lord, are beaten, are scourged. For "the Lord does not wish the death of the sinner, but that he should return and live". And therefore the "kind and merciful Lord" repays the sins of the fathers upon the sons, so that—since the fathers, that is, "the devil and his angels", and the rest, "the princes of the world and rulers of these darknesses" (for these too are made fathers of sin, just as the devil is)—since, I say, these fathers are unworthy to be rebuked in the present age, but in the future receive what they deserve, their sons, that is, those whom they have persuaded to sin and who nonetheless have been enlisted by them into the partnership and companionship of sin, these receive what they have done, so that they may pass more purified to the age to come and no longer be made companions of the devil in punishment. Because, therefore, God is merciful and "wishes all men to be saved", for this reason he says: "I will visit their misdeeds with a rod of iron and their sins with scourges. But my mercy I will not take away from them". The Lord, then, visits and requires the souls which this most evil father has begotten by persuasion to sin, and says to each one of them: "hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and the house of your father". He visits you, then, after sin, and admonishes you, and with scourge and rod he visits you for the sin which the devil your father put upon you, that he may repay it to you "into your bosom", that is, while you dwell in the body. And thus it is fulfilled that the "sins of the fathers" are repaid "into the bosoms of the sons, unto the third and fourth generation". For "God" is "jealous" and does not wish the soul which he has betrothed to himself in faith to remain in the defilement of sin, but wishes her quickly to be purged, wishes her swiftly to cast off all her uncleannesses, if perhaps anything has stolen upon her. But if she remain in sins and say: we will not hear the voice of the Lord, but doing we will do our own wills and will burn offerings "to the queen of heaven", as is reproached through the prophet: then she too is reserved for that sentence of wisdom which says: "since indeed I called and you would not hear, but mocked my words; therefore I too will laugh at your destruction", or for that which is set before them in the Gospel, the Lord saying: "depart from me into eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels". I desire that, while I am in this age, the Lord may visit my sins and here repay them to me, so that there he may say also concerning me, Abraham, as he said concerning poor Lazarus to the rich man: "remember, son, that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things. But now here he is at rest, but you are tormented". For this reason, therefore, when we are rebuked, when we are chastised by the Lord, we ought not to be ungrateful, but let us understand that we are rebuked in the present age for this, that in the future we may obtain rest, as the Apostle also says: "but when we are chastised by the Lord, we are rebuked, lest we be condemned with this world". Finally, for this reason too the blessed Job willingly received all torments and said: "if we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not also endure evil things?" "The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so has it been done. Blessed be the name of the Lord". But he also repays "mercy unto thousands to those who love him". For those who love do not need rebuke, nor indeed do they sin, as the Lord too says: "he who loves me keeps my commandments". And therefore "perfect love casts out fear". On this account, then, for those who love, mercy alone is set; for "blessed are the merciful, for God will have mercy upon them" in Christ Jesus our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".
AGAINST CELSUS 5.6

It is obvious that the Jews follow the law where God is represented as saying, "You shall have none other gods but me; you shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness of anything in the heaven above and in the earth beneath and in the waters under the earth; you shall not bow down to them nor worship them." And they worship none other than the supreme God who made heaven and everything else. It is clear then that since those who live according to the law reverence him who made the heavens, they do not reverence the heavens together with God. Furthermore, none of those who serve the Mosaic law worship the angels in heaven. And in the same way that they do not worship the sun, moon and stars, "the world of heaven," they avoid worshiping heaven and the angels in it.
AGAINST CELSUS 7.64

Christians and Jews are led to avoid temples and altars and images by the command "You shall fear the Lord your God and him only shall you serve." … And not only do they avoid them, but when necessary they readily come to the point of death to avoid defiling their conception of the God of the universe by any act of this kind contrary to his law.
COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 10.221

Now Christ is especially jealous for the house of God in each of us, not wishing it to be a house of merchandise or that the house of prayer become a den of thieves, since he is Son of a jealous God. This is the case if we understand such words from the Scriptures in a reasonable manner, which were spoken metaphorically from the human viewpoint to set forth the fact that God wishes nothing alien to his will to be mingled with the soul of any, but especially with the soul of those who wish to receive [the teachings of the] most divine faith.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

He adds, moreover, and says: "you shall not adore them nor worship them". To worship is one thing, to adore another. A person can sometimes adore even unwillingly, as some, flattering kings, when they have seen them given over to devotions of this kind, feign that they adore idols, though in their heart it is certain that an idol is nothing; but to worship is to be enslaved to these things with the whole affection and zeal. Both, therefore, the divine word cuts away, so that you neither worship with affection nor adore in outward show. Yet it must be known that, when you have resolved to keep the charge of this precept and to repudiate all the other gods and lords, and to have besides the one God and Lord no one as either god or lord, this is to have declared war without treaty upon all the rest. When, therefore, we come to the grace of baptism, renouncing all other gods and lords, we confess God the Father alone and the Son and the Holy Spirit. But confessing this, unless we "love the Lord our God with the whole heart and with the whole soul" and cleave to him "with the whole strength", we have not been made "the Lord's portion", but, set as it were on a certain border, we both suffer offense from those we have fled, and do not render favorable the Lord to whom we have fled, whom we do not love "with the whole and entire heart". And therefore the prophet mourns over us, whom he sees wavering with inconstancy of this kind, and says: "woe to the double-minded", and again: "how long do you go lame on both your knees?" But the Apostle James also says: "a double-minded man is inconstant in all his ways". We are, then, we who follow our Lord with a faith neither whole nor perfect, and have withdrawn from alien gods, set as it were in a certain middle border, and by those we are struck at as fugitives, and by our own Lord, as unstable and doubtful, we are not defended. Or is this not what the prophets too spiritually figure concerning the lovers of Jerusalem, when they say: "your lovers themselves have become your enemies"? So, then, understand that your soul too has had many lovers, who delighted in her beauty, with whom she played the harlot. Concerning whom she also said: "I will go after my lovers, who give me my wine and my oil", and the rest. But now she has come to that time when she says: "I will return to my former husband, because it was better for me then than now". You have returned, then, to your former husband; without doubt you have given offense to your lovers, with whom you were committing adulteries. Unless, therefore, you now abide with your husband in whole faith, and are glued to him with your whole love, out of the many crimes which you have committed every movement of yours and glance of yours is suspect to him, and your very gait, if it be too careless. He can see nothing further in you that is wanton, nothing dissolute and prodigal. But when you turn your eyes even a little away from your husband, at once there must needs come a remembrance of former things. Therefore, that you may both blot out former things and that trust may be able to be had in you for the rest, you must not only do nothing unchaste, but not even think it. For see what is written: "When" it says "an unclean spirit has gone out from a man, it goes through dry places, seeking rest, and finds none. And then it says: I will return into my house, whence I came out. And if, coming, it finds it empty, swept, and adorned, it goes and brings with it seven other spirits worse than itself, and entering into that house it dwells therein. And the last state of that man shall be worse than the first". If we heed these things, how can we give even in a small matter a place to negligence? For an unclean spirit dwelt in us before we believed, before we came to Christ, when still, as I said above, our soul was fornicating away from God and was with its lovers, the demons. But after she said: "I will return to my former husband" and came to Christ, who from the beginning "created her according to his own image", the adulterous spirit necessarily gave place when it saw the lawful husband. We have been received, then, by Christ, and our house has been "cleansed" from former sins and "adorned" with the ornaments of the sacraments of the faithful, which those who have been initiated know. But this house does not at once merit to have Christ as its inhabitant, unless its life and conduct be so holy, so pure and undefiled, that it may merit to be a "temple of God". For it must be no longer a house, but a temple, in which God may dwell. If, then, it neglect the grace received and entangle itself in worldly affairs, straightway that unclean spirit returns and claims for itself the empty house. And, that it may not be able to be expelled again, it brings "with it seven other spirits worse", and "the last state of a man of this kind becomes worse than the first", because it had been more tolerable for a soul that once played the harlot not to have returned to its former husband than, having returned after the confession of the husband, to become an adulteress again. There is, then, no "fellowship", as the Apostle says, "of the temple of God with idols", no "concord of Christ with Belial". If we are God's, we ought to be such that there may be fulfilled that which God says concerning us: "for I will dwell in them and walk among them, and they shall be to me a people", and as in another place the prophet says: "go out from the midst of them and be separated, says the Lord, you who bear the vessels of the Lord. Go out and touch not the unclean thing, and I will receive you, and I will be to you a father, and you shall be to me sons and daughters, says the Lord almighty". For this reason, therefore, he says: "there shall be for you no other gods besides me, nor shall you make for yourself an idol nor any likeness, whatever things are in heaven, and whatever are in the earth, and whatever are in the waters; neither shall you adore them nor worship them".
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 8

"For I am the Lord your God, a jealous God". See the kindness of God, how, in order to teach us and make us perfect, he himself does not refuse the frailty of human affections. For who, hearing of a "jealous God", would not straightway wonder and think it a fault of human frailty? But God both does and suffers all things for our sake, and, that we may be able to be taught, he speaks in affections known and familiar to us. Let us see, then, what this is that he says: "I am a jealous God". But that we may more easily be able to contemplate things divine, let us be taught by human examples, according to those things we discoursed of above. Every woman is either under a husband and subject to the laws of the husband, or is a harlot and uses the liberty of sinning. He, therefore, who goes in to a harlot knows himself to have gone in to a woman who is prostituted and lies open to all who wish; and therefore he cannot be indignant if with her he sees other lovers also. But he who uses lawful marriage does not suffer his wife to use the power of sinning, but is kindled with jealousy to preserve the chastity of the marriage, whereby he may become a lawful father from her. By this example, then, let us understand that every soul is either prostituted to demons and has very many lovers—so that at one moment there enters into her the spirit of fornication, and when that departs there enters the spirit of avarice, after this comes the spirit of pride, then of wrath, then of envy, then also of vainglory, and very many others with these. All these so play the harlot with the unfaithful soul that the one does not envy the other, nor are they moved to jealousy toward one another. And why do I say that the one does not exclude the other? Nay, they even invite one another and of their own accord summon one another, as we already said a little before, that it is written in the Gospel concerning that spirit which "went out from a man, and returning brought with it seven other spirits worse than itself, that they might dwell together in one soul". So, then, the soul that is prostituted to demons suffers no jealousy from her lovers. But if she be joined to a lawful husband, to that husband to whom Paul joins and unites souls in marriage, as he himself says: "for I have determined to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, to Christ", and concerning whom it is written in the Gospels that "a certain king made a marriage for his son"—into the marriage, then, of this husband when the soul has given herself, and has obtained by lot a lawful matrimony with him, even if she was once a sinner, even if she played the harlot, yet if she has handed herself over to this husband, he suffers her to sin no further. He cannot bear that the soul which has obtained a husband by lot should again dally with adulterers: his jealousy is aroused over her, he defends the chastity of the marriage. And "God" is called "jealous" because he does not suffer the soul made his own to mingle with demons. Otherwise, if he see her violating the rights of the marriage and seeking occasions for sin, then, as it is written, he gives her "a bill of divorce" and dismisses her, saying: "where is the bill of divorce of your mother, by which I dismissed her?" To which he adds also and says: "behold, for your sins you have been sold, and for your iniquities I have dismissed your mother". He who speaks these things is "jealous" and, moved with jealousy, says these things; for after the acknowledgment of himself, after the illumination of the divine word, after the grace of baptism, after the confession of faith, and the marriage confirmed by sacraments so many and so great, he does not wish us to sin any further, he does not suffer the soul, of which he is himself called either the bridegroom or the husband, to sport with demons, to fornicate with unclean spirits, to wallow in vices and uncleannesses; and if perhaps it sometime unhappily happen, at least that she may be converted and return and repent. For this is a new kind of his goodness, that even after adultery he receives the soul, provided she returns and repents from the heart; as he himself also says through the prophet: "if a woman go out from her husband and sleep with another man, shall she return again to her husband? Shall she not be defiled with defilement? But you have fornicated with many shepherds, and yet you were returning to me". Likewise elsewhere he says: "and after you had fornicated in all these things, I said: return to me; and not even so did you return, says the Lord". This "jealous God", then—if he requires and desires your soul to cleave to him, if he keeps you from sin, if he rebukes, if he chastises, if he is indignant, if he is angry and, as it were, uses a certain jealousy toward you—recognize that there is for you hope of salvation. But if, chastised, you do not come to your senses, if, rebuked, you are not amended, if, scourged, you despise it, know that, if you have so far advanced in sinning, his jealousy will depart from you, and that will be said to you which through the prophet Ezekiel is said to Jerusalem: "therefore my jealousy shall depart from you, and I will be angry over you no more". See the mercy and the loving-kindness of the good God. When he wishes to have mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as through Jeremiah he says: "with grief and with scourge you shall be chastised, Jerusalem, lest my soul depart from you". If you understand these things, it is the voice of a God who has mercy, where he is angry, where he is jealous, where he applies griefs and scourges. "For he scourges every son whom he receives". But do you wish to hear the terrible voice of an indignant God? Hear what he says through the prophet: when he had enumerated the many wicked things which the people had committed, he adds also these: "and for this reason" he says "I will not visit upon your daughters when they fornicate, nor upon your daughters-in-law when they commit adultery". This is the terrible thing, this the extremity: when we are no longer rebuked for our sins, when we are no longer corrected when we transgress. For then, when we have exceeded the measure of sinning, the "jealous God" turns his jealousy away from us, as he said above: "for my jealousy shall be taken away from you, and I will be angry over you no more". So much concerning that which was said: "a jealous God".
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 14: ON REPAYING THE FATHERS' SINS UPON THE CHILDREN

WHAT DOES IT MEAN THAT GOD, WHO IS PROCLAIMED AS JUST, HAS PROMISED TO REPAY THE SINS OF THE FATHERS UPON THE CHILDREN TO THE THIRD AND FOURTH GENERATION? — Anyone who doubts that God does nothing and says nothing unjust is out of his mind. Therefore, if the words of the Lord are not suppressed, but everything that relates to this same question is set forth, what seems obscure will come to light, and what is thought hardly just will be recognized as devout. For whoever suppresses the words of a question is either ignorant or shifty, preferring accusation to teaching. Further, the Lord indeed promised that He would repay the sins of the fathers upon the children, but upon those who hate Him, that is, those who, involved in their fathers’ evils, have served idols just as their fathers did. For he is an enemy of God who transfers the honor of His name to a creature. Just as the sons of the righteous, being themselves righteous, dignify the line of righteousness in themselves, while both the righteousness of the fathers and their own are exalted; so also the sons of the utterly wicked, being themselves wicked, increase hatred, because they are children of the evil and have copied their wickedness to the ruin of many. God therefore appears to speak with terror; but it is true, and it has its basis. For who does not detest both an evil man and the son of an evil man in a double way, just as he judges both a good man and the son of a good man deserving of double honor? He therefore promised to repay to the third and fourth generation so that, if after an evil father the son does not follow his father’s treachery, but the grandson becomes an imitator of his grandfather’s evils, he may know that he will not be exempt from the severity of judgment; or if the grandson, not following his grandfather but his father’s footsteps, loves the Covenant of God, the great‑grandson may not be ignorant that the sentence reaches to him, if he rivals the disloyalty of his great‑grandfather. By this revealing of the Law God wished to deter wicked fathers, so that, recognizing how much evil the pursuit of idolatry produces, they might be recalled to reverence for the Creator by affection for their children; or so that the children, fearing lest they experience their fathers’ sins, might obey the Law of God. But those who add to their wickedness began to interpret this differently, saying, “Our fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge,” so that, feeling secure about exemption, because the sins would be repaid to their children, they would have no devotion either in spirit or in flesh. Therefore it is said to them, “The son shall not die for the father, nor the father for the son; but the soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18:2, 4). In order that they might learn that it would not be without penalty for them, but that the sins of the fathers are repaid to the children in this way: since they have followed the wickedness of their parents and have repeated the evils which should have been blotted out, they are punished more bitterly. After God showed what evil idolatry produces, He immediately added what good follows for those who love Him, saying, “And showing mercy to thousands upon thousands of those who love Me and keep My commandments” (Exod. 20:6): so that the good of a father is repaid not only up to the great‑grandson, but up to thousands upon thousands. Suppose, for instance, that someone from the seed of David loves God, knowing for certain that David lived a thousand years earlier: to this man the mercy of God is added, so that in time of need, with two reasons to support him, he may merit to receive mercy, because he himself is a worshiper of God, and because he is of the seed of one who loved God. And in this the mercy of God is praiseworthy, that He repays to those who hate Him only up to the third and fourth generation, and not to thousands upon thousands: so that, if evil is drawn out into a fifth generation, from there it again begins to have its starting‑point, so that from that point it is counted up to a third and fourth generation. But someone will say: It seems more just that more should be repaid to the originator than to the imitator. Vengeance is rightly given to the originator; but what is said about more being repaid to the sons is a punishment upon the fathers. And if you seek the reason, by the coming of the Law sinners become more guilty, like Lamech and those after Lamech. Yet it seems to some that the sins of the fathers were repaid to the children in this way: when they were led into captivity because of their fathers and remained there up to the fourth generation. If this is true, He repaid the sins of the fathers not only to those who hated Him, but also to those who loved His name: for Daniel was taken away, and the three youths, and Baruch, and Ezekiel, and Ezra was born there. It clearly appears, then, that what we said above fits the question that has been proposed.
Commentary on Isaiah

For we ought not to take as fathers, whose iniquities and sins are now repaid to us, those from whose seed our bodies were born. Otherwise Moses himself, who had said that the sins of the fathers are to be repaid to the sons to the third and fourth generation of those who hate God (Exod 20), interprets his own sentence, saying: The sons shall not die for the sins of the fathers: but each shall die in his own sin (Deut 24:16). Ezekiel approves the same sentence, that that parable is by no means to be spoken: The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons are set on edge (Ezek 18:2), but that only his teeth are set on edge who has eaten, and that the sinning soul perishes, and does not pay for another's sins. From this we understand that those are to be taken as fathers, whether in the good sense or in the contrary, to whom each is added when he has departed from this life.
Commentary on Ezekiel

Now divine Scripture warns that what was said in Exodus, I am the Lord your God; a jealous God, who render the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation for those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands for those who love me and keep my precepts, and again, The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses, and Moses called on the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he called on him, saying: Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true, and keeping righteousness and mercy to thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins, and he will not cleanse the guilty, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and upon the sons of the sons to the third and fourth generation, ought to be taken thus, as a parable and a proverb, so that it sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; which we also said above on the parable of the two eagles. Hence the Lord in Psalm 77 (78): I will open, he says, my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning; and in the Gospel he sets forth the parable of the sowing, and of the darnel, and of the mustard seed, which, though it is the least of all seeds, rises up into a great tree, in such a way that he presents one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; and we, up to the present day, think that the two testimonies of Exodus which we set down above are not a parable, but set out a simple statement. And although we would not dare to say anything, nor would the earthen vessel speak against the potter, 'why have you made me thus or thus', yet we suffered a hidden stumbling block, because it seemed an injustice on God's part that one should sin and another pay for the sins. For if he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished; but from what follows, for those who hate me, the stumbling block of the threat, or of the precept, is resolved: for they are not punished to the third and fourth generation because their fathers transgressed, since it is rather the fathers, who were the sinners, who ought to have been punished, but because they proved to be imitators of their fathers and hated God, by an inherited evil, the impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. At this place the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament are accustomed to say against the Creator: How good and righteous is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, resting and silent at the sins of the fathers, repays those who have not sinned; nay rather, how great is the cruelty in him, that he should extend his wrath even to the third and fourth generation! To them we shall reply that even in this the clemency of God the Creator is shown: for it is not a mark of ferocity and severity to hold back wrath until the third and fourth generation, but a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin; for when he says, The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much compassion, and adds, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and the sons of the sons, he indicates this: that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish at once but defers the sentence of punishment. But if the vengeance on sinners is deferred to the third and fourth generation, what more will he do with the righteous and the holy? There follows: And keeping righteousness and mercy to many thousands for those who keep his commandments and do his precepts. It is written in Proverbs: As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it; from which it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape. And this is the sense of this passage: just as, if anyone should wish to say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge, it is ridiculous and has no logical consequence, so it is unjust and perverse that the fathers should sin and the sons and grandsons be tormented. There are those who expound what is written in Exodus, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, in such a way as to refer the statement to the human soul, saying that the father in us is the light prick of the senses and the incitements of the vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if you carry out in deed what you have thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you not only do what is evil and wicked but glory in your crimes, according to what is written: The impious man, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises. God therefore by no means punishes the first and second goads of thoughts, which the Greeks call προπαθείας [pre-passions, the first movements of the mind], without which no human being can exist, but only if someone has resolved to do what he has thought, or has been unwilling to correct by repentance the very things he has done; whence it is written: No human being is without sin, not even if his life be of a single day. But the years of his life are numbered; and in another place: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart?; and again: The stars too are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he has devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not free of sin, what is to be said of human beings who, surrounded by fragile flesh, must say with the Apostle: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?, and that word, that when we have done all things we must say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done, and: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has kept watch in vain? Now in proof of this point, that the first impulse of thoughts, or rather the slight prompting of the mind, is by no means punished by God, but only if you complete in deed what you have conceived in the mind, that passage of Genesis must be brought forward: Ham sinned in mocking his father's nakedness, and the sentence was received not by him who laughed but by his son Canaan: Cursed, he says, be Canaan; a servant he shall be to his brothers. For what righteousness is there in this, that the father should have sinned and the sentence be pronounced against the son? Likewise what the Apostle sets down in the opposite direction, that the woman is saved if her son remains in faith and holiness and chastity, would seem not to have the righteousness of a sentence, namely that if the sons and grandsons are good, the parents are saved; for how many parents are holy and have wicked sons, and, on the contrary, how many are sinners and beget holy sons? But it is the fifth commandment of the Decalogue; therefore it must be asked how one ought to understand the which is the first commandment, since the first commandment is stated to be "You shall have no other gods besides me." Now some have read which is the first commandment with a promise in this way, as though the commandments before it did not contain a promise; for they think that upon this one there lies for the first time the promise "that it may be well with you and that you may be long-lived upon the earth which the Lord your God gives you."

But these seem not to have observed that a promise is set down also upon the second commandment; for it says, "You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor a likeness of anything, whatever is in the heaven above and whatever is on the earth below and whatever is in the waters beneath the earth; you shall not bow down to them, nor shall you serve them. Perhaps, then, since the Decalogue is spoken of as the first legislation to the people after their coming out of Egypt, each of the ten commandments is first, being spoken among the first of those that follow.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 114: AGAINST THE PAGANS

AGAINST THE PAGANS. — The tradition of the pagans, having been invented by man, cannot be denied; but that our Law was given by God is an evident fact. For on the mountain the majesty of God appeared to give the Law to men. And that faith might be placed in this, He first sent many signs and wonders done in Egypt, which even today books testify to, stored by Ptolemy in the library of Alexandria. Therefore, then, He consented to give the Law, that no one might doubt that it was God who delivered it. For the majesty of God was seen openly and plainly by all, with such brilliance and terror that no other god besides Him was believed to exist, and that what He commanded was held worthy of all observance. And that all things might agree with the divine order, let the given Law be examined, to see whether there is anything unjust in it, anything dishonorable, anything ridiculous. Therefore it was fitting that God should be made known; not that He should appear in a corner by deceit, He who cannot be limited; nor in a mirror, where what is seen is other than it appears through enticing fraud; nor would He deliver precepts to be kept which, because they were dishonorable, would be performed in darkness. For since the knowledge of the one God had been obliterated in the world by the habit of sinning, because falsehood had supplied a veil for the truth, the merciful and gracious God, unwilling that His work should become accountable to destruction, consented to visit the human race. He did not appear as those did who wished falsely to be called gods; but as He is the Truth of God, so He revealed Himself, that He might remove the error which, by the proclamation of false gods, had corrupted the understanding of the world. In short, more than six hundred thousand men, having gone out of Egypt, seeing and knowing that this Lord was above all from the revealing of unspeakable glory, were afraid to approach Him, but from afar, with knees bent, they worshiped Him (Exod. 20:18). Afterwards, as other signs followed besides those which He had done in Egypt, in all these wonders He was revealed as the one God. These things became known in almost all tongues; these were a terror to neighboring nations. What such thing is there among the gods of the Gentiles? To what nation, to what people have they shown their glory? What signs or powers have they performed as testimony of their divinity? Where or when are they proved to have spoken?

Thus "at his threshold and door his master shall pierce his ear," in order that he might remember the decision by which he chose slavery.
Commentary on Galatians

We must also inquire what difference there is between "age" and "age of the age," or "ages of ages," and where it is used for a short span of time, and where for eternity: for in Hebrew "age," that is, OLAM (עלם), when it has the letter VAV placed in it, signifies eternity, but when it is written without VAV, the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee. For this reason too that Hebrew who, because of his wife and children, loving his master, is subjected to servitude with his ear pierced, is ordered to serve "for ever" (in sæculum) (Exod. 21), that is, up to the fiftieth year. And the Moabites and Ammonites (Deut. 23) do not enter the church of the Lord up to the fifteenth generation, and "for ever": because every hard condition was dissolved at the coming of the Jubilee.
