Like to this also is that which is said by God through Moses: "Behold, I have set you in a hole of the rock, and you shall see My back parts." Therefore this rock, which is Christ, is not closed on every side, but has a hole. And the hole of the rock is that which reveals God and makes Him known to men. No one, then, sees the Father except the Son; no one, then, sees the last things of God — that is, the things which come to pass in the last times — except one placed in the hole of the rock, namely when he has learned those things by the revelation of Christ.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 2.3

For it is well known that he, that is, the one who gave the oracles to Moses, says, "You shall not see my face but my back." Certainly these statements must be understood by the aid of that symbolism which is appropriate to the understanding of divine sayings, and those old wives' fables, which ignorant people invent on the subject of the front and back parts of God, must be utterly rejected and despised. Nor indeed must anyone suppose that we have entertained some impious thought in saying that the Father is not visible even to the Savior, but he must consider the exact meaning of the terms we use in controverting the heretics. For we have said that it is one thing to see and be seen, another to perceive and be perceived or to know and be known. To see and be seen is a property of bodies, which it would certainly not be right to apply either to the Father or to the Son or to the Holy Spirit in their relations one with another. For the Trinity by its nature transcends the limits of vision, although it grants to those who are in bodies, that is, to all other creatures, the property of being seen one by another. But incorporeal and above all intellectual nature is capable of nothing else but to know and be known, as the Savior himself declares when he says, "No one knows the Son save the Father, neither does any know the Father save the Son, and he to whom the Son wills to reveal him." It is clear then that he did not say, "No one sees the Father save the Son" but "No one knows the Father save the Son."

(For it, &c.) If thou do not support me, I shall not be able to govern. (Haydock) --- Possess us. Take us for thy peculiar inheritance. (Menochius)

(Haydock) --- It relates chiefly to contracts of marriage, which God forbids the faithful to enter into with the Chanaanites, and with other idolatrous nations, lest they should follow their example. Solomon is reprehended for transgressing this law, (3 Kings xi. 1,) and such marriages are called abominations. (1 Esdras ix. 1.; x. 2, 10.; Josephus) --- But if any of those people became converts, the reason of the prohibition ceased. Hence a captive woman might be married, (Deuteronomy xxi. 11,) and Salmon took Rahab to wife. If Samson and Esther married with heathens, it might be done by God's dispensation, for weighty reasons. (Tirinus) --- Fornication. On account of the dissolute behaviour of those idolaters, their worship is often condemned under this name, Jeremias ii. and iii.; Ezechiel xvi. S.) and St. Augustine (q. 186,) infer, however, from this text, that the second tables had not the same honour as the first. The contrary appears from Deuteronomy x. 4, He (God) wrote....as before. Salien., year of the world 2544, in which year of the world he fixes the death of Job, the great prophet of the Gentiles.

Horned. That is, shining, and sending forth rays of light like horns. (Challoner) --- Septuagint, "encircled with glory." St. Paul (2 Corinthians iii. 7,) says, the Hebrews could not look steadfastly at the face of Moses, on account of the glory of his countenance. Hence, he was forced to have a veil, which the apostle observes, was not taken off from the old law till Christ appeared. The Jews and heretics still read the law and the gospel with a veil over their eyes and heart, without understanding them, as they are hidden to those who perish, 2 Corinthians iv. 3. The Jews are much enraged at some Christians, who have represented Moses with horns, as if, they say, he were a devil, or his wife an adulteress. (Stacchus and Drusius.) --- Hebrew, "his skin was radiant" all over his face. These rays commanded respect and awe from the people, who had before said contemptuously, Moses---the man, (chap. xxxii. 1,) as they shewed that God was with him. They had not appeared before, though he had often conversed with the Lord: but now, having seen the glorious vision, they adhered to him during the remainder of his life, particularly when he enforced the obligations of the law to the people. (Haydock) --- The Arabs make their hair stand up like little horns, when they are about 40 years old. (Patric. ii. 4. Navig.) Homer mentions the like custom, and Diomed laughs at Paris calling him the pretty-horned. (Iliad xi.) Many of the ancient heroes and gods are represented with horns, particularly Bacchus, whose history reminds us of many particulars, which belong to Moses. He was born or educated in the confines of Egypt, was exposed on the waters, in a box; had two mothers, and very beautiful. While his army enjoyed the light, the Indians were in darkness. He was preceded by a pillar, had women in his train, dried up rivers with his thyrsus or wand, which had crawled, like a serpent, &c. (Huet. &c.) St. Epiphanius (her. 55,) says the Idumeans adored Moses. Their idol is called Choze by Josephus, (Antiquities xviii. 11,) which may be derived from Chus, the ancestor of Sephora, as Bacchus and Iacchus may denote "the son Bar, or the god Chus," Jah-Chus, who was adored in Arabia; so that Moses, Choze, and Bacchus, probably mean the same person. Chus peopled that part of Arabia where the Hebrews sojourned, Numbers xii. 1. (Calmet)

And having, &c. At first, he spoke uncovered. (Menochius) --- The Protestants insert the word till in Italics, to insinuate that Moses spoke with a veil on, as St. Paul mentions; (Haydock) and Calmet would translate, "for Moses had ceased to address the people, and had put a veil upon his face," as soon as he perceived that they could not bear the blaze of his countenance. This he did out of modesty, that they might not be afraid of coming to speak freely to him, (Jansenius) though it was also mysterious, as St. Paul remarks. For even until this day, when Moses is read, the veil is upon their heart, (2 Corinthians iii. 15,) as it is upon that of heretics, who cannot see the church. (St. Augustine in Psalm xxx.) f: Commentary on Ezekiel

Now divine Scripture warns that what was said in Exodus, I am the Lord your God; a jealous God, who render the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation for those who hate me, and show mercy to thousands for those who love me and keep my precepts, and again, The Lord descended in a cloud and stood beside Moses, and Moses called on the name of the Lord, and the Lord passed before his face, and he called on him, saying: Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much mercy and true, and keeping righteousness and mercy to thousands, taking away iniquities and injustices and sins, and he will not cleanse the guilty, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and upon the sons of the sons to the third and fourth generation, ought to be taken thus, as a parable and a proverb, so that it sounds one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; which we also said above on the parable of the two eagles. Hence the Lord in Psalm 77 (78): I will open, he says, my mouth in parables, I will utter propositions from the beginning; and in the Gospel he sets forth the parable of the sowing, and of the darnel, and of the mustard seed, which, though it is the least of all seeds, rises up into a great tree, in such a way that he presents one thing in the words and holds another in the sense; and we, up to the present day, think that the two testimonies of Exodus which we set down above are not a parable, but set out a simple statement. And although we would not dare to say anything, nor would the earthen vessel speak against the potter, 'why have you made me thus or thus', yet we suffered a hidden stumbling block, because it seemed an injustice on God's part that one should sin and another pay for the sins. For if he renders the sins of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, it seems unjust that one should sin and another be punished; but from what follows, for those who hate me, the stumbling block of the threat, or of the precept, is resolved: for they are not punished to the third and fourth generation because their fathers transgressed, since it is rather the fathers, who were the sinners, who ought to have been punished, but because they proved to be imitators of their fathers and hated God, by an inherited evil, the impiety growing from the root into the branches as well. At this place the heretics who do not receive the Old Testament are accustomed to say against the Creator: How good and righteous is the God of the Law and the Prophets, who, resting and silent at the sins of the fathers, repays those who have not sinned; nay rather, how great is the cruelty in him, that he should extend his wrath even to the third and fourth generation! To them we shall reply that even in this the clemency of God the Creator is shown: for it is not a mark of ferocity and severity to hold back wrath until the third and fourth generation, but a sign of mercy to defer the punishment of sin; for when he says, The Lord God, compassionate and merciful, patient and of much compassion, and adds, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons and the sons of the sons, he indicates this: that he is of such great mercy that he does not punish at once but defers the sentence of punishment. But if the vengeance on sinners is deferred to the third and fourth generation, what more will he do with the righteous and the holy? There follows: And keeping righteousness and mercy to many thousands for those who keep his commandments and do his precepts. It is written in Proverbs: As a sour grape is harmful to the teeth and smoke to the eyes, so is iniquity to those who practice it; from which it is clear that it is not the teeth of others that ache and are set on edge, but the teeth of those who have eaten the sour grape. And this is the sense of this passage: just as, if anyone should wish to say, The fathers have eaten a sour grape, and the teeth of the sons have been set on edge, it is ridiculous and has no logical consequence, so it is unjust and perverse that the fathers should sin and the sons and grandsons be tormented. There are those who expound what is written in Exodus, rendering the iniquities of the fathers upon the sons to the third and fourth generation, in such a way as to refer the statement to the human soul, saying that the father in us is the light prick of the senses and the incitements of the vices; the son, if the thought has conceived the sin; the grandson, if you carry out in deed what you have thought and conceived; and the great-grandson, that is, the fourth generation, if you not only do what is evil and wicked but glory in your crimes, according to what is written: The impious man, when he has come into the depth of evils, despises. God therefore by no means punishes the first and second goads of thoughts, which the Greeks call προπαθείας [pre-passions, the first movements of the mind], without which no human being can exist, but only if someone has resolved to do what he has thought, or has been unwilling to correct by repentance the very things he has done; whence it is written: No human being is without sin, not even if his life be of a single day. But the years of his life are numbered; and in another place: Who will boast that he has a chaste heart?; and again: The stars too are not clean in his sight, and against his angels he has devised something perverse. But if that sublime nature is not free of sin, what is to be said of human beings who, surrounded by fragile flesh, must say with the Apostle: Wretched man that I am! Who will deliver me from the body of this death?, and that word, that when we have done all things we must say, We are unprofitable servants; we have done what we ought to have done, and: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord guards the city, he who guards it has kept watch in vain? Now in proof of this point, that the first impulse of thoughts, or rather the slight prompting of the mind, is by no means punished by God, but only if you complete in deed what you have conceived in the mind, that passage of Genesis must be brought forward: Ham sinned in mocking his father's nakedness, and the sentence was received not by him who laughed but by his son Canaan: Cursed, he says, be Canaan; a servant he shall be to his brothers. For what righteousness is there in this, that the father should have sinned and the sentence be pronounced against the son? Likewise what the Apostle sets down in the opposite direction, that the woman is saved if her son remains in faith and holiness and chastity, would seem not to have the righteousness of a sentence, namely that if the sons and grandsons are good, the parents are saved; for how many parents are holy and have wicked sons, and, on the contrary, how many are sinners and beget holy sons? Therefore all that we said above is to be taken according to this sense: that the sins of parents and begetters are punished in the branches, not in the root. Let it suffice for the present to have said this about the proverb, or the parable: that the Law and the Prophets, that is, Exodus and Ezekiel, or rather God himself, who spoke both here and there, should by no means seem to disagree in their statements, or to correct here what he had said badly there. But if anyone can find either a better sense or another one, which removes the stumbling block of testimonies contrary to one another, it is rather his opinion that is to be accepted.

QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 64: ON THE THREE DAYS AND THREE NIGHTS

HOW IS IT PROVED THAT THE SAVIOR ROSE FROM THE DEAD AFTER THREE DAYS AND NIGHTS? — In this matter, if you seek the number of days and nights in strict sequence, you will gain no true understanding. For Moses fasted forty days and forty nights (Exod. 34:28), and yet a complete numerical count is not found: for when he went up by day and came down by day, he clearly did not fulfill the entire number; but because where there is day, night is also reckoned, and where there is night, day is likewise counted, so that the part is taken for the whole, they are called forty days and forty nights. Therefore it is with what the Savior said: “As Jonah was in the belly of the sea monster three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth” (Matt. 12:40). And because there are three nights, three days are also to be taken. Night is indeed something that might seem new or perhaps unreasonable, since night depends on day: for before light was made, from which “day” is named, and before evening was appointed, which is followed by night, it is by no means doubted that the Lord’s Passion is confirmed to have taken its beginning from the night; this is not absurd. For just as light, that is day, is an image of life, so night is a likeness of death, that is, darkness: as Scripture clearly shows the children of light, and conversely those of darkness. Nor is it surprising that, although everywhere day precedes night and light precedes darkness, here alone the things that follow are set before those that precede; or that in such a matter the order of things is disturbed and changed, as we have already indicated. For the night of death appears rather to be what truly counts, more than the day. Therefore the beginning is taken from the night, because the prince of darkness could not otherwise be entered into except by night; that is, he could not be conquered: and so that in some manner the Lord of light, that is of eternal life, might for a time be subjected to the prince of darkness or death, so that he might free both those of the past and those of the future from death. For death would not be utterly abolished, nor would the gloom of darkness ever be dispelled, if it had not seen the Lord enter in. Indeed, by such great light the hidden realm of death, in which he ruled, vanished, nor can he be utterly conquered except by one who is taken either in himself or in his own. Rightly then in such a matter night alone holds the primacy, in such a way that it loses its power: and so that the unbelieving Jews remain in eternal night, and the author of such a great crime, indeed, of such sacrilege, be not the day, but the night; a day is subjected to the preceding night, contrary to the usual course of things, just as God and Lord of all things was subjected to the prince of wicked death, so that he might free all from the snares of death. If to anyone this still seems in some way contrary, let him carefully consider lest he begin to judge more harshly that God, assuming the person of a servant, not to say of a man, gave himself over to death. Why then do you seek order here, where you see everything contrary to order? For what is that light which was in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it (Jn. 1:5)? The Lord of light, who yet was apprehended. For whoever knows that he is apprehended so that he may be struck down, counts that time as death. There is also the following day on which he was examined and crucified. There is also the night that falls upon the Sabbath, and the Sabbath itself. There is also the evening after the Sabbath; this is what was commanded to the Jews by Moses in figure, that they should enter the Sabbath in the evening, on which the Lord rose: which embraces the Lord’s Day; for night is not counted without day, nor day without night. In this way, after three days and after three nights, the Lord rose.
