HOMILIES ON EXODUS 12

A reading from Exodus has been recited to us, one that may either spur us on to the search for understanding or drive us back from it. It spurs on minds that are studious and free; it drives back those that are idle and preoccupied. For it is written: "Aaron and all the sons of Israel saw Moses, and his face was glorified and the color of his countenance, and they were afraid to approach him." And a little after: "Moses," it says, "placed a veil over his face. But when he entered into the sight of the Lord, to speak with him, he laid the veil aside." Now the Apostle, expounding these things with that magnificent understanding which he employs in the rest, of which he said: "but we have the mind of Christ," says: "for if the ministry of death, formed in letters upon stones, was in glory, so that the sons of Israel could not gaze upon the face of Moses because of the glory of his countenance, which is done away: how shall not the ministry of the spirit be rather in glory?" And again a little later he says: "and not as Moses put a veil over his face, that the sons of Israel might not gaze upon the face of his countenance. For their perceptions were dulled; for until this present day, when Moses is read, the veil is placed over their heart." Who would not marvel at the greatness of the mysteries? Who would not be filled with dread at the mark of the dulled heart? The face of Moses was glorified, but the sons of Israel could not "gaze upon the face of his countenance," the people of the synagogue could not "gaze" upon it. But if anyone can have a manner of life and a way of living more eminent than the rest of the common crowd, he is able to behold the glory of his countenance. For even now, as the Apostle says, "a veil is placed over the reading of the Old Testament," and even now Moses speaks with glorified countenance, but we cannot behold the glory that is in his countenance. And the reason we cannot is that we are still the common people and have no more of zeal, no more of merit, than the rest of the multitude. But since the holy Apostle says: "yet the same veil remains over the reading of the Old Testament," the pronouncement of so great and such an Apostle would cut off from us every hope of understanding, had he not added: "but when anyone shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away." Therefore he says that the cause of the veil's removal is our turning to the Lord. From which we ought to gather these indications: that so long as, when we read the divine Scriptures, the understanding lies hidden from us, so long as the things that are written are obscure and closed to us, we have not yet turned to the Lord. For if we had turned to the Lord, without doubt the veil would be taken away.

But let us see also what this very thing, "to turn to the Lord," may be. And that we may know more plainly what it is to be turned, we must first say what it is to be turned away. Everyone who, when the words of the law are recited, is occupied with common tales, is turned away. Everyone who, "when Moses is read," carries anxiety about the affairs of the world, about money, about profits, is turned away. Everyone who is bound tight by cares for possessions and stretched out by desire for riches, who is eager for the glory of the age and the honors of the world, is turned away. But even one who seems indeed a stranger to these things, yet stands by and hears the words of the law and is intent in face and eyes, yet wanders in heart and thoughts, is turned away. What then is it to be turned? If we turn our backs on all these things and, in zeal, in deeds, in mind, in solicitude, give our labor to the word of God, if we "meditate on his law day and night," if, setting all else aside, we are at leisure for God and exercise ourselves in his testimonies—this is to be turned to the Lord. If you wished your son to know the letters that men call liberal, to know the discipline of grammar or of rhetoric, would you not render him free and unoccupied from all else, would you not make him, setting the rest aside, devote his labor to this one study, would you not see that he lack nothing at all—tutors, teachers, books, expenses—until he carries off the perfected work of the study he has purposed? Which of us has so turned himself to the studies of the divine law, which of us has given such labor? Who seeks the divine letters with as much zeal and toil as he has sought the human? And what do we complain of, if we are ignorant of what we do not learn? Some of you, as soon as they have heard the things that are read recited, straightway depart. There is no inquiry among yourselves about the things that were read, no comparing together, nowhere a remembering of that commandment by which the divine law admonishes you: "ask your fathers and they will tell you, your elders and they will declare to you." Others do not even patiently wait for this very thing, until the readings are recited in the church. And others, even if they are recited, do not attend to them, but in the more remote places of the Lord's house are occupied with secular tales. Of whom I have made bold to say that, "when Moses is read," there is now no longer "a veil over their heart," but a kind of partition and wall has been set up. For if he who is present, who hears and is intent and reconsiders and examines what he hears, and questions and learns what he cannot attain—if he can scarcely reach the freedom of knowledge, then he who hides away his ears, that he may not hear, and turns his back upon the face of the reader, how is he to be said to have a veil laid over his heart, to whom not even the very veil of the letter—by which the sense is veiled, which is the sound of the voice—has come near? It is therefore an evident figure, of how the face of Moses is made glorious; for the things he speaks have glory, but this is covered and hidden, and all his glory is within.

Consider also of what sort this is: that in the law the face of Moses is indeed reported as glorified, though it be covered with a veil; but his hand, put "within his bosom," is recorded as "made leprous like snow." In which there seems to me to be most fully depicted the form of the whole law; for in his face is designated the word of the law, in his hand its works. Since, therefore, "by the works of the law no one was to be justified," nor could the law bring anyone "to perfection," for that reason the hand of Moses is made "leprous" and is hidden away "in his bosom," as though destined to have no perfect work; but his face is glorified, yet is covered with a veil, because his word has the glory of knowledge, but hidden. Whence also the prophet says: "unless you hear in secret, your soul shall weep," and David says: "the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom you have made manifest to me." In the law, therefore, Moses has his face alone glorified, and his hands have no glory, nay rather even disgrace; but neither do his feet. In short, he is commanded to loose his sandal; thus there was no glory in his feet—though this too came about not without the form of some mystery; for the feet are the last part of a man. It was shown, therefore, that in the last times Moses would loose his sandal, so that another might receive the bride, and that she would be called "the house of the unshod" "unto this present day." Moses, therefore, has nothing else glorious in the law except his face alone; but in the Gospels he is wholly glorified, entirely. For hear what it says in the Gospels: "when Jesus had ascended into a high mountain, taking with him Peter and James and John, and was transfigured there before them; and behold," it says, "there appeared Moses and Elijah in glory, speaking with him." Here it is not reported that his face was glorified, but that he wholly "appeared in glory," speaking with Jesus; and there is fulfilled for him that promise which he received on Mount Sinai, when it was said to him: "you shall see my hinder parts." He saw, therefore, his hinder parts. For he saw the things that were done in the latter and last days, and he rejoiced. For just as Abraham longed to see the day of the Lord "and saw it and rejoiced," so also Moses longed to see the day of the Lord "and saw it and rejoiced"; and necessarily "he rejoiced," because now he descended from the mountain glorified not in face alone, but ascended from the mountain wholly glorified. "Moses rejoiced," without doubt, because he now beheld present, and confirming his own words, the one of whom he had said: "the Lord your God will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, like myself; him you shall hear in all things." And that he might not hesitate in anything, he hears the Father's voice saying: "this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." Moses long ago said: "him you shall hear": now the Father says: "this is my Son, hear him," and points out present the one of whom he speaks. Moses seems to me also to rejoice for this reason: that he too now in a certain manner lays aside "the veil, being turned to the Lord," when the things he foretold are evidently fulfilled, or when the time comes that the things he had covered over might, through the Spirit, be revealed.

Yet the holy Apostle's meaning must be reconsidered, and it must be pondered what he had in view when, having said: "but if anyone shall have turned to the Lord, the veil shall be taken away," he added: "now the Lord is the Spirit," by which he seems as it were to interpret what the Lord is. For who does not know that "the Lord is the Spirit"? But surely in this place it was not the Lord's nature or substance that was being treated, that he should say "the Lord is the Spirit"? Let us see, then, whether not only "when Moses is read," but also when Paul is read, "a veil" may be "placed over" our "heart." And plainly, if we hear negligently, if we bring no zeal to erudition and understanding, not only the Scripture of the law and the prophets, but even that of the Apostles and the Gospels is covered from us with a great veil. But I fear lest, through excessive negligence and dullness of heart, the divine volumes be for us not only veiled but even sealed, so that, "if a book to be read is given into the hands of a man who does not know letters, he says: I do not know letters; if it is given into the hands of a man who knows letters, he says: it is sealed." Whence it is shown that we must not only apply zeal to learning the sacred letters, but must also entreat the Lord and "day and night" beseech him, that the Lamb "from the tribe of Judah" may come and himself, taking the "sealed book," may deign to open it. For he it is who, "opening the Scriptures," kindled the hearts of the disciples, so that they said: "was not our heart burning within us, when he opened to us the Scriptures?" May he, therefore, even now deign to open to us what it is that he inspired his Apostle to say: "now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." I indeed, so far as I can perceive according to the smallness of my understanding, think that the Word of God, according to what concerns the hearers—as we have often already said—is named now "the way," now "the truth," now "the life," now "the resurrection," now also "flesh," but now "spirit." For although he truly received the substance of flesh from a virgin, in which he both endured the cross and inaugurated the resurrection, yet there is a place where the Apostle says: "even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer." Since, therefore, even now his word summons the hearers to a subtler and spiritual understanding, and wishes them to perceive nothing carnal in the law, he says that whoever wishes "the veil to be taken away" from his heart "let him turn to the Lord"—not as to a Lord according to the flesh—for there is this too, since "the Word was made flesh"—but as to a Lord according to the spirit. For if he turns as to a Lord according to the spirit, he will come from carnal things to spiritual, and will pass from servitude to liberty: for "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And that what is said may become still more evident, let us make use also of other meanings of the Apostle. To certain ones, whom he had perceived to be incapable, he says: "I judged myself to know nothing else among you save Christ Jesus, and him crucified." To such ones as these he did not say that "the Lord is the Spirit," nor did he say to them that Christ is the "wisdom" of God. For "they could not recognize Christ according to that which is wisdom," but according to that which is "crucified." But those to whom he said: "we speak wisdom among the perfect, yet a wisdom not of this age nor of the princes of this world, who are brought to nothing, but we speak the wisdom of God hidden in a mystery," did not need to receive the Word of God according to that which "was made flesh," but according to that which is "wisdom hidden in a mystery." So, therefore, in this place also, to those who are summoned from the carnal to the spiritual understanding, it is said: "now the Lord is the Spirit; and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty." And that he might show that he himself has now arrived at the liberty of knowledge and has been stripped of the servitude of the veil, he adds to these words and says: "but we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord." If, therefore, we too beseech the Lord that he may deign to take the veil from our heart, we can grasp the spiritual understanding—provided, however, that we turn to the Lord and seek the liberty of knowledge. But how can we find liberty, we who serve the age, who serve money, who serve the desires of the flesh? I rebuke my own self, I judge my own self; I convict my own faults; let those who hear look to what they think of themselves. I meanwhile say that, so long as I am in bondage to any one of these things, I am not turned to the Lord, nor have I attained liberty, so long as such affairs and solicitudes bind me tight. Of that affair and solicitude by which I am bound tight, I am the servant; for I know it is written that "each one is delivered as a servant to that by which he is overcome." Even if the love of money does not overcome me, even if care for possessions and riches does not bind me, yet I am greedy of praise and pursue human glory, if I hang upon the faces and words of men—what this man thinks of me, how that man regards me, that I may not displease him, that I may please him. So long as I seek these things, I am their servant. But I would wish at least by this to be sufficiently in earnest, if I might become free, if I might be released from the yoke of this foul servitude and arrive at liberty according to the Apostle's admonition, who says: "you were called unto liberty, do not become the servants of men." But who will grant me this manumission? Who will free me from this most shameful servitude, save he who said: "if the Son shall free you, you shall be truly free"? But indeed I know that a servant cannot be granted liberty unless he serves faithfully, unless he loves his Lord. And therefore let us too serve faithfully and "with our whole heart and with our whole soul and with our whole strength love the Lord our God," that we may be worthy to be granted liberty by Christ Jesus his Son our Lord, "to whom be glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."
QUESTIONS ON THE OLD AND NEW TESTAMENTS, QUESTION 8: WHY MOSES' FACE SHONE COMING DOWN THE MOUNTAIN

WHY DID MOSES, COMING DOWN FROM THE MOUNTAIN WITH THE TABLES OF THE LAW, HAVE A FACE SO BRIGHT THAT IT COULD NOT BE FIXED ON HIM? — Having received authority over sinners, he came down from the mountain with honor, his face glorious. For the Law was given against sinners. Moses therefore, because he had not sinned, appeared glorious, to such an extent that he could not be seen by sinners. For it was shown in him that sinners do not deserve to behold the glory of God. After the idol of the molten calf and the breaking of the tablets on which the Law had been given, Moses again went up the mountain with tablets; and when he came down after receiving the Law on them, his face became glorious, so that the children of Israel could not gaze upon his face, nor could Aaron, because he too had sinned. But with a veil placed over his face he spoke to them, so that they would remain unworthy of the glory of God as long as they continued in sins (Exod. 34:29). Therefore the Apostle says, “When one turns to God, the veil is removed” (2 Cor. 3:16), so that, cleansed by the gift of God, they might become worthy to contemplate the glory of God. In the breaking of the tablets that he had previously received, he prefigured the depraved people of the Jews, because by persisting in sins they would become unworthy of God’s promise. But in the fact that the Law was given again, another people was signified, for whom the Law given on the mountain would be of benefit.
ON FIRST PRINCIPLES 1.1.2

For so long as a man does not attend to the spiritual meaning "a veil lies upon his heart," in consequence of which veil, in other words his duller understanding, the Scripture itself is said or thought to be veiled. This is the explanation of the veil which is said to have covered the face of Moses when he was speaking to the people, that is, when the law is read in public. But if we turn to the Lord, where also the Word of God is and where the Holy Spirit reveals spiritual knowledge, the veil will be taken away, and we shall then with unveiled face behold in the holy Scriptures the glory of the Lord.
The Book of Pastoral Rule, Part 3, Chapter 39

But the preacher should know how to avoid drawing the mind of his hearer beyond its strength, lest, so to speak, the string of the soul, when stretched more than it can bear, should be broken. For all deep things should be covered up before a multitude of hearers, and scarcely opened to a few. For hence the Truth in person says, "Who, thinkest thou, is the faithful and wise steward, whom his Lord has appointed over his household, to give them their measure of wheat in due season?" Now by a measure of wheat is expressed a portion of the Word, lest, when anything is given to a narrow heart beyond its capacity, it be spill. Hence Paul says, "I could not speak unto you as unto spiritual, but as unto carnal. As it were to babes in Christ, I have given you milk to drink, and not meat." Hence Moses, when he comes on from the sanctuary of God, veils his shining face before the people; because in truth He shews not to multitudes the secrets of inmost brightness. Hence it is enjoined on him by the Divine voice that if any one should dig a cistern, and not cover it, and an ox or ass should fall into it, he should pay the price, because when one who has arrived at the deep streams of knowledge covers them not up before the brutish hearts of his hearers, he is adjudged as liable to penalty, if through his words a soul, whether clean or unclean, be caught on a stumbling-stone. Hence it is said to the blessed Job, "Who hath given understanding unto the cock?"

n: Sabbath. The frequent repetition of this precept, cannot escape the notice of the attentive reader. The sabbath was a distinctive mark of the Jews, and was generally observed by them with the utmost care, and even with scrupulosity. (Haydock) --- They were not allowed to do on it any thing that had the appearance of servility, if it could be avoided without serious inconveniences. But in any urgent necessity of the sick, &c., they might provide meat, and do other work, that could not be done before. They might also repel an enemy, water cattle, &c. Though a mere rest be positively ordered, the design of it shewed that the day was to be spent in religious duties, reading the Bible, &c. Josephus assures us, many were so diligent herein, as to know almost the whole law by heart. (Tirinus)

No fire, to dress meat. The Rabbins say it is lawful to light a fire, to warm oneself, or for light. But they generally employ some other to do it for them. The Samaritans and Caraites look upon this as an evasion. (Calmet) --- It was customary to light candles and dress meat before sun-set on Friday. On other festivals, even the greatest, this was not required, as they were not instituted chiefly in memory of God's rest, as the sabbath was, chap. xii. 16. (Haydock)
Vestments, in which the vessels of the tabernacle were folded up. (Vatable)
And women, by the hands of their husbands, as the Hebrew and Septuagint intimate. --- Tablets, (dextralia) ornaments worn on the right hand or arm.
Spun. The wool, it seems, was dyed first, unless it were naturally of these colours. See Exodus xxv. 5. (Calmet)

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

We had indeed already spoken before about the tabernacle, to the best of our ability; but since the description itself is often repeated in the book of Exodus — for it is set forth both when God commanded Moses how it ought to be made, and again when Moses commanded the people to offer materials for the work to be constructed, as this reading contains, which has just now been recited to us; but also afterwards the individual items are enumerated, when they are fashioned by Bezalel and the other wise men, and again when they are brought into the sight of Moses, and once more when they are dedicated by the Lord's command. Moreover, a mention of these things is made also in other books or places, and it is frequently repeated, inasmuch as it is necessarily brought to mind. Now, then, that discourse has been recited to us where it says: "and Moses said to all the synagogue of the sons of Israel, saying: this is the word which the Lord commanded, saying: take from among your own selves a redemption for the Lord. Everyone who has conceived it in his heart, let him bring the first offerings to the Lord: gold, silver, bronze, hyacinth, purple, doubled scarlet, and twisted fine linen, goats' hair, and rams' skins dyed red and hyacinthine skins, imperishable woods, and sardius stones and stones for carving on the shoulder-piece and on the full-length robe; and let everyone wise in heart among you come and work all the things which the Lord has commanded". When I consider myself first and examine myself, I am loath to set my hand to opening these things. For I fear that perhaps, even if the Lord should deign to reveal them, if indeed He deigns to reveal them to anyone — for concerning myself I have not dared to say it — I fear, I say, and I greatly doubt, whether he will find hearers; and since this is so, lest perhaps it be required of him who shall attempt to explain, where or how or before whom the Lord's pearls are cast. But since you greatly expect that some of the things which have been read should be discussed, and since my Lord has commanded me, saying: "you ought to have put my money at the table, and I, when I came, would surely have exacted it with interest", I will ask Him that He deign to make my word His own money, so that I may lend to you not my money, not my gold, but His own; that I may speak to you by His word and by His "understanding", and bring these things to the table of your hearing. See you now to it, as you receive the Lord's money, how you may prepare its interest for the Lord when He comes. Now the interest of the word of God is to have in the practice of life and of deeds those things which the word of God has commanded. If therefore, hearing the word, you make use of it and act according to the things you hear, and live according to these things, you are preparing interest for the Lord; and it can come to pass that each one of you may make from "five talents" ten, and may hear from the Lord: "well done, good and faithful servant, you shall be having power over ten cities". Only see to this, that none of you either gather up the money he has received "in a napkin" or bury it "in the earth", for you well know what the outcome of such a man is at the coming of the Lord. We shall therefore attempt a few things out of many, indeed even fewer out of the few, seeing that both our discourse must be weighed and your hearing.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

First of all, then, let us see what it is that Moses says to the sons of Israel: "take from among your own selves a redemption for the Lord; everyone who has conceived it in his heart, let him offer the first offerings to the Lord". Moses does not wish you to offer to God something that is outside you: "from your own selves", he says, "take, and bring the first offerings to the Lord, according as each one has conceived it in his heart". Gold and silver are commanded to be brought, bronze and the other materials; how can I bring this from my own self? Surely gold is not born within me, or silver and the other things that are commanded? Does not each one bring these forth from his storerooms and from his chests? What is it, then, that Moses says: "bring from your own selves, and each one according as he has conceived it in his heart"? That gold indeed and silver and the other materials, from which the tabernacle was constructed, are agreed to have been brought forth from the chests and storerooms of each one; but the spiritual law requires gold for the tabernacle which is within us, and silver which is within us, and demands all those remaining materials which we both can have within us and bring forth from ourselves. For the Scripture says that: "the word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart; for, if you confess the Lord Jesus and believe in your heart that God raised Him from the dead, you shall be saved". If therefore "you have believed in your heart", your heart and your understanding is gold; you have therefore offered gold to the tabernacle, the faith of your heart; but if you have also "confessed" with speech, you have offered the word of confession, silver. For this reason, then, Moses, who is the spiritual law, says: "take from your own selves". These things you take from your own self, these are within you, these, even if you are naked, you can have. But also what he added: "each one according as he has conceived it in his heart", looks to this. For you will not be able to offer anything to God from your understanding or from your word, unless first you have conceived in your heart the things that are written; unless you have been attentive and have listened diligently, your gold cannot be genuine, nor your silver; for it is required that it be "tested". Hear the Scripture saying: "the words of the Lord, chaste words, silver tested by fire, purified sevenfold". If therefore you have conceived in your heart the things that are written, your gold, that is, your understanding, will be genuine, and your silver, which is your word, genuine. What, too, shall we say about bronze? Bronze is also needed for the construction of the tabernacle. Bronze indeed seems able to be taken for strength and to be set in place of fortitude and constancy; but lest anyone say: this is to divine rather than to explain, where what is said is not fortified by the authority of the Scriptures, I think, then, that bronze can be taken for the voice. For speech is one thing, the voice another. Speech is called an utterance grounded upon reason; but the voice is, for example, whether one speaks in Latin, whether in Greek, whether more loftily, whether more subdued. But you demand that we prove these things too from the Scriptures, as is necessary. Hear what the Apostle says: "if", he says, "I speak with the tongues of men and of angels, but have not charity, I am one thing, as sounding bronze or a tinkling cymbal". So then, to speak with tongues and to translate from one language into another is an offering of bronze. For the tabernacle of the Lord must have all things, and nothing must be lacking in the house of God. There is, therefore, as we said, an offering of bronze, the voice. Now the voice is that which turns the meaning of another into another language; but speech is that which brings forth one's own meaning. Let all these things, therefore, be offered to God; let the understanding be offered to God, and the speech, and the voice.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

What shall we say about the rest? For they are many, and to discuss each one is a huge task. But what will it profit, that they be spoken with our own huge labor, yet be spurned and perish, spurned by preoccupied hearers who attend upon the word of God for scarcely the point of a single hour? For "unless the Lord builds the house, they have labored in vain who build it". Nevertheless we, as has already been said above, deliver the Lord's money to the table; let each one of the hearers see how he receives the things that are delivered. "Let each one", he says, "according as he has conceived it in his heart, bring the first offerings to the Lord". As for what he called "first offerings", I ask what are the first offerings of gold, or what the first-fruits of silver? And how do first-fruits seem to be contributed from scarlet and purple and fine linen? Or how does one offer "according as he has conceived it in his heart"? This now strikes each one of us; let us see at the same time also how we have conceived in our heart, as many of us as are here present just now, and the word of God is being expounded. There are those who conceive in their heart the things that are read; there are those who do not at all conceive the things that are said, but their mind and heart is either in business or in the affairs of the world or in the reckonings of gain; and especially the women — how, do you think, do they conceive in their heart, who chatter so much, who make such an uproar with their tales that they do not permit there to be silence? Now what shall I discuss concerning their mind, what concerning their heart, if they are thinking either of their infants or of wool or of the necessities of the house? I truly fear that they may follow those women of whom the Apostle says: "who learn to go about the houses, not only talkative, but also curious, speaking the things that are not fitting". How, then, do such women as these conceive in their heart? One does not conceive in his heart unless he is empty in heart, unless he is free in mind and wholly attentive; unless he keeps watch in his heart, he cannot conceive in his heart and offer gifts to God. And even if we have neglected this hitherto, from this time at least let us be more attentive and diligently intent, that we may be able to conceive with the mind. For it is just that each one be found to have his own portion in the tabernacle of the Lord. For it does not escape the Lord what each one offers. How glorious it is for you, if it be said in the tabernacle of the Lord: that gold, for example, with which the ark of the covenant is overlaid, is his; the silver, from which the bases and columns are, is his; the bronze, from which the rings and the basin and some of the bases of the columns were made, is his; but also those stones of the shoulder-piece and of the oracle are his; the purple with which the high priest is adorned is his, and the scarlet is his, and each of the rest, one by one. And again, how unseemly, how wretched it will be, if the Lord, coming to inspect the building of the tabernacle, should find in it nothing of your gift, should recognize nothing offered by you. Have you lived so undevout, so unfaithful, that you have longed for nothing of your memorial to be in the tabernacle of God? For just as "the prince of this world" comes to each one of us and seeks whether he may find in us anything of his own deeds, and, if indeed he finds it, claims us for himself; so also, on the contrary, if the Lord, coming, should find anything of yours in His tabernacle, He defends you for Himself and calls you His own. Lord Jesus, grant me that I may deserve to have some memorial in Your tabernacle. I would wish, if it could be, that there be something of mine in that gold from which the mercy-seat is fashioned, or from which the ark is overlaid, or from which the lampstand of light and the lamps are made. Or if I have no gold, that I may at least be found to offer something of silver, that may serve for the columns or for their bases; surely at least that I may deserve to have something of bronze in the tabernacle, from which the rings are made and the rest that the word of God describes. And would that it were possible for me to be one of the princes and to offer gems for the adornment of the high priest's shoulder-piece and oracle. But since these things are above me, at least may I deserve to have goats' hair in the tabernacle of God, only that I be not found empty and unfruitful in all things. "Each one", therefore, "according as he has conceived it in his heart". See whether you are conceiving, see whether you are holding fast, lest perhaps the things that are said flow away and perish. I wish to admonish you by the examples of religion; you who are accustomed to take part in the divine mysteries know how, when you receive the body of the Lord, you guard it with all caution and reverence, lest any small part of it fall down, lest anything of the consecrated gift slip away. For you believe yourselves guilty, and rightly do you believe it, if anything of it should fall down through negligence. But if you employ such caution in preserving His body — and rightly do you employ it — how do you think it is of less guilt to have neglected the word of God than His body? First offerings, therefore, are commanded to be offered, that is, first-fruits. He who offers what is first, necessarily has himself what remains. See how much we ought to abound in gold, how much in silver and in all the rest that are commanded to be offered, that we may both offer to the Lord and have a surplus for ourselves. For first of all, my understanding ought to understand God and offer to Him the first-fruits of its understanding, so that, when it has understood God well, it may consequently recognize the rest. Let the speech do this too, let all things that are in us do this. But let us see the rest as well. "Hyacinth and purple and doubled scarlet and twisted fine linen". These are four things, from which are made either the vestments of the high priest or the rest that are prepared for the sacred adornment. Concerning these certain men before us have also spoken, and just as it is not fitting to steal what belongs to another, so I think it fitting to make use of another's good sayings while acknowledging it. These four things, then, as it seemed also to our predecessors, hold the figure of the four elements from which both the world and the human body are composed, that is, of air, fire, water, and earth. Hyacinth, therefore, is referred to air — for its very color indicates this — as scarlet is to fire. Purple holds the figure of water, as one that takes its dye from the waters; fine linen, of earth, because it arises from the earth. We therefore also have all these things in us, and because we are commanded to offer the first-fruits of these to the Lord, therefore he says: "take from your own selves, and you shall offer the first-fruits to the Lord".
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

But I think this must be considered, that, whereas Moses spoke of the rest simply, he added to scarlet alone "doubled", and to fine linen "twisted". It is asked, therefore, why the other materials, by which the remaining elements are indicated, he named simply, but scarlet, by which fire is designated, he alone set down as "doubled". These things are difficult to understand and much more difficult to expound. Nevertheless, as the Lord shall grant, we shall attempt to explain. For some things must be spoken and some things kept in reserve. Let us see, then, for what reason he called "scarlet doubled". This color, as we said, indicates the element of fire. Now fire has a twofold power, one by which it illuminates, another by which it burns. This is the reasoning of the literal sense; let us come also to the intellectual meanings. Even in these matters fire is twofold; there is a certain fire in this age, and there is one in the age to come. The Lord Jesus says: "I have come to send fire upon the earth": this fire illuminates. The same Lord again says in the age to come to the "workers of iniquity": "go into the eternal fire, which my Father has prepared for the devil and his angels": that fire burns. Nevertheless this fire, which Jesus came to send, indeed "illuminates every man coming into this world", yet it has also something that burns, as those confess who say: "was not our heart burning within us, when He opened the scriptures to us?" At the same time, therefore, it both burned and illuminated in "opening the scriptures". But I do not know whether that fire also in the age to come, which burns, has anything too that illuminates. There is, therefore, as we have shown, a twofold nature of fire, and for this reason "doubled scarlet" is commanded to be offered. Let us see, then, how we can offer this doubled fire for the building of the tabernacle. If you are a teacher, you build the tabernacle by constructing the church of God; God therefore says also to you what He said to Jeremiah: "behold, I have given my words in your mouth as fire". If therefore, teaching and building the church of God, you only rebuke and censure and chastise and reproach the sins of the people, but bring forth no consolation from the divine scriptures, explain nothing obscure, touch nothing of deeper knowledge nor open anything of more sacred understanding, you have indeed offered scarlet, but not doubled. For your fire only burns and does not illuminate. And again, if, teaching, you open the mysteries of the law, discuss the secrets of hidden things, but do not reprove the sinner, do not correct the negligent, do not maintain the severity of discipline, you have indeed offered scarlet, but not doubled. For your fire only illuminates, it does not kindle. He therefore who "offers rightly" and "divides rightly" offers doubled scarlet, so that with the light of knowledge he mingles a little fire of severity.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

Now let us see what "twisted fine linen" too means. For here also he gave something of addition beyond the other elements. We said that fine linen holds the form of earth, which is our flesh. He does not wish, therefore, the flesh to be offered to God floating in luxury and loosened by delights, but he commands it to be twisted and constrained. Who, then, is he who twists his flesh? Assuredly he who said: "I mortify my body and subject it to servitude, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself become reprobate". Thus, then, is it to offer twisted fine linen also, to wear down the flesh by abstinence, by vigils and by the labor of meditations. Goats' hair also is offered. This kind of beast in the law is commanded to be offered for sin; but hair is a species that is dead, bloodless, lifeless. He who offers this shows that in himself the sense of sin is already dead, and that sin no longer lives or reigns in his members.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13
Rams' skins also are offered. Certain men before us have also set the ram for fury. And because the skin is a token of a dead animal, he who offers rams' skins to the Lord shows fury dead in himself.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

After these things: "and the men", he says, "took from their women, all to whom it seemed good in their understanding, and brought gems and earrings and rings and hair-clasps and armlets". You see here too how those bring gifts to God who see with the heart, who conceive understanding in the heart, who have the mind intent and devoted to the word of God. These, then, bring gifts, and they bring them even from their women: "earrings", he says, "and gems and armlets". We have already often said that, according to the allegorical interpretation, the woman is taken as the flesh and the man as the rational sense. Good, therefore, are these women who obey their husbands; good is the flesh which no longer fights against the spirit, but complies and consents, and therefore "if two or three of you agree, concerning whatever thing you shall ask, it shall be done for you", the Lord said. They offer, therefore, "earrings from their women". You see how the hearing is offered to the Lord. But armlets too are offered to the Lord: right works and good works, which are performed through the flesh. These the rational sense offers to the Lord. But hair-clasps also are offered. He offers hair-clasps who knows well to discern what is to be done, what is to be avoided, what pleases God, or what displeases, what is just, what is unjust. These are the hair-clasps that are offered to the Lord. Here, then, the women offer earrings to the Lord, because they are wise women. For there came, he says, wise women, and made whatever things were necessary for the vestments of the high priest. But those women who offered their earrings that the calf might be made were foolish, women who "turned away their hearing indeed from the truth, but turned it to fables and impiety"; and therefore they offered their earrings that the head of a calf might be made. But in the book of Judges too we find likewise another idol made from women's earrings. These, then, are blessed women, blessed is that flesh, which offers to the Lord its earrings and its armlets and its rings and all the works of its hands which it performs in the commandments of the Lord.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

It is added after these things that "he too with whom imperishable woods were found", brought them to the Lord. If anyone "loves Christ the Lord in incorruption", he offers imperishable wood to God. Blessed, therefore, is he with whom is found either an incorrupt understanding or an incorrupt body, and offers this to God. Hence too he said very well: "with whom imperishable woods were found". For "imperishable woods" are not found with everyone. Of gold he did not say, nor of silver, with whom it was found; for understanding and speech can be found with everyone. But neither did he say this of the four colors; for it belongs to all to consist, according to the body, of four elements. But "imperishable woods", that is, the grace of incorruption and virginity, can be found with only a rare one, as the Lord too says: "not all receive this word, but those to whom it is given".
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

But also the "princes", he says, "offered" their gifts. What are these gifts which the princes offer? "Gems", he says, "they offered, emerald stones and stones of filling and stones for the shoulder-piece". Stones of filling are called those which are placed in the oracle, that is, which are set on the breast of the high priest, inscribed with the names of the tribes of Israel. This which is called the oracle, that is, the rational, which is set on the breast of the high priest, has the form of the rational sense which is in us. In this are said to be placed the "stones of filling", which yet cling and are connected to the shoulder stones and are held bound together by these. The adornment of the shoulder-piece is a token of good deeds. Deeds, therefore, are joined with reason and reason with deeds, so that there may be a harmony in both: "for he who shall do and teach, he shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven". Let there be in us, therefore, speech depending upon deeds, and let deeds adorn the speech; for this refers to the adornment of the high priest. But to accomplish these things princes are required; this adornment belongs to those who have advanced so far that they deserve to preside over peoples.
HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

The princes also offer oil, to serve for a twofold use, for the lamps and for the anointing. For the lamp of those who preside over peoples ought not to be hidden or "put under a bushel, but upon a lampstand, that it may give light to all who are in the house". But the princes also offer "the composition of incense", which is to be compounded by Moses "for a sweet odor to the Lord", so that they too may say that "we are a good odor of Christ".
AGAINST EUNOMIUS 11.5

"He was entrusted," he says, "with the construction of things by the Father." But if he had been talking about some artizan executing his work at the pleasure of his employer, would he not have used the same language? For we are not wrong in saying just the same of Bezaleel, that being entrusted by Moses with the building of the tabernacle, he became the constructor of those things there mentioned, and would not have taken the work in hand had he not previously acquired his knowledge by Divine inspiration, and ventured upon the undertaking on Moses' entrusting him with its execution. Accordingly the term "entrusted" suggests that His office and power in creation came to Him as something adventitious, in the sense that before He was entrusted with that commission He had neither the will nor the power to act, but when He received authority to execute the works, and power sufficient for the works, then He became the artificer of things that are, the power allotted to Him from on high being, as Eunomius says, sufficient for the purpose.

n: Vows, or voluntary oblations to Moses, according to the Hebrew. (Calmet) --- These donations are called first-fruits, because they were the best of all things, and the first offerings that were made by the people, in the desert. (Tirinus) --- They shew great alacrity in performing this action, as it was to make some atonement for their liberality in honour of the golden calf. (Haydock) --- But as matter alone will not suffice, unless it be properly managed, so neither will the letter of the Scripture instruct us, unless God teach us, by his pastors, Ephesians iv. 11. (Worthington) --- From this place to the end, the Roman edition of the Septuagint is very confused. That of Alcala agrees better with the Vulgate than the Alexandrian or Aldine. See Grabe. Almost all the three following chapters might be comprised in these words. The workmen did all according to God's prescription. Moses perhaps gave them plans of what each was to execute; and hence Calmet accounts for these repetitions. (Haydock)
Bar, not mentioned, (chap. xxvi. 28,) but specified by Josephus ([Antiquities?] iii. 5,) at the west end of the tabernacle, going across the breadth of the planks. (Tostat)
Which heads, according to the Hebrew and Septuagint. On some parts of the pillars the wood appeared.

f: HOMILIES ON EXODUS 13

And after the people had offered, "Moses", he says, "called every wise man" for the fashioning, and the architect, that they might put together and fashion each of the things that are written. "But also the women", he says, "the wise women he called", that they might make the things which were suitable in the tabernacle of the Lord. You see, then, that all the things which are made are made by wise persons; both women are called wise and men are called wise. For "all the works of the Lord" are made "in wisdom". Each one, therefore, comes "wise in understanding" and makes the works of the Lord. It does not suffice for us if we only offer, but there is need that we also work with wisdom those things that are in us, that we may know how to mingle gold with fine linen and to double scarlet or to mingle it with purple. For what does it profit you, if you have these things and know not how to use them, nor recognize how you ought to fit and bring forth each thing in its own time and in its own place? And therefore we must give effort to being wise and being able to bring forth these things which we hear from the holy scriptures in their time and to fit and to compose them, and from these to adorn "the tabernacle for the God of Jacob", through Christ Jesus our Lord, to whom is "glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen".
On the Tabernacle 2.2, AT EXODUS 26:6

Since the number fifty designates true rest in the Holy Spirit, and a ring seems to have neither beginning nor end, and gold is the most precious of metals, excelling all others in its brightness, what is expressed in the fifty golden rings except the perpetual brightness and bright perpetuity of the highest repose? And the rings grip the loops of the curtains in such a way that one tabernacle might be made out of them all when the glory of the heavenly kingdom graciously pours itself into the pure minds of the faithful, so that with the glue of such healing inspiration the church is made perfect out of the two peoples, or perhaps we should say out of all Christ's elect.
On the Tabernacle 2.6

And since the reprobate perish in eternity while the righteous are reigning with the Lord, rightly is it said further on that this side of the tabernacle looks to the sea. Now this signifies the Red Sea, in which Pharaoh with his host was drowned and from which Israel, having been saved by the Lord, went up to Mt. Sinai where they made the tabernacle. Therefore the western side of the tabernacle looks back to the sea when after the perfection of good works the holy church is crowned in Christ and gazes freely upon the failings or the punishments of the impious, which [Christ] has decreed by his own command.
LETTER 164

Sometimes, however, under one figure of either an act or an utterance, two terms may have one meaning. Thus the boards which were fitted together into the construction of the ark signify both the faithful and the eight souls who were saved in the same ark. Similarly, in the Gospel, in the parable of the sheepfold, Christ himself is both the shepherd and the door.
On the Tabernacle 2.10

Here, therefore, we must assume that a bar was stretched across the ten cubits of the width of the tabernacle, from the top of the boards in front to the top on the other side. [It was] firmly positioned with a head on the boards on each side in such a way that by means of it that side of the tabernacle which rested not on boards but on pillars might also remain immovable, no less firmly fixed than the other [side], even when the wind was blowing against it.If you should also wish to understand the sacrament of this bar, in a figurative manner it unambiguously signifies our Redeemer himself, who passed through from corner to corner, as it were. He reached out from the Jewish people, which he had previously chosen for himself, to make atonement also for the sake of the salvation of the multitude of the Gentiles. Hence, just as in the prophets he can for good reason be called the "cornerstone," so also in the law can he be called the "corner bar." He is "cornerstone," evidently, in relation to the temple which is constructed for God out of living stones. He is "corner bar" in relation to the tabernacle which is built for him out of imperishable wood, that is, out of the souls of the elect, which are free from the stain of corruption.

n: Half, duos semis cubitos, ver. 6, and chap. xxv. 10. (Tirinus)
Covering... This indicated that the Scriptures were to be studied with diligence, as they have a literal and a mystical sense. (St. Gregory of Nyssa)
Over-against, or under, chap. xxv. 27. (Tirinus)
Censers. Hebrew Kapoth, means broad deep dishes or bowls. (Calmet) --- Wherein, meaning the golden vessels aforesaid. (Haydock)

f: Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 6

And we know that in the tabernacle of God not only bowls but also, by the Lord's command, cups were made. By bowls, indeed, abundant teaching is designated; by cups, however, small and limited knowledge. One person, full of the teaching of truth, intoxicates the minds of his hearers. By what he says, therefore, he surely offers a bowl. Another cannot fully express what he perceives, but because he proclaims it in some way, he surely offers a taste through a cup. Therefore, placed in God's tabernacle, that is, in the holy Church, if you cannot minister bowls through the wisdom of teaching, give to your neighbors cups of a good word insofar as you are able according to divine generosity. Insofar as you perceive yourselves to have progressed, draw others along with you; desire to have companions on the way to God.

n: Mirrors. Formerly all sorts of metal, silver, copper, tin, &c., were used for mirrors, till the Europeans began to make them of glass. The best were made of a mixture of copper and tin. (Pliny, [Natural History?] xxxiii. 9.) --- Watched. Hebrew, served like soldiers: fasting and praying, according to the Septuagint and Chaldean. These devout women came thither with great alacrity, to shew their affection towards God, and to consecrate to his service what had hitherto served to nourish vanity. Such were the virgins, mentioned [in] 2 Machabees iii. 19, and those who were abused by the sons of Heli, 1 Kings ii. 22. Ann, the prophetess, and our blessed Lady[Virgin Mary], were thus also employed in the temple, Luke ii. 37. Women kept watch, singing and dancing before the palace of the Persian kings. (Calmet) --- When the tabernacle was fixed at Silo, small apartments were probably built for the convenience of these pious women. (Tirinus)
Brass. The Hebrew does not say the pillars were of brass, but only the bases. The body was of wood, encircled with silver, ver. 12. See chap. xxvii. 10. (Calmet)

The, &c. Some render the Hebrew, "The bases of the pillars were of brass, the hooks of the pillars and circles were of silver, their chaptrels were covered with silver." Bonfrere supposes that the pillars were of the Ionic order, and that the chaptrels here designate the summit or abacus; while the hooks (vuim) mean the voluta, (Menochius) or bolster, representing the head-dress of virgins in their long hair. (Vitruvius) (Haydock)

Ithamar, some time after this, (Numbers i. 50,) was appointed to deliver the necessary vessels to the Levites; part of whose duty it was to take down the tabernacle and set it up again, and to keep an account of all things. (Menochius)
Gifts, voluntarily. The following verse mentions what arose from the tax of half a sicle per head, chap xxx. 13.

And it, &c. Hebrew is rather more express, "And the silver given by those who were numbered, was a hundred talents, 1775 sicles of the weight of the sanctuary, ver. 26. They gave each half a sicle, paid by all those who were 20 years old and upwards, amounting to 603,550 men." Hence the talent would weigh exactly 3000 sicles, (Calmet) or 12,000 drachmas. Some say that the common talent weighed 100 pounds, and that of the sanctuary 120, each pound containing 25 sicles. (Du Hamel)
Seventy. Hebrew confines the number of talents to 70, and allows "two thousand and four hundred sicles." The Greek interpreters vary.

f: Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 17

For Moses places the bronze laver in which the priests ought to be washed and enter the holy of holies, because the law of God first commands us to be washed through compunction, so that our uncleanness may not be unworthy for penetrating the purity of God's secrets.
Forty Gospel Homilies, Homily 17

But then we truly preach right things to others if we show our words by deeds, if we ourselves are pierced with divine love, and wash with tears the daily stains of human life, which can in no way pass without fault. But then we are truly pierced with compunction about ourselves if we carefully consider the deeds of the fathers who went before, so that from beholding their glory, our own life may become vile in our own eyes. Then we are truly pierced with compunction when we diligently search the commandments of the Lord, and through these we ourselves strive to advance, through which we know those whom we venerate have already advanced. For hence it is written of Moses: He placed also the bronze laver in which Aaron and his sons were to wash when they entered the holy of holies, which he made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle. For Moses places the bronze laver in which the priests ought to be washed and enter the holy of holies, because the law of God first commands us to be washed through compunction, so that our uncleanness may not be unworthy for penetrating the purity of God's secrets. Which laver is rightly said to have been made from the mirrors of the women who ceaselessly kept watch at the door of the tabernacle. For the mirrors of the women are the commandments of God, in which holy souls always behold themselves, and detect if there are any stains of defilement in them. They correct the faults of their thoughts, and as if arranging resisting countenances, they compose them as from a reflected image, because while they diligently attend to the Lord's commandments, in them they doubtless recognize both what pleases and what displeases the heavenly spouse in themselves. As long as they are in this life, they can in no way enter the eternal tabernacle. But yet the women keep watch at the door of the tabernacle, because holy souls, even while they are still weighed down by the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless with continual love await the entrance of eternal entry. Therefore Moses made the laver for the priests from the mirrors of the women, because the law of God provides the washing of compunction for the stains of our sins, while it presents for our contemplation the heavenly commandments through which holy souls have pleased the heavenly spouse. If we diligently attend to these, we see the stains of our inner image. But seeing the stains, we are pierced with the sorrow of repentance; and being pierced with compunction, we are washed as in the laver made from the mirrors of the women.

n: Vestments. Hebrew distinguishes, "the clothes of service" destined to fold up the tabernacle and vessels, from "the holy garments of Aaron."

Threads. Hebrew, "wires to work it in the blue....with cunning work." The ancients had the art of beating gold into thin plates, with which they adorned the horns of their victims, &c. (Virgil, Æneid iv.) See Numbers xvi. 58. (Calmet)
Fastened to the girdle. This is not specified in the Hebrew. The Vulgate has abridged some verses, in these chapters, to avoid repetitions.
Pomegranate, alternately, chap. xxviii. Clement of Alexandria observes, that the 366 bells denote the leap year, in which Christ began to preach. (Tirinus)

Of fine linen, or cotton, and of common linen, as Pollux describes it. The Samaritan copy adds, "Breeches of linen, of byssus, of violet, of scarlet, of purple, of embroidery work, according to the command of the Lord."
Veneration, of which it was deserving. Hebrew, "the crown of holiness." It reminded the high priest of his consecration to the Lord, and of the sanctity with which he ought to appear before him.

Finished, exactly according to God's prescriptions. --- Blessed them, the people, who had contributed so liberally; and the workmen, who had performed their task so much to his satisfaction. (Calmet) --- He also blessed the sacred vessels, as they were destined for the worship of God. (Haydock)

f: On the Tabernacle 3.4, AT EXODUS 28:7

From this it appears to have been the case that the borders of two pieces were joined together from top to bottom on both sides into a doubled garment. In [this] way … half of the garment would be visible to the eyes of those looking at it from the outside while the other half would be concealed on the inside, but the joined borders of the two would come all the way down to the lowest point below. What else are we to understand by means of this type, except that while we are displaying good works on the outside before our neighbors, we must keep them unblemished on the inside before the Lord?

n: Month of the second year, ver. 15. The first day of every month was kept with some degree of solemnity, though it was not a day of rest. (Numbers xxxiii. 11.; 1 Kings xx. 5.; &c.) (Calmet)

Priesthood. Hebrew, "And thou shalt put upon Aaron the holy garments, and anoint him, and sanctify him, that he may serve me in the priest's office: (14) and thou shalt bring his sons, and put on them their tunics; (15) and thou shalt anoint them, as thou didst anoint their father, that they may perform the office of priests to me for ever, in their generations." As the priesthood was hereditary in Aaron's family, this first unction might suffice for all. Yet, the new high priests were always anointed till the days of our Saviour, chap xxix. 7.
Cover of purple, goat skins, &c.

Testimony, or tables of the law. The pagans enclosed various symbolical figures, cakes, &c., in their mystic arks. (St. Clement of Alexandria) But how different were they from the sacred records of religion! (Calmet)
Roof, covering both the holy of holies and the sanctuary. (Menochius)
Laver. This is a repetition of ver. 7, (Calmet) shewing that the command was fulfilled. (Haydock)

Glory. The cloud which had rested over the tent, appointed for prayer, came now to the grand tabernacle, in the midst of the camp. (Calmet) --- By its superior lustre, it signified that the glory of God was there. (St. Augustine, q. 173.)

Moses, out of respect, abstained from entering that day. (Calmet) --- The cloud of legal observances, though designed to prefigure Christ and the gospel, seems however to hinder the Jews from recognizing them. (St. Augustine) (Tirinus)
A fire. The same cloud overshadowed the camp by day, and enlightened it by night. (Chaldean; Chap. xiii. 22.)

intro: THE BOOK OF EXODUS. INTRODUCTION. The second Book of Moses is called Exodus from the Greek word Exodos, which signifies going out; because it contains the history of the going out of the children of Israel out of Egypt. The Hebrews, from the words with which it begins, call it Veelle Shemoth: These are the names. (Challoner) --- It contains the space of 145 years, till the beginning of the second year after the liberation of the Israelites. (Tirinus) --- Their slavery is described in the first chapters; and is supposed to have continued ninety years. (Du Hamel) --- The laws prescribed by God to his people, the sacrifices, tabernacle, &c., were all intended to prefigure the Christian dispensation. (St. Augustine, City of God vii. 31.) --- Moses himself was a type of Jesus Christ, who was rejected by the synagogue, and received by the Gentiles, as the Jewish Legislator was abandoned by his mother, and educated by the Egyptian princess. She delivers him back to his mother; and thus the Jews will, at last, acknowledge our Saviour. (Du Hamel) --- God deigns to address his people in the character of a powerful Eastern monarch, and requires the like attention. He appoints his ministers, like guards, to attend before his tabernacle, &c. The laws which he enacts, are such as suited the Jewish people: they were not able to rise all at once to perfection; but these laws guide them, as it were, on the road. They are infinitely more perfect than those of the surrounding nations. (Calmet)
